title: Required Lease Contents and Copies
bodyText: A written rental agreement must be signed by you or your agent and the tenant or the tenant's agent, and you must give the tenant one copy free at signing and further copies within a reasonable time on request (a reasonable fee is allowed for extras). On request you must also give a prospective tenant a copy of the lease they would sign. Every written lease must address: duration; rent (as a single all-in figure) and how and when it is paid; occupancy by children or pets; services included; required fees and their purposes; required deposits and the conditions for refund; charges for late or partial payment and for a dishonored check; your inspection rights; who, or how many people, will occupy; who pays which utilities; a signed inventory and condition record; a summary of the state public-nuisance statute; how a tenant can report a nuisance or a code violation; and the tenant's rights to display the U.S. flag and religious or cultural items. Using a lease that does not conform is unlawful, and any nonconforming provision is void. With no written lease, the law presumes no restriction on children or pets, maintenance and trash service at no charge, no late or dishonored-check charges, and a return of the premises in move-in condition except normal wear.

title: Application and Screening Fees
bodyText: If you collect an application, credit-report or background-check fee from an applicant and then rent the unit to someone else without actually doing the thing the fee paid for (processing the application, pulling the report), you must refund that fee. You may not charge an application, credit-report or background-check fee for a minor (under 18) who is a member of the applicant's household - household meaning people living together who are related by blood, adoption, marriage or domestic partnership. State law sets no cap on the amount of an application fee.

title: Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: Anything you collect to cover unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear, or cleaning is a security deposit - whatever you call it. All deposits plus any surety bond, including prepaid last month's rent, are capped at three months' rent. A tenant may buy a surety bond instead if you agree, but you cannot require one. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends you must give an itemized written accounting and return the balance, in person where rent is paid or by mail. Keeping the balance past 30 days exposes you to the whole deposit plus up to the same amount again, depending on your good faith. Only a reasonable cleaning charge may be made nonrefundable; any other nonrefundable label or waiver of these rules is void. The tenant's claim to the deposit outranks your creditors. When you sell or transfer the property you must either transfer the deposit to the buyer with written notice to the tenant, or return it; on a voluntary sale where the lease continues, you must transfer it (NRS 118A.349(1)(c)); before recording the deed you must transfer the balance to the buyer in writing or tell the buyer in writing that you returned it. The buyer must accept the existing deposit and cannot demand more during the lease. On request you must give a signed receipt for any deposit, rent or other payment, and the tenant may hold back rent until you do. No deposit interest is required.

title: No Deposit Interest Requirement
bodyText: State law does not require you to pay interest on an ordinary security deposit or to hold it in a separate or interest-bearing account. One exception: if a tenant with a disability asks to make a reasonable modification and you require an additional deposit to secure restoration of the unit, that additional deposit must be necessary for the restoration, may not exceed its actual cost, and must be held in an interest-bearing account, with the interest paid to the tenant.

title: Habitability Duty
bodyText: You must keep the unit habitable at all times. A unit is not habitable if it violates housing or health codes on health, safety, sanitation or fitness, or substantially lacks: effective waterproofing and weather protection of roof, walls, windows and doors; plumbing that met code when installed and works; an approved water supply with hot and cold running water connected to an approved sewage system; adequate heating that met code when installed and works; electrical lighting, outlets, wiring and equipment that met code when installed and work; enough clean garbage receptacles at move-in, with trash removal arranged by you unless the lease says otherwise; building, grounds and areas you control clean, sanitary and reasonably free of debris, rodents, insects and vermin at move-in; floors, walls, ceilings, stairways and railings in good repair; and any ventilation, air-conditioning, elevators and appliances you supply in good repair. A tenant may agree to do specified repairs only if the agreement is made in good faith and does not reduce your duties to other tenants - and it is not in good faith if the tenant agreed because you refused a repair you owed. You may not charge a tenant any fee for repairs that are your duty, including a home-warranty deductible or copay, unless the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the condition deliberately or negligently.

title: Tenant Remedies for Repairs and Essential Services
bodyText: If you breach the lease or fail to keep the unit habitable, the tenant must give written notice; you then have 14 days to fix a remediable problem or make best efforts. If you do not, the tenant may terminate immediately, recover actual damages, or seek court relief - and for a material habitability failure may withhold rent without late fees until you fix or try in good faith to fix it - though withheld rent is a defense to eviction only if the tenant deposits it into a justice-court escrow account. For repairs costing less than the greater of $100 or one month's rent, the tenant may instead give written notice and, if you don't use your best efforts to comply within 14 days (or sooner if an emergency requires), have the work done and deduct the reasonable cost from rent, capped at that amount per 12 months; you may name in the lease the person, firm or class of qualified firms who must do such work, and if they are unavailable the tenant uses another qualified person. If you willfully or negligently fail to supply heat, air-conditioning, running or hot water, electricity, gas, a working door lock or another essential service, making the unit unfit, the tenant's written notice gives you 48 hours (excluding weekends and holidays); then the tenant may buy the service and deduct it, recover damages, withhold rent if current, or move to comparable housing with rent abated and excess cost recoverable. What the lease says you will supply counts: failing to supply an essential service it promises (a utility, air-conditioning) can trigger the essential-services remedies, and appliances and air-conditioning you supply must be kept in good repair as part of habitability. For a condition the tenant's own household or guests caused deliberately or negligently, the tenant cannot terminate, repair and deduct, withhold rent or use the essential-services remedies.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: You may recover possession only through a court action or summary proceeding, or when the tenant has surrendered or abandoned the unit. Locking a tenant out, removing them, or willfully cutting or causing interruption of an essential service lets the tenant recover possession on an expedited court complaint (filed within 5 judicial days, heard within 3), terminate, or pursue the essential-services remedies - plus actual damages and up to $2,500 fixed by the court. The summary-eviction statute's permission to lock out after an uncontested pay-or-quit notice is expressly subject to this ban, so treat any lockout without a court order as prohibited.

title: Landlord Rules and Regulations
bodyText: A house rule binds the tenant only if it serves the convenience, safety or welfare of you or the tenants, protects the property from abuse, or fairly distributes services; is reasonably related to that purpose; applies to all tenants fairly; is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do; is in good faith and not a way around your own obligations; does not affect rent, utilities or other charges; does not take away a pet the lease allows before the lease ends; and the tenant had notice of it. A rule adopted after signing that materially changes the bargain binds the tenant only with their written consent or 30 days' advance written notice.

title: Duties on Sale of the Property
bodyText: After a voluntary sale or transfer, the lease continues and the new owner steps into the old landlord's rights, duties and liabilities unless the new owner and tenant agree otherwise. Within 30 days after the transfer the new owner must give the tenant a notice with the new owner's contact information for rent, stating that the lease continues and the amount of deposit the new owner holds, and warning that failing to pay rent to the new owner or comply with the lease is a breach that may lead to eviction. Manager and owner disclosures must also be kept current, and bind a successor.

title: Rent Timing During a Government Shutdown
bodyText: During a federal, state or tribal government shutdown, a lease term requiring rent at a specified time cannot be enforced against a tenant who is a federal, state or tribal worker, or a household member of one, and you must accept that period's rent up to 30 days after the shutdown ends. A worker who gives you proof of that status during a shutdown is outside the pay-or-quit summary-eviction process, may ask in writing to stay in possession until 30 days after the shutdown ends, and every no-cause termination notice you serve must tell the tenant about that right. Retaliating against a tenant who uses this protection is prohibited. If the shutdown lasts 30 days or more, you may petition the court for relief on undue-hardship grounds (mortgage and foreclosure risk, your other financial obligations); if granted, the parties may modify the lease or you may terminate and start eviction proceedings.

title: Key-Control Policy for Large Complexes
bodyText: If you own a complex of more than 50 units on one parcel in a county of 100,000 or more people (or more than 30 units in a smaller county), you must: require a criminal background check of any job applicant whose position gives access to unit keys or codes; adopt written policies for storing, issuing, returning and securing keys (and for using and deactivating electronic keys); and keep on the premises a log of every key issued and returned, together with those policies. A tenant or the district attorney can sue for declaratory and injunctive relief, actual damages and attorney's fees. Financial institutions and licensed real estate brokers and salespeople are excluded from "landlord" for this rule.

title: Work Cards for Staff in 55-and-Older Housing
bodyText: If your units are intended and operated exclusively for people 55 and older, you may not employ anyone who will work 36 or more hours a week with access to all units unless they hold a current sheriff-issued work card (renewed every 5 years and on changing employers). Licensed property managers, independent contractors, inmate work-program participants and court-ordered community-service workers are exempt.

title: Prohibited Lease Terms
bodyText: A lease may not make the tenant: waive rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act; authorize a confession of judgment; pay your attorney's fees (a prevailing-party fee clause is allowed); exculpate or limit your liability, or indemnify you, for liability based on your own or your agents' acts or omissions; or give you a different termination notice than you must give them. Such a term is void and the tenant may recover actual damages caused by its inclusion. A court may also refuse to enforce, or limit, an unconscionable lease or term. Separately, a lease may not call a deposit nonrefundable (except a reasonable cleaning charge), may not prohibit display of religious or cultural items, and a lease that does not conform to the required-content rules is unlawful to use. A lease also may not shorten the notice periods the eviction statutes require.

title: Domestic Violence Termination Documentation
bodyText: If a tenant, co-tenant or household member (someone related by blood or marriage and living with the tenant) is the victim of domestic violence, harassment, sexual assault or stalking, the tenant or any co-tenant may end the lease by written notice, effective at the end of the current rental period or 30 days after notice, whichever is sooner, describing the reason and attaching the required documentation, if the events happened within the 90 days before the notice (NRS 118A.345). The terminating tenant owes only rent through termination and other outstanding obligations; you may keep prepaid rent for the final period (refunding any excess), and you may not withhold the deposit because of the early termination. Don't give the adverse party any information about the tenant's whereabouts. After notice, the tenant may require a new lock at their cost (you may rekey a working lock or replace the mechanism with one of equal or better quality); don't give the adverse party a key, or access to reclaim property unless a law enforcement officer is present. For a domestic-violence termination the tenant may use a protection order, a police report, or an affidavit in the statutory form signed by a qualified third party: a state-licensed physician, board-certified psychiatrist, psychologist, social worker, psychiatric-nursing RN with a master's degree, or licensed marriage and family therapist or clinical professional counselor; a trained, state-resident domestic-violence agency employee who is licensed to provide health care under NRS title 54, or the agency's executive director or a board member; or state-resident clergy of a tax-exempt religious organization. For harassment, sexual assault or stalking only a police report or a temporary or extended protective order qualifies. You may not tell a prospective landlord the tenant broke the lease early, and the tenant need not disclose it either. The person named as the adverse party can be sued for your economic losses from the early termination.

title: Retaliation Prohibited
bodyText: You may not, in retaliation, terminate or refuse to renew a tenancy, raise rent, cut essential services, or bring or threaten an eviction because the tenant: complained in good faith to a code-enforcement agency, or to you or law enforcement about a violation of the landlord-tenant act or a criminal statute; organized or joined a tenants' union; triggered a code citation; raised habitability in a court or administrative proceeding; refused to consent in writing to a rule adopted mid-lease that must wait out its notice period; complained about or exercised fair-housing rights; is or has a household member who is a victim of domestic violence, harassment, sexual assault or stalking, or used the termination right for those victims; or, as a government worker in a shutdown, paid rent within the allowed extension. The tenant gets the self-help-eviction remedies (including up to $2,500) and a defense to eviction. It is not retaliation if the code violation was mainly the tenant's fault, the termination is for cause, a citation requires the unit to be vacant for repairs, or a rent increase applies uniformly to all tenants.

title: Calls for Emergency Help Protected
bodyText: You may not evict, fine or take any other adverse action against a tenant based solely on the tenant or someone in the unit calling police, fire, rescue or emergency medical services, if they reasonably believed an emergency response was needed or a crime may have occurred - no matter how many earlier calls there were. A local government also may not treat such calls as a nuisance against you. You may still act on a nuisance or lease breach that a responding officer discovers or reports. A tenant, a landlord or the district attorney can sue for injunctive relief, actual damages and attorney's fees.

title: No Landlord Lien on Household Goods
bodyText: A lien or security interest in a tenant's household goods to secure rent is unenforceable unless created by attachment or garnishment, and distraint for rent is abolished. Do not put a lien clause in the lease, and do not hold a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent - doing so exposes you to the self-help-eviction damages, including up to $2,500.

title: Ending a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: A lease for a fixed term ends at its expiration without notice. A periodic tenancy can be ended without stating a cause by written notice of at least 7 days for a week-to-week tenancy and at least 30 days for any other periodic tenancy. The 5-day notice for a tenancy at will applies only to property outside the landlord-tenant act, so never use it for a residential tenant. A government worker affected by a shutdown may ask to stay until 30 days after it ends. In a periodic tenancy other than week to week, a tenant who is 60 or older or has a disability may also ask in writing, with proof, to stay 30 more days, and may petition the court if you refuse. Every such notice must tell the tenant about both rights. A 5-day notice applies instead where the tenant has failed to perform basic or lease obligations, and the 60-and-over extension does not apply to it. Notices must be served as the eviction statutes require, and a lease cannot shorten these periods.

title: Nonpayment of Rent: Pay-or-Quit and Summary Eviction
bodyText: If rent is unpaid, you may serve a written notice to pay or surrender by close of business on the seventh judicial day after service (for rent reserved weekly or less in a tenancy that has lasted 45 days or less, you may instead use noon of the fourth full day; if that notice can't be delivered in person, you must post it on the premises and send it by overnight mail, and the sheriff or constable will serve it only with the tenant's written acknowledgment, signed at move-in, of the short-term eviction procedure). The notice must name the court and tell the tenant how to contest it by filing an affidavit, what happens if the court rules against them, and that they can seek relief for an unlawful lockout. After serving it you may not refuse rent because collection fees, attorney's fees, other costs, a late or dishonored-check charge, or a deposit is still unpaid. In the court proceeding the tenant may counterclaim and can be ordered to deposit rent with the court; failing to deposit within 24 hours ends the right to a hearing. After an eviction judgment for unpaid rent on an unexpired lease, the tenant has 5 days to pay the judgment and costs and be restored. Summary eviction is not available against a government worker who proves shutdown status.

title: Breach Notices: Cure and No-Cure Grounds
bodyText: For most lease breaches you serve a written notice to perform or surrender within 5 days; the tenant saves the lease by performing within that time, and no notice is needed if the breach cannot be cured. For assigning or subletting contrary to the lease, committing waste, running an unlawful business, maintaining a nuisance that unreasonably obstructs others' use and injures other tenants, or violating the controlled-substances laws on the premises (other than simple possession), a 3-day notice to surrender applies with no cure. If you win a drug-based eviction the tenant contested, you are entitled to reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: A summary-eviction court file is sealed automatically when the case is dismissed, ten judicial days after the eviction is denied, or 31 days after a tenant files a contest affidavit if you have not filed your complaint within 30 days. A court may also seal a file on a stipulation to set aside the eviction, or on the tenant's motion in the interests of justice. A sealed eviction is treated as never having occurred, and a notice to surrender may not be made publicly available except as part of an unsealed court file.

title: Serving Notices on a Tenant
bodyText: Except where the summary-eviction statute lets you or your agent deliver a notice, eviction notices must be served by a sheriff, constable, licensed process server or an attorney's agent: by handing a copy to the tenant; or, if the tenant is away, by leaving it with a person of suitable age at the home or workplace and mailing a copy; or, failing that, by posting it on the property, giving a copy to anyone living there, and mailing a copy. Proof of service must be filed before the court can order removal. Written notices to a tenant under the landlord-tenant act must be served "in the manner provided" by that same statute - the safe course is to use those methods, and a qualified server, for rent-increase, rule-change and repair notices too. Under a lease of the tenant's primary residence, a notice of default, eviction or the right to cure can't be given electronically, even if the tenant agreed to electronic notices.

title: Fair Housing
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, deposits or fees, advertise a preference, misrepresent availability, or interfere with anyone's housing rights because of race, religious creed, color, national origin, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, ancestry, familial status or sex. You must allow a tenant with a disability to make reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense (you may require restoration at move-out, reasonable wear excepted) and must make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services. You may not raise the usual deposit because a modification was requested; an additional restoration deposit is allowed only if necessary, no more than the actual cost, and held in an interest-bearing account with the interest paid to the tenant. A fair-housing violation is a defense to eviction, and a tenant may complain to the Nevada Equal Rights Commission or sue for actual and punitive damages and attorney's fees. A narrow exemption covers an owner of no more than three single-family houses renting without a licensed broker, and an owner-occupied building of up to four units whose owner has not, in the past 12 months, been the principal in three or more sales or rentals of a dwelling or the agent in two or more - but the advertising ban applies to them too.

title: Assistance and Support Animals
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent to a person with a disability solely because an animal that assists, supports or provides service to them will live in the unit - support animals are covered, not only trained service animals. You may require proof, which a statement from a health care provider that the animal performs a function easing the effects of the disability satisfies. No state statute or regulation expressly bans a pet fee or deposit for these animals. Waiving pet rules and fees is generally treated as a reasonable accommodation under fair-housing law, and the lease's assistance-animal clause promises it; federal guidance on the point has been withdrawn, so the promise is the product's choice as much as a legal requirement.

title: Abandonment and the Duty to Re-Rent
bodyText: If you reasonably believe a tenant who is behind on rent has abandoned the unit, you may serve a written notice of that belief; unless within 5 days the tenant pays the rent due and gives you written notice of intent not to abandon with an address for service, the unit is deemed abandoned and the lease terminated. The notice must explain this rule and state the property address, the date of deemed abandonment, and where to pay; it must be served like an eviction notice and may be combined with a pay-or-quit notice. Leftover belongings alone do not make your belief unreasonable. When a tenant abandons, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rent; the former tenant owes your actual damages, but if you make no effort, only damages up to the point you had reason to believe the unit was abandoned.

title: Towing Vehicles from the Property
bodyText: To tow an unauthorized vehicle, the owner or person in lawful possession of the property must give oral notice to the police or sheriff stating when the vehicle was removed, from where, and where it was taken, and - except on single-family residential property - must have a sign in plain view declaring parking prohibited or restricted and showing the police or sheriff's number. Towing costs fall on the vehicle owner, but the vehicle owner can file an expedited court complaint within 21 days, and if the tow was unlawful the person who authorized it pays the towing and storage costs. In a single-family rental, the tenant may be the person in lawful possession of the driveway.

title: Tenants When the Property Is Sold at Foreclosure
bodyText: If a single-family residence (up to four units) is sold at foreclosure or trustee's sale, a tenant in actual occupation can be removed only after receiving a notice of change of ownership and a notice period of at least 60 days (or one rental period for tenancies shorter than a month). During that period the lease binds the new owner and the tenant, the notice must give the new owner's rent contact and warn that nonpayment is a breach, the tenant may leave at any time without further obligation, and no eviction record may be entered for a tenant who leaves within it.

title: Access Disputes
bodyText: If a tenant unlawfully refuses access the lease or statute allows, you may get a court order compelling access or terminate the lease, and recover actual damages. If you enter unlawfully, enter unreasonably, or make repeated demands that harass the tenant, the tenant may get an injunction or terminate the lease, and recover actual damages. Outside emergencies, a court order, abandonment or surrender, or statutory remedial work, you have no other right of access.

title: Smoke Detector Law - Which Buildings
bodyText: State law requires a smoke detector in every dwelling unit of an apartment building with three or more units, placed as the fire authority approves; apartment buildings and condominiums with three or more units must also seal corridor air-supply openings to units unless the corridor system meets fire-marshal requirements. The statute does not reach single-family homes, duplexes or a single condominium rented on its own, though local codes may. There is no statewide rule allocating testing or battery replacement, and disabling a detector is no longer a state-regulation misdemeanor - so put both in the lease. A criminal statute still punishes anyone who willfully and maliciously removes, damages or destroys apparatus for communicating fire alarms (NRS 202.580(1)); whether it reaches a unit's smoke detector is not settled. In Clark County and Washoe County the local building and fire officials, and their adopted fire codes, are the authority. State statutes set no carbon-monoxide alarm requirement for long-term rentals, though local codes may. A person who holds a county or city authorization to rent a unit for transient (short-term) lodging must equip it with a fire extinguisher, a smoke alarm and a carbon-monoxide alarm.

title: Returned Checks: Fees and Remedies
bodyText: If a tenant's check bounces, you may recover the amount of the check and, if the tenant does not pay it in cash within 30 days after you mail a written demand by certified mail, damages of three times the check amount, but not less than $100 or more than $500. A separate statute caps at $25 the fee a seller may collect for each check accepted for goods or services that bounces or on which the drawer stops payment; whether it reaches rent is unsettled, so keep the lease's returned-payment charge at $25 or less. The lease must state whatever charge you will impose, and after a pay-or-quit notice you cannot refuse rent because that charge is unpaid. If a tenant stops payment on a rent check, the criminal statute treats a failure to act within 5 days after your notice of nonpayment as evidence of intent to defraud. That notice must go by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the address on the check, and must state the statute's penalties (NRS 205.380(3)-(4)). You must also give every tenant the statute's written stop-payment notice; the Nevada lease includes it (NRS 205.380(5)).

title: Misrepresenting a Service Animal
bodyText: It is a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of up to $500, to fraudulently misrepresent an animal as a service animal or service animal in training. The crime covers only service animals - animals trained to perform tasks - not emotional-support or other support animals, and it gives a landlord no civil remedy. A support animal's status is handled through the documentation a landlord may request under the fair-housing rules.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: If a former tenant's deposit refund goes unclaimed - for example, the refund check is never cashed and the tenant cannot be found - the amount is presumed abandoned 3 years after the tenant's right to demand it arose, unless the tenant has communicated with you about it in the meantime. Your record of issuing the refund check is itself evidence that you owe the money. You then hold it as unclaimed property and must report it and pay it to the State rather than keep it: the report is due before November 1 each year, covers the 12 months before July 1, and is filed and paid electronically through the State's portal unless you obtain a waiver. If you have a usable mailing address and the amount is $50 or more, you must first send the former tenant written notice, 60 to 120 days before filing (also by email if they agreed to email delivery), and file an affidavit that you did. You may deduct a dormancy charge only if a written contract with the tenant allows it and you regularly impose the charge, and never more than $5 a month. You remain responsible for the report even if someone else prepares it.

title: Political Signs in HOA and Condo Communities
bodyText: If the rental is in a common-interest community (a homeowners' or condominium association), the association may not prohibit a unit's owner or an occupant - which includes your tenant - from displaying political signs in the part of the property the owner or occupant has the right to use exclusively. Protected signs are those supporting or opposing a candidate, political party or ballot question in a federal, state, local or association election. Each may be no larger than 24 by 36 inches, only one sign per candidate, party or ballot question is protected, and signs must follow any law on posting political signs. While a tenant occupies the unit, you as the owner may not display a political sign there unless the tenant consents in writing. The rule binds the association and its governing documents; it does not address what your lease may say about signs.

title: Removing a Squatter or Unauthorized Occupant
bodyText: A person who enters your property without the authority of you, your representative or your tenant and does not leave after a written notice to surrender is guilty of forcible detainer, as is anyone who holds possession by force or threats. For a squatter there is a fast court process. Serve a written notice to surrender the way eviction notices are served. It must name the court and tell the occupant: that they may contest by filing an affidavit before the court closes on the fourth judicial day after service; that the court may order the sheriff or constable to remove them within 24 hours; and that property left behind will be stored safely and may be disposed of after 14 calendar days, with inventory, moving and storage costs payable before release. When the notice expires, file an affidavit of complaint with a copy of the notice and proof of service. If the occupant did not contest, or the contest raises no legal defense, the court must order removal within 24 hours; if it raises a defense, a hearing is held within 7 judicial days. An occupant who entered peaceably under an invalid lease or someone else's fraud may be given up to 20 days to leave. Keep property left behind in safe storage for 21 days after the removal or surrender before disposing of it: the notice says 14 days, but the removal section separately requires 21 days' storage. Vehicles go through the abandoned-vehicle law. If every unauthorized adult occupant has been arrested for housebreaking or unlawful occupancy, you may instead retake possession and change the locks, posting a notice with the court and contest details for at least 21 days and filing a copy with the court within 1 day. You may recover three times your actual damage to real and personal property from a person guilty of forcible entry or forcible detainer. Your tenant, as an occupant you authorized, may use the same process. For a tenant or former tenant, use the eviction procedures for tenants instead.

title: Lease Translation When You Advertise in Another Language
bodyText: If, in your business, you advertise a rental in a language other than English and negotiate the lease in that language - orally or in writing, yourself or through an employee or agent - you must give a translation of the lease in that language to the tenant, and to anyone else who may sign it, before it is signed. This applies to a lease or rental agreement of at least one month for a dwelling used as a residence. The translation must include every term and condition; names, addresses, numbers, dollar amounts, dates and words with no accepted translation may stay in English. A later document that substantially changes the parties' rights needs a translation too; routine house rules and furniture inventories do not. If you don't comply, the tenant may cancel (rescind) the lease, and a knowing violation is a deceptive trade practice.

title: Repair Orders and Receivership for Multifamily Rentals
bodyText: If you rent out two or more units on one parcel, your county (outside cities) or city must act when it finds that the property violates a habitability standard, a housing or building code, or a habitability, building-safety or fire-safety law badly enough to substantially endanger the health and safety of residents or the public. It must order you to repair, rehabilitate or abate the condition by a deadline. The notice and order is posted on the property and sent by certified mail to you and each affected resident, and it states that you may not retaliate against any tenant. If you don't comply, the county or city can sue to have the property declared substandard and obtain a repair order and civil penalties, and the local government or a nonprofit representing tenants can ask the court to appoint a receiver after 30 days' posted and mailed notice. Once a receiver is appointed you may not collect rent, interfere with the receiver, or encumber or transfer the property; the receiver collects the rents, makes the repairs and may borrow against the property. The court will order you to pay the local government's costs and attorney's fees. If tenants cannot safely stay, it will also order moving costs and up to 120 days of rent differential as relocation benefits, plus a first right to return; a tenant who caused the conditions gets no relocation benefits.

title: Health District Rules for Rental Units
bodyText: In a county served by a district board of health, the board may adopt and enforce regulations on health hazards in rental dwelling units - any biological, physical or chemical exposure, condition or public nuisance that may harm health - and recover its enforcement costs. If it has adopted regulations on the condition of rental units, you must give a copy to a tenant who asks for one. A tenant who gave you written notice of a habitability failure that you did not fix, or reasonably try to fix, within the statutory time may send a copy of that notice to the district board of health. If an inspection finds that you or the tenant failed to keep the unit habitable, the board may take enforcement action or refer the matter to its administrative hearing process.

title: Former Drug-Lab Properties
bodyText: A building that was used to manufacture a controlled substance illegally, such as methamphetamine, is a public nuisance if it has not been deemed safe for habitation by the board of health and the owner either lets it be used for any purpose before a certified or licensed entity has removed or remediated the contamination, or fails to have that done within 180 days after the manufacturing stops. Maintaining a public nuisance is a misdemeanor, so do not rent such a property until it has been remediated and deemed safe. The statutes set no separate duty to disclose a former drug lab to a tenant. The statute that makes certain facts immaterial in a sale, lease or rental excludes a former methamphetamine lab unless a certified or licensed entity has removed or remediated the contamination or the board of health has deemed the property safe (NRS 40.770(1)(b), (6)). After either step, the fact is not material to the rental.

title: No Mold Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Nevada statutes do not require a residential landlord to disclose mold, and they set no separate mold-remediation duty. Mold is handled through your general duty to keep the unit habitable and to comply with housing and health codes. In a county with a district board of health, the board can also regulate health hazards in rental units.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Nevada statutes do not require a residential landlord to test for radon or to disclose it.

title: No Bed Bug Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Nevada statutes set no bed bug disclosure, inspection or treatment rule for residential rentals. As part of habitability, the unit must be reasonably free of insects and vermin at move-in. The only bed bug statute covers hotel rooms.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Nevada statutes do not give a residential tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger, and they do not require a landlord to allow one.

title: No Immigration-Status Rule for Landlords
bodyText: Nevada statutes do not require or forbid a residential landlord to ask about a tenant's immigration or citizenship status. State and federal fair housing law still bars discrimination based on national origin and ancestry, so apply any screening question the same way to every applicant.

title: No Statewide Source-of-Income Rule
bodyText: Nevada law does not prohibit a landlord from refusing a housing voucher or other lawful source of income; source of income is not a protected class under the state fair housing law. Check local law before declining a voucher.

title: Servicemembers: Lease Protections
bodyText: Nevada statutes give a servicemember no state right to end a residential lease early; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act governs that, and it applies whatever the lease says. When a tenant presents military orders with a request to end the lease or pause an eviction, get legal advice before refusing it.

title: Rent-Reporting Programs Are Voluntary
bodyText: The state Housing Division may run a free, voluntary program for reporting tenants' rent payments to a credit reporting agency. You may not require a tenant to take part in that program, and you may not impose any penalty or other consequence on a tenant for not taking part.

title: If You Can't Deliver Possession on Time
bodyText: If you fail to deliver possession as the lease requires, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may end the lease on at least 5 days' written notice (you return all prepaid rent, the recoverable deposit and any payment made to secure the lease), demand performance and sue for possession against you or anyone wrongfully in possession and recover actual damages, or pursue any other remedy (NRS 118A.370). You aren't liable for damages if you used due diligence to evict a holdover tenant or fix the condition keeping the tenant out.

title: Older or Disabled Tenants: Relocation and Death of a Co-Tenant
bodyText: A tenant who is 60 or older or has a physical or mental disability may end the lease on 30 days' written notice, given within 60 days after relocating, if their condition requires a move for care or treatment that can't be provided in the dwelling; a co-tenant may do the same if also 60 or older or disabled, or if they became a tenant on or after the date the relocating tenant signed (NRS 118A.340). Such a tenant may also end the lease on 60 days' written notice, within three months after the death of their spouse or co-tenant. The notice must set out the facts and, for a relocation, include reasonable verification of the condition and the need to move. A tenant's death does not by itself give you a right to end the lease.

title: Annual Property Tax Statement to Tenants
bodyText: Each July, and whenever the rent changes, give the tenant a written statement showing, for each periodic rent payment, the amount that represents property taxes you paid and the remainder. If you pay taxes on several properties together, apportion the tax among the rented properties by area and reduce it to the rent period (NRS 118.165). The duty does not apply where a written agreement requires the tenant to pay the property tax or otherwise provides for calculating it and notifying the tenant of its amount, or to lodging without its own kitchen and toilet, hotel or motel rooms, concessions within a larger business, or property whose rent is a share of sales or profit. The Department of Taxation enforces it.

title: Nevada Late Fee Rules
bodyText: A Nevada late fee must be reasonable, stated in the lease and no more than 5% of the periodic rent; in a tenancy longer than week to week it can't be charged until rent is at least 3 calendar days late; and the maximum can't be increased because of a late fee charged earlier (NRS 118A.210(4)). No late fee or other charge may be imposed on rent a tenant lawfully withholds because of a habitability or essential-services failure (NRS 118A.355(1)(d), 118A.380(1)(c)), and a lease term requiring rent at a set time can't be enforced against a qualifying government worker or household member during a shutdown; you must accept that rent up to 30 days after the shutdown ends (NRS 118A.310(2), unless a court grants relief under 118A.315). Use these limits as a guardrail when you enter the fee.

title: Notice Before Raising Rent
bodyText: You may not raise rent without serving the tenant written notice at least 60 days before the first increased payment, or at least 30 days before for a periodic tenancy of less than a month (NRS 118A.300).

title: Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options
bodyText: If fire or casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment of the property, the tenant may move out immediately and tell you within 7 days that they are ending the lease, which then ends on the date they moved out; or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the drop in fair rental value or lack of use (NRS 118A.400). If the lease ends, return all prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit, accounting for rent as of the date they moved out. None of this applies if the tenant, a household member or someone there with the tenant's consent caused the fire or casualty deliberately or negligently.

title: Disclose Foreclosure Proceedings Before Signing
bodyText: If the property is the subject of any foreclosure proceedings, you must disclose that in writing to a prospective tenant before they enter into the lease (NRS 118A.275). The law does not require the disclosure to be in the lease or attached to it; give it in writing before the tenant signs, for example in a separate notice. Treat a recorded notice of default as a foreclosure proceeding and disclose it too. A willful failure to disclose is a deceptive trade practice. The lease's optional foreclosure clause records that the disclosure was made, and stating in writing that there are no proceedings is a sensible record, but neither replaces the disclosure before signing.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Nevada has no just-cause eviction rule for houses and apartments. A fixed-term lease ends at its expiration without notice, and a periodic tenancy can be ended without a reason on written notice of at least 7 days (week to week) or 30 days (other periodic tenancies); no length of tenancy changes this. The limits are situational: you may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy, raise rent, cut services or bring or threaten an eviction in retaliation for protected acts such as a good-faith code or landlord-tenant complaint, joining or organizing a tenants' union, raising habitability in a proceeding, or exercising fair-housing or domestic-violence rights (a termination for cause is not retaliation); a tenant who is 60 or older or has a disability (except in a week-to-week tenancy) can ask for 30 more days, and a qualifying government worker can stay until 30 days after a shutdown ends; fair housing law applies, and a violation is a defense to eviction; the domestic-violence termination statute keeps your right to end a tenancy for unrelated reasons; after a foreclosure sale of a building of up to four units the tenant gets a change-of-ownership notice and at least 60 days (one rental period if rent is due more often than monthly); and when apartments are converted to condominiums, tenants get 120 days' notice and a first offer to buy. Mobile home parks have their own termination rules.

title: Eviction Court Rules: Landlord Duties
bodyText: Court rules add duties for a landlord who brings an eviction. Statewide, a summary-eviction notice must be specific about the ground it alleges. In a formal unlawful-detainer case the court may not shorten the tenant's time to answer below 10 days, the trial can't be held sooner than 21 days after service, and, except in extraordinary circumstances, a hearing on a temporary writ of restitution can't be held sooner than 14 days after service; the writ also needs a court-approved bond. The justice courts' local rules add more. In the Las Vegas, Henderson, North Las Vegas and Pahrump justice courts, the notice must name that justice court specifically (a reference to the justice of the peace or a county courthouse is not valid), and the complaint must be filed with the notice and proof of service. Henderson, North Las Vegas and Pahrump also require notices to be typed or clearly legible and unaltered, bar filing the complaint before the notice period ends, and require a postmarked certificate of mailing where mailing is required. Henderson, North Las Vegas and Pahrump treat a notice as expired if the complaint is not filed within 30 days after the notice period ends. Las Vegas allows 45 days, but requires the court-approved notice and complaint forms, and a surrender notice there lapses unless the eviction notice is served within 30 days after the time to comply ends. By statute, the court file is sealed if you have not filed your complaint within 30 days after the tenant files a contest affidavit, so file within 30 days of the tenant's affidavit and in any case within 30 days after the notice period ends. Under these courts' local rules, an order for summary eviction that is not executed expires after 30 days unless the court orders otherwise. These courts hold rent a tenant withholds for a habitability failure in escrow, and a tenant who does not deposit it loses that defense.

title: Electronic Leases, Signatures and Notices
bodyText: Nevada's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets a lease, a signature or a written record be electronic, but only between parties who have agreed to do business electronically, and a party who agreed may refuse to do later transactions electronically (that right cannot be waived). If the sender prevents the recipient from storing or printing an electronic record, the record is not enforceable against the recipient, and a lease that must be in writing can be denied effect if the electronic copy can't be kept and accurately reproduced by everyone entitled to it. Where another law requires a notice to be sent by a specified method, it must still be sent that way: written notices to a tenant under the landlord-tenant act are served as the eviction statutes prescribe. A notice of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of a tenant's primary residence never satisfies a writing requirement if it is given electronically, and the parties cannot agree otherwise.

title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Neglect
bodyText: If a tenant's failure to meet the tenant's basic obligations can be fixed by repair, replacing a damaged item or cleaning, you may give written notice specifying the problem and asking the tenant to fix it within 14 days (or sooner in an emergency). If the tenant doesn't use best efforts to comply, you may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner and give the tenant an itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost or the fair and reasonable value of the work. The bill is payable as rent on the next rent due date, or, if the lease has ended, immediately or out of the security deposit. This is one of the few entries the access statute allows without the tenant's consent. No lease clause is needed for this right.

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: Nevada defines rent as all periodic payments to you for occupancy, including reasonable and actual late fees set forth in the lease, and every mandatory periodic fee must be included in the single rent figure the lease states (a qualifying utility charge is the one exception). A bill for repair or cleaning you did after the tenant failed to fix a problem is payable as rent on the next rent date. A one-time fee is not a periodic payment, so it is not rent. After you serve a pay-or-quit notice, you may not refuse rent because collection fees, attorney's fees, other non-rent costs, a late or dishonored-check charge or a deposit is unpaid, and this lease does not let an unpaid late fee alone end the tenancy. Whether an unpaid late fee alone can support a pay-or-quit notice is not settled here; base a nonpayment notice on unpaid periodic rent.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Nevada prescribes few forms for residential landlords. A tenant ending the lease because of domestic violence may use an affidavit from a qualified third party in substantially the statute's form. A single-family lease not signed by a licensed property manager must carry the statutory disclosure about occupancy presumptions at the top of the first page, in type at least twice the size of any other text. Summary-eviction notices must contain the statements the eviction statute lists (the court with jurisdiction, how to contest, what happens if the court rules against the tenant, and the lockout remedies), but no statewide form is prescribed; the Las Vegas Justice Court requires its court-approved notice and complaint forms. A lender collecting rents after an assignment may notify tenants on a statutory form, and a trustee's or execution sale of an occupied home requires a separate notice posted and mailed to the tenants.

title: No Separate Quiet-Enjoyment Statute
bodyText: Nevada's landlord-tenant act has no separate quiet-enjoyment covenant, but it protects the tenant's possession directly. You may recover possession only through a court proceeding or after surrender or abandonment; locking the tenant out, removing them or willfully interrupting an essential service lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover actual damages plus up to $2,500. You may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant, and an unlawful or unreasonable entry, or repeated demands for entry that harass the tenant, let the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover actual damages. Retaliation against a tenant's protected acts is also barred.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Nevada statutes do not regulate using algorithmic or software pricing tools to set residential rents or sharing rent data between landlords. General antitrust law may still apply.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Nevada statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells. The lease's alteration and installation terms govern. Laws on recording and surveillance were not reviewed.

title: No Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Nevada has no statute barring a landlord from having a tenant sign a residential lease with blank spaces, or requiring the lease to be complete at signing. The landlord-tenant act lists what a written lease must contain, and you must give the tenant a free copy of the signed lease when it is signed. Fill in every blank before anyone signs: a blank filled later invites a dispute over what was agreed.

title: Damage a Tenant Causes
bodyText: A tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or knowingly let anyone else do so. For a tenant's breach you may recover your actual damages and get a court order; end the lease on a 5-day notice if the tenant doesn't fix a fixable breach (or at once if it can't be fixed, unless a tenant unable to fix it lets you enter and fix it and pays the reasonable cost); or, after 14 days' written notice, have the repair or cleaning done yourself and bill the reasonable cost as rent on the next rent date (or deduct it from the deposit after the lease ends). Committing or permitting waste is a ground for a 3-day notice to surrender with no cure. You may charge the tenant for repairs of a condition the tenant, a household member or a guest caused deliberately or negligently. When they caused the condition, the tenant cannot use it to end the lease, to repair and deduct, to withhold rent, or for the essential-services remedies, and if it is determined that their deliberate or negligent acts caused a fire or casualty, the casualty rules (ending the lease or reducing the rent) don't apply. No Nevada statute addresses rent lost while repairs are made; claim it as damages, and the lease's optional tenant-caused-damage clause provides for it.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText: Since July 1, 2026, each county of 100,000 or more people and each city of 60,000 or more must have an ordinance allowing accessory dwelling units on property zoned for single-family residential use. The ordinance may not, as a condition of approving a unit, ban a separate kitchen, require more than one extra parking space (where existing and street parking is enough), impose stricter side or rear setbacks than the main home, or require street work except in limited cases, and it may not prohibit the owner from renting the unit as housing; it may prohibit renting it as short-term (transient) lodging. No more than two accessory units are authorized on a property. If a covered county or city did not adopt a consistent ordinance before July 1, 2026, accessory dwelling units are authorized on any parcel zoned for residential use without restriction. An approved unit must meet residential building, housing and health codes, not commercial ones. The rule does not apply in the Tahoe region governed by an interstate regional plan. Smaller counties and cities are not required to adopt an ordinance. Once rented, an accessory unit is a dwelling unit like any other, and the landlord-tenant law applies in full. Check the local ordinance (not reviewed) and any homeowners' association rules.

title: Notice, Knowledge and Agreed Delivery Methods
bodyText: Nevada's landlord-tenant act defines notice broadly: a person has notice of a fact if the person actually knows it, has received a notice or notification of it, or reasonably should know it from all the facts and circumstances (NRS 118A.190(1)). That definition matters where the act turns on notice, such as whether you had notice that a tenant abandoned the unit. But where the act prescribes a written notice to the tenant, the method is fixed: it must be served in the manner provided for eviction notices, by a sheriff, constable, licensed process server or an attorney's agent through personal delivery, substituted delivery plus mailing, or posting plus mailing (NRS 118A.190(2), 40.280). A lease can't substitute a text message, email or app message for those notices, and a notice of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of a primary residence can't be given electronically even if the tenant agreed (NRS 719.250(4)(b)). Where a statute specifies a delivery method, an electronic record must still be sent by that method (NRS 719.250(2)(b)). Notices from the tenant to you may be delivered or mailed to your place of business named in the lease, or to any place you hold out for receiving rent, and are effective on delivery or mailing (NRS 118A.190(3)); you may invite additional methods, such as email, for the tenant's convenience. For notices that no statute prescribes, such as routine maintenance updates, the lease may set an agreed method, including electronic delivery if both parties agree, and sending an extra courtesy copy by text or email alongside a statutory notice does no harm. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Telling Tenants About Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: Nevada's only general rule requiring a landlord to tell tenants about a proceeding against the property is the foreclosure disclosure: you must disclose in writing to a prospective tenant if the property is the subject of any foreclosure proceedings, and a willful failure is a deceptive trade practice (NRS 118A.275). No statute requires you to tell current tenants about a lawsuit, a code-enforcement order, a condemnation or another proceeding that could affect them. Other notices come to tenants from someone else. In a residential foreclosure by trustee's sale, the trustee must post on the property and mail to each tenant in actual occupation a statutory "Notice to Tenants of the Property" at least 15 days before the sale, explaining that the tenant may move out or stay and possibly face eviction (NRS 107.087(3)); after the sale the new owner must serve a change-of-ownership notice before any eviction (NRS 40.255(2), (4)). When a utility plans to cut service to a multiunit complex or a mobile home park for the owner's default, it must use its best efforts to post a notice on each unit's door at the same time it notifies the owner (NAC 704.360(9), 704.393(6)). When your interest in the property ends by sale, death, receivership or otherwise, you must give tenants the successor's contact information and transfer or return the deposits (NRS 118A.244). Condemnation of the unit is a legal cause for ending the tenancy (NRS 118A.060(4)). Condominium conversions and mobile home park closures have their own notice rules. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Detector Tampering Fee
bodyText: Nevada's statutes and the held fire-marshal regulations set no fee or civil penalty for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon-monoxide detector. A criminal statute punishes anyone who willfully and maliciously removes, damages or destroys apparatus for communicating fire alarms (NRS 202.580(1)); whether it reaches a single unit's smoke detector is not settled. Your protection is the lease: forbid removing or disabling detectors and require prompt notice of a detector that doesn't work. For the cost, charge the tenant the reasonable cost of repairing or replacing a detector only when the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the problem deliberately or negligently. You may not charge a tenant for repairs or maintenance that are your habitability duty (NRS 118A.290(4)), and where state law requires detectors (each unit of an apartment building with three or more units, NRS 477.140(1)) keeping them working is part of that duty; the exception is a condition caused by the tenant's own deliberate or negligent act or omission or that of a household member or guest (NRS 118A.290(5)). You may also recover your actual damages for the tenant's breach (NRS 118A.420) or, after 14 days' written notice, replace the device and bill the reasonable cost as rent on the next rent date (NRS 118A.440). Avoid a fixed 'tampering fee' unrelated to your cost: no statute authorizes one, and a charge for a habitability item outside NRS 118A.290(5) is barred. Case law and local fire codes were not reviewed.

title: Substitute Housing and Relocation Costs
bodyText: Nevada does not make you provide a hotel room or another unit when a tenant asks during repairs. Instead the tenant has a self-help remedy: if the lease or the law requires you to supply heat, air-conditioning, water, hot water, electricity, gas, a working door lock or another essential item or service and you willfully or negligently fail to, making the unit unfit, and you do not fix it or use best efforts within 48 hours (excluding weekends and legal holidays) after written notice, the tenant may move to comparable housing while you are out of compliance; rent for the unit fully abates during that time and the tenant may recover the reasonable cost of the other housing above the abated rent (NRS 118A.380(1)(d)). That remedy is not available for a condition the tenant, a household member or a guest caused deliberately or negligently (NRS 118A.380(5)). After a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease by notifying you within 7 days, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay reduced rent, unless the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the fire or casualty deliberately or negligently (NRS 118A.400). Relocation costs can also be ordered against an owner by local government: when a county or city receivership case finds that a multifamily rental (two or more units on a parcel) substantially endangers residents who cannot safely stay, the court orders moving costs and up to 120 days of rent differential, plus a first right to return (NRS 244.369055, 268.42845); a county that relocates tenants because of a dangerous structure or other nuisance may recover the cost from the person primarily responsible (NRS 244.3607); and a court abating a chronic nuisance in a city may order the owner to pay tenants' reasonable relocation expenses (NRS 268.4124(3)(c)). Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Entering to Care for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText: Nevada gives you no special right to enter a unit to feed, care for or remove a tenant's animal. Outside an emergency you may enter only after at least 24 hours' notice, at reasonable times during normal business hours, unless the tenant expressly agrees to shorter notice or other hours for that particular entry (NRS 118A.330(3)), and you have no other right of access except under a court order, after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit, or for statutory remedial work (NRS 118A.330(4)). A lease clause giving advance permission to let a caretaker in whenever the tenant is away does not replace that per-entry consent. What you can do: in a genuine emergency, such as an animal in distress, you may enter without consent (NRS 118A.330(2)); you can ask the tenant at the time to agree to a specific entry; and you can call animal control or the police, who must take possession of an animal being treated cruelly (NRS 574.055(1)), with a magistrate able to issue a warrant to enter where animal laws are being broken (NRS 574.060(3)). Collecting the name of an animal-care contact at move-in is sensible, but use it to reach the tenant's chosen person, not as a key to the unit. Whether a particular situation is an emergency is decided on its facts; case law and local animal ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText: You must keep in good repair the ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances you supply or are required to supply (NRS 118A.290(1)(i)), and the lease must state the services included (NRS 118A.200(3)(d)). The law does not say whether an item you leave in the unit but disclaim counts as supplied. The cautious course is to remove an item you will not maintain; if you leave it, list it in the lease as not supplied. Never exclude anything the habitability statute or a housing or health code requires, such as heating, plumbing, hot and cold water, electrical equipment and garbage receptacles (NRS 118A.290(1)), or an essential item such as air-conditioning, hot water or a functioning door lock that the lease or the law requires you to supply (NRS 118A.380). You may not charge the tenant for repairs that are your duty, including a home-warranty deductible (NRS 118A.290(4)), and a lease term limiting your liability for your own acts or omissions is void (NRS 118A.220(1)(d)). Local housing codes may require cooling or other equipment (not reviewed).

title: Asbestos in Rentals
bodyText: Nevada law sets no duty to disclose asbestos to a tenant before leasing and no asbestos inspection rule for rentals. Asbestos work is regulated: the control of asbestos includes encapsulating, enclosing or removing asbestos or material containing it, and repairing, renovating or demolishing a building containing it (NRS 618.750(2)). Only a person licensed by the Division of Industrial Relations may engage in such a project (NRS 618.790), unlicensed work is a misdemeanor (NRS 618.850), and the contractor must notify the state's Enforcement Section at least 10 days before on-site work begins (NAC 618.954). The statute exempts a person working in his or her own residence (NRS 618.755(1)); the regulations do not say whether that reaches a unit you rent out, so hire a licensed contractor for asbestos work in a rental. Work on nonfriable materials such as vinyl asbestos tile, exterior asbestos roofing or siding and drywall joint compound is exempt from the abatement regulations if done with the listed safe practices (NAC 618.951). If you find that airborne asbestos in your building exceeds 0.01 fibers per cubic centimeter as an 8-hour average, you must post a written notice to all occupants in a conspicuous place, including all entrances, and notify the Enforcement Section immediately (NAC 618.907(1)-(2)). Your habitability duty still applies (NRS 118A.290(1)). A 2025 bill that would have listed asbestos among habitability conditions (AB 223) was vetoed. Federal asbestos rules and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Renting in an HOA or Condo Community
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a landlord to disclose a homeowners' or condominium association's obligations, budget or governing documents in a lease of a unit. The association's rules still reach your tenant: if the governing documents so provide, the executive board may fine a tenant, or bar the tenant from using the common elements for a reasonable time, for violating them (NRS 116.31031(1)). It may not impose a fine unless, at least 30 days before the alleged violation, the unit's owner and, if different, the person to be fined received written notice of the provisions involved (NRS 116.31031(4)(a)). Give your tenant a copy of the association's rules and the relevant governing-document provisions at signing, and keep proof. Check the declaration and rules for leasing restrictions before you lease; an association may restrict renting only as its declaration and NRS 116.335 allow. The resale disclosure package applies to sales, not leases.

title: Attorney's Fees: Prevailing Party Only
bodyText: A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney's fees, but it may provide that reasonable attorney's fees may be awarded to the prevailing party if there is a court action. A one-way fee clause is void, and the tenant may recover any actual damages it caused (NRS 118A.220(1)(c), (2)). The library's Default by Tenant clause carries a prevailing-party sentence of the permitted kind; do not add a separate one-way fee, collection-cost or legal-cost charge. Some statutes award fees whatever the lease says: a tenant who wins a claim over the single-rent-figure rules recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees (NRS 118A.405); a landlord who wins a contested summary eviction for drug-law violations is entitled to reasonable attorney's fees for that hearing (NRS 40.254(3)); either side may recover fees in a claim over adverse action for a call for emergency help (NRS 118A.515(5)); and court costs go of course to the prevailing party in an action to recover real property (NRS 18.020(1)). Without a fee clause or a specific statute, a court may award fees to a prevailing party who recovered no more than $20,000, or where the other side's claim or defense was brought without reasonable ground or to harass; those general rules do not apply where a written agreement entitles the prevailing party to reasonable fees (NRS 18.010(2), (4)). Whether the 15 percent cap on contract attorney's fees in actions to collect a consumer debt (NRS 97B.160) reaches unpaid rent is not settled by the text; keep any fee claim reasonable and documented.

title: No Automatic Renewal Rule
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not regulate automatic renewal of a residential lease: there is no required reminder notice before a lease renews, no type-size or formatting rule for a renewal clause, and no general consumer auto-renewal law that reaches a lease. A renewal clause is an ordinary contract term, subject to the landlord-tenant act. If you use one, the cautious course is to give both sides the same notice period to stop the renewal, because a lease may not require the tenant to give you a different notice of termination than you must give the tenant (NRS 118A.220(1)(e)). Any rent increase for the renewal term still needs written notice at least 60 days before the first increased payment, or 30 days for a periodic tenancy of less than a month (NRS 118A.300). Without a renewal clause, a tenant who stays on with your consent after the term ends becomes a month-to-month tenant (week to week if rent is paid weekly) on the same terms unless you specifically agree otherwise (NRS 118A.470). Refusing to renew in retaliation for protected tenant activity is prohibited (NRS 118A.510). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Balcony or Deck Inspection Law
bodyText: Nevada's statutes and the state regulations reviewed have no periodic inspection requirement for balconies, decks, exterior stairways or other elevated elements of rental buildings, and no inspection report to give tenants. Your duty comes from habitability: floors, walls, ceilings, stairways and railings must be maintained in good repair (NRS 118A.290(1)(h)), and a condition that violates a building or housing code concerning health or safety makes the unit not habitable (NRS 118A.290(1)), with the tenant's repair remedies running from written notice. A severe enough condition at a property with two or more rental units can also lead a county or city to order repairs and, if you do not comply, seek a receiver (NRS 244.36904, 268.4283). In a condominium or other common-interest community, unless the declaration provides otherwise, a balcony or porch serving a single unit is a limited common element allocated to that unit (NRS 116.2102(4)); check the declaration for who must repair it. Local building codes may require inspections (not reviewed).

title: Bed Bugs and Pests: Who Does What
bodyText: Nevada has no bed bug statute for rentals, so cooperation on reporting and treatment is a lease term. The limits: at the start of the tenancy, the building, grounds and other areas under your control must be reasonably free of rodents, insects and vermin (NRS 118A.290(1)(g)), and you must keep the unit habitable throughout the tenancy (NRS 118A.290(1)). You may not charge the tenant for repairs, maintenance or other work that is your habitability duty, except for a condition the tenant, a household member or a guest caused deliberately or negligently (NRS 118A.290(4)-(5)). Whether an infestation that arises mid-tenancy without the tenant's fault is your duty depends on the housing and health codes; the optional clause assigns its cost to you, the cautious course. The tenant must keep its part of the premises as clean and safe as the condition of the premises permits (NRS 118A.310(1)(b)) and may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry for necessary repairs or services (NRS 118A.330(1)). Except in an emergency, give at least 24 hours' notice and enter only at reasonable times during normal business hours (NRS 118A.330(3)).

title: Arbitration Clauses in a Lease
bodyText: Nevada enforces written agreements to arbitrate (NRS 38.219), but an arbitration clause in a lease is void and unenforceable unless the lease includes a specific authorization showing that the person affirmatively agreed to that clause (NRS 597.995(1)-(2)). The only exceptions are collective bargaining agreements and wills or trusts, so the rule reaches every residential lease. A clause that sits in the ordinary lease text is not enough; the cautious course is a separate signature or initials placed directly with the arbitration clause. Before a dispute arises, the parties may not give up the right to be represented by a lawyer in the arbitration (NRS 38.217(2)(d)). No Nevada statute says whether a pre-dispute arbitration clause in a residential lease is also a forbidden waiver of the tenant's remedies under the landlord-tenant act (NRS 118A.220(1)(a)), and possession is recovered only through a court action or summary proceeding (NRS 118A.480), with the tenant's expedited lockout and shutoff remedy also in court (NRS 118A.390). This library therefore offers no arbitration clause. If you use one anyway, keep possession actions and the tenant's expedited court remedies outside it, allow attorney's fees only to the prevailing party (NRS 118A.220(1)(c)), and get the separate authorization signed. Federal law also makes a written arbitration provision in a contract involving interstate commerce enforceable, except on grounds that would undo any contract (FEDERAL: 9 U.S.C. § 2). Whether that federal rule reaches a particular lease and overrides Nevada's separate-authorization rule is a question for case law, which was not reviewed; getting the separate signed authorization is the cautious course either way. Local court rules were not reviewed.

title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText: Nevada lets a person who owns or controls private property prohibit or restrict the smoking, cultivation, processing, manufacture, sale, delivery or transfer of cannabis there (NRS 678D.510(1)(c)), so your lease may ban those activities anywhere on the property. The statute does not list possession or non-smoked use, such as edibles, inside the unit; no statute forbids a lease from banning them, but none expressly allows it, so the library's clause covers only the listed activities. Adults may grow no more than six plants, in a locked enclosed area not visible to the public, and growing is illegal within 25 miles of a licensed adult-use retail store or without the consent of the person in lawful possession of the property (NRS 678D.200(3)(e), 678D.310(1)). During a tenancy that person is the tenant, so if you want to forbid growing, the lease must say so. The adult-use law does not affect the medical-cannabis law, which has no landlord provision (NRS 678D.510(2)); whether you may restrict a registered patient's medical use is not settled by statute, so consider any disability-accommodation request case by case. The state indoor smoking ban does not apply to private residences (NRS 202.2483(3)(g)), so a smoking ban must come from the lease. Because adult use within the legal limits is exempt from state prosecution (NRS 678D.200), treat a breach of a cannabis term as a lease violation and use the 5-day notice to perform or quit (NRS 40.2516), not the 3-day notice for drug crimes. Local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Carpet Cleaning and the Deposit
bodyText: Nevada's statutes have no rule specific to carpets: no professional-cleaning requirement or ban, no age or depreciation test. The deposit rules govern. At the end of the tenancy you may claim from the deposit only what is reasonably necessary for unpaid rent, for repairing damage the tenant caused beyond normal wear, and for the reasonable costs of cleaning, itemized in a written accounting within 30 days (NRS 118A.242(4)). So the reasonable cost of cleaning carpets the tenant left dirty is deductible; stains, burns or tears caused by negligence, carelessness or abuse are damage you may charge to repair; but carpet worn out by ordinary use is normal wear, which you may not charge (NRS 118A.110, 118A.242(4)). You have two ways to plan for cleaning: an optional clause requiring the tenant to have the carpets professionally cleaned at move-out (lawful if the carpets were professionally cleaned before the tenancy and you deduct only the reasonable cost actually paid when the tenant doesn't), or a nonrefundable cleaning charge in a reasonable amount stated in the lease, which is the only nonrefundable part of a deposit allowed and counts toward the three-months'-rent limit (NRS 118A.242(1), (8)). A clause that lets you deduct carpet cleaning as a penalty or regardless of need risks being void (NRS 118A.242(8)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Waiving Casualty and Re-Rent Rules
bodyText: Casualty: when fire or casualty substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, the landlord-tenant act lets the tenant move out and end the lease, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part with a proportional rent reduction, and requires you to return prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit if the lease ends (NRS 118A.400). Those are rights under the act, so a lease may not waive them (NRS 118A.220(1)(a)). The section does not apply if the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the fire or casualty deliberately or negligently (NRS 118A.400(3)). Your own right to terminate after such a casualty is yours to use or not; the library's casualty clause states it. Mitigation: the duty to make reasonable efforts to re-rent after a tenant abandons, which limits the former tenant to your actual damages, is in NRS 118.175, outside the landlord-tenant act, so the act's waiver ban does not reach it by its terms, and chapter 118 has no anti-waiver rule of its own. Whether a lease may waive the re-rent duty is not settled by statute (case law not reviewed). Cautious course: never include a term waiving the re-rent duty, or one keeping the tenant liable for rent on a unit made unusable by casualty; such terms invite an unconscionability ruling (NRS 118A.230). The library's Default by Tenant clause promises reasonable mitigation efforts to the extent the law requires.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a landlord to disclose, attach or show a tenant a certificate of occupancy, or to say in the lease whether one was issued. Certificates of occupancy come from local building codes (not reviewed) and, for mobile homes, from the state manufactured-housing law: a mobile home posted as unsafe or substandard may not be occupied until repairs are completed and a certificate of occupancy has been issued (NRS 461A.150(3), 461A.170(1)(b)).
