A unit that violates housing or health codes on health, safety, sanitation or fitness for habitation is not habitable (NRS 118A.290(1)), so do not rent a unit that lacks a required certificate. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Cold-Weather Vacating Rule
bodyText: Nevada has no statute or regulation requiring a tenant to warn you before leaving a unit empty in cold weather, or to keep heat on or drain pipes to prevent freezing, and none that limits evictions or move-outs during winter. Parts of Nevada do freeze, so the general rules matter. You must keep adequate heating facilities in good working order as part of habitability (NRS 118A.290(1)(d)). The tenant must use the heating, plumbing and other facilities in a reasonable manner and must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises (NRS 118A.310(1)(e)-(f)), so frozen-pipe damage caused by a tenant's neglect can be charged as tenant-caused damage. If you want advance warning of a long winter absence, or want the tenant to keep the heat at a minimum setting while away, put it in the lease; the library's optional Notice of Extended Absence clause covers the notice. A utility energy-conservation regulation mentions lowering the thermostat to 55 degrees when a unit is empty in a heating season, but it lists conservation measures for utility programs and imposes no duty on tenants or landlords. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Collection Fees
bodyText: No Nevada statute authorizes or caps a lease fee for collecting overdue rent or other money a tenant owes. The limits that do apply: any fee the lease requires must be stated in the lease with its purpose (NRS 118A.200(3)(e)), and the library's Required Fees clause is where it goes; a collection fee may not cover your attorney's fees except through a prevailing-party clause (NRS 118A.220(1)(c)); and after you serve a pay-or-quit notice you may not refuse rent because collection fees, attorney's fees or other non-rent costs are unpaid (NRS 40.253(11)). If you refer a debt to a licensed collection agency, the agency may add a fee, charge or expense only if law or contract authorizes it or the parties agreed to it, and only if you added it to the debt before referral, the agency added it and described it in its first written communication, or a court has found it proper (NRS 649.375(1)(b)). An agency owned or operated by, affiliated with, or owned by a relative of the property manager of an apartment building may not collect debts owed to that property manager (NRS 649.375(1)(i)(3)). A fixed collection fee that does not reflect actual cost risks being struck as a penalty or as unconscionable (NRS 118A.230; case law not reviewed). The library offers no collection-fee clause for Nevada.

title: Common-Area and Exit Lighting
bodyText: In any building other than a single-family detached house, the owner or operator must equip every exit corridor and other means of exit with emergency lighting of a type the fire authority approves that permits safe evacuation (NRS 477.120(1)(a)); the authority is the State Fire Marshal in smaller counties and the local building and fire officials in counties of 100,000 or more (NRS 477.100). Beyond that, Nevada's statutes set no lighting level for hallways, stairways, parking areas or grounds. Habitability covers lighting inside the unit (electrical lighting, outlets, wiring and equipment that met the law when installed and are kept in good working order), stairways and railings in good repair, and the buildings, grounds and other areas under your control clean and sanitary at the start of the tenancy (NRS 118A.290(1)(e), (g), (h)). No statute addresses common-area lights wired to a tenant's meter. If you bill tenants for common-area electricity, the charge is a mandatory fee that must be built into the single rent figure; the separate utility-fee exception covers only service provided in the tenant's own unit (NRS 118A.200(6), (8)). If shared lights run through a tenant's meter, say so in the lease's utility section, which every written lease must include (NRS 118A.200(3)(j)). Local building and housing codes may set more (not reviewed).

title: No Government Approval Needed for a Private Lease
bodyText: No Nevada statute makes a private residential lease depend on a government officer's approval. State law has no communal or native land tenure, no approval or registration step before a lease takes effect, and no rule holding back rent or possession until an officer signs. Your lease is effective between you and the tenant on its own terms. Land held in trust for a tribe or tribal member, and leasing within a reservation or colony, are governed by federal and tribal law, which this library does not cover; get advice directed at that before leasing such land. Case law was not reviewed.

title: Condemned or Unsafe Units: No General Rent Bar, but Rent Can Stop
bodyText: Nevada's statutes have no general rule barring you from collecting rent or a deposit after a unit is condemned, placarded or ordered vacated. The one express rent bar is in receivership: once a court appoints a receiver for a substandard multifamily rental (two or more units on a parcel), you and your agents and employees may not collect rent from any tenant; the receiver collects it and spends it on the court-ordered repairs (NRS 244.36906(1), 268.4285(1)). Short of that, the tenant's remedies can stop the rent. A written notice from a government agency that inspects for building, housing or health code violations lets the tenant withhold rent, without separate notice to you, if you do not fix the condition, or try in good faith to, within the time the agency allows (NRS 118A.355(4)(b)); rent fully abates while the tenant uses substitute housing after an essential-service failure (NRS 118A.380(1)(d)); and after a fire or casualty the tenant may end the lease or pay rent reduced for the unusable part, with prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit returned if the lease ends (NRS 118A.400). Condemnation of the unit counts as cause for ending a tenancy (NRS 118A.060(4)). A building used to manufacture a controlled substance such as methamphetamine is a public nuisance if it has not been deemed safe for habitation and you let it be used before certified remediation (NRS 202.450(4)), so do not rent it until then. If a unit cannot lawfully be occupied, get legal advice before collecting rent for that period. Local ordinances on condemnation and placarding may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: A lease may not authorize anyone to confess judgment on any claim arising out of the lease; such a term is void and the tenant may recover any actual damages its inclusion caused (NRS 118A.220(1)(b), (2)). Nevada's general confession-of-judgment procedure, a sworn written statement by the debtor filed with the court clerk, applies except as otherwise provided by law (NRS 17.090 to 17.110), and the landlord-tenant act is such a law for claims under a residential lease. Do not include a confession, cognovit or warrant-of-attorney clause, and do not ask a tenant to sign a confession of judgment as a condition of renting.

title: Habitability: What Nevada Has and Lacks
bodyText: Nevada's habitability law is the landlord-tenant act's list of conditions and its notice-based remedies (NRS 118A.290, 118A.350 to 118A.380): written notice, then 14 days to fix a lease or habitability failure or 48 hours (excluding weekends and legal holidays) for heat, water, power, a working lock or another essential service, with termination, damages, repair and deduct, rent withholding through the court's escrow, and substitute housing as the tenant's tools. Many rules found in other states are not in Nevada's statutes or the state regulations reviewed: no minimum indoor temperature or heating season; no air-conditioning requirement or tenant right to install a cooling unit (supplied air-conditioning must be kept in repair); no duty to supply a stove or refrigerator; no water-heater temperature or turnover rule; no window-guard or radiator-cover rule; no list of required locks or rekeying between tenants; no carbon-monoxide alarm statute for long-term rentals (the model fire and building codes the State Fire Marshal adopts by reference, NAC 477.281, were not reviewed and may address alarms); no lease statement promising habitability; no writing or completion-date rule for repair promises; no presumption that you breached the duty; no small-landlord exemption from the remedies; no duty to provide a hotel or other housing when a tenant asks during repairs; no right to end a lease because a repair costs too much; no general bar on collecting rent after condemnation (only once a receiver is appointed); no rule splitting a rent reduction between a tenant and a housing subsidy; no general requirement that a tenant pay rent into court before raising a defense or counterclaim (but the court must order a deposit if judgment is delayed, NRS 118A.490, and a rent-withholding defense requires the withheld rent in the court's escrow, NRS 118A.355(5)); and no sprinkler disclosure, balcony inspection, code-variance notice or private-well testing rule. Some gaps are filled elsewhere: the habitability duty itself reaches any housing or health code violation affecting health or safety (NRS 118A.290(1)); counties and cities can order repairs and appoint receivers for multifamily rentals (NRS 244.36904, 268.4283); and fire and building codes adopted by the State Fire Marshal and local governments apply. A 2025 bill that would have expanded the habitability list and the tenant's remedies (AB 223) was vetoed and is not law. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Other Rules Nevada Does Not Have
bodyText: Four rules found in some other states do not exist in Nevada's statutes or the Nevada regulations reviewed. (1) No double-letting rule: nothing specifically bans renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period or gives the shut-out tenant a special remedy; the failure-to-deliver-possession remedies apply (rent abates; the tenant may end the lease on 5 days' written notice or sue for possession and damages, NRS 118A.370), along with general contract and fraud law, so keep one calendar and one signed lease per unit. (2) No statutory right to end a lease because the application was false: no statute gives a remedy for a material misstatement, so apart from general contract and fraud law (not reviewed) it can be acted on as a lease breach only if the lease makes accuracy of the application a lease term (the library's rental-application accuracy clause). (3) No smoke-detector liability shield: nothing makes having or lacking a working smoke detector inadmissible in an injury case or stops an insurer from reducing a payment because of it. (4) No general type-size, bold-print or initialing rule for leases: the lease type-size rules are the required disclosure at the top of the first page of a lease for a single-family residence (a structure of up to four units, NRS 118A.200(10)) not signed by a licensed property manager, which must be in a font at least twice as large as any other in the lease (NRS 118A.200(4)), and, where a utility is billed outside the single rent figure, an asterisk or other symbol at least half the font size of that figure tied to a statement on the same page (NRS 118A.200(8)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Checked Across the Whole Code
bodyText: Three questions some states answer outside their landlord-tenant act, checked across all of Nevada's statutes. (1) Squatters: Nevada does have a specific fast remedy. A person who entered without the authority of the owner or tenant and will not leave after a written notice to surrender commits forcible detainer, and a special notice-and-affidavit court process lets the sheriff or constable remove them (see the row on removing a squatter or unauthorized occupant). (2) Cash rent receipts: there is no separate cash-receipt rule, but the general rule covers cash: on the tenant's request you must give a signed written receipt for the deposit or bond and for any other payment, including rent, and the tenant may withhold rent until you tender it. In a manufactured home park, a landlord may not make a tenant who pays cash apply the change to the next payment. (3) Landlord registration as a condition of eviction: no Nevada statute or court rule requires a landlord to show a rental registration or license to get a possession order. A state business license may be required for the business itself (see the row on landlord registration and business licenses). But two general business statutes can stop you bringing the case. If you rent under an assumed or fictitious name different from the legal name of each owner, no action on that business may be commenced or maintained unless the certificate was filed with the county clerk before the action began (NRS 602.010(1), 602.070). And an out-of-state LLC or corporation doing business here without registering with the Secretary of State may not commence or maintain any action until it registers, though the lease stays valid and it may defend a suit (NRS 86.544(1), 86.548(2), (3); NRS 80.010(1), 80.055(2), (6)). Owning property without more is not doing business under those chapters (NRS 86.5483(1)(i); NRS 80.015(1)(i)); whether renting it out is, is a case-law question. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Construction Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText: Under Nevada's construction lien law, any improvement built, altered or repaired on property is treated as done at the instance of every owner with an interest in it, so a contractor or supplier the tenant hires can lien your interest, not only the tenant's leasehold. The lien law also counts a lessee with charge or control of the property as the owner's agent, so a lease sentence saying the tenant is not your agent does not by itself protect you. Your statutory protection is a notice of nonresponsibility. As a lessor you must record it with the county recorder within 3 days after the lease takes effect or by the time all parties sign the lease, whichever comes first (otherwise within 3 days after you learn of the work), and serve it on the tenant within 10 days after recording and on the tenant's prime contractor within 10 days after the tenant signs with that contractor, by personal delivery or certified mail, return receipt requested. The notice must state, among other things, whether you told the tenant in writing that it must comply with the lessee-security rule. That rule requires a tenant, before starting work, to record a notice of posted security and either fund a construction disbursement account run by a construction control for at least the full contract price or record a surety bond. If the tenant does not comply, you lose the protection of your notice. All the owners may instead record a waiver of these rights. Because the rules are technical and case law was not reviewed, the cautious course is to forbid tenant-ordered work without your written consent, and before consenting to any significant work, record and serve the notice and require the tenant's posted security. The optional lease clause on liens for tenant work states the tenant's side of this.

title: Deceptive Trade Practices and Landlords
bodyText: Nevada's Deceptive Trade Practices Act (NRS 598.0903 to 598.0999) reaches landlords expressly in two places: a willful failure to disclose in writing to a prospective tenant that the property is in foreclosure is a deceptive trade practice (NRS 118A.275), and so is a knowing failure to give a translated lease when you advertise and negotiate a rental in another language (NRS 598.09227). More generally, the Act covers acts done knowingly in the course of a business, including failing to disclose a material fact, or violating a statute, in connection with the sale or lease of goods or services; using coercion, duress or intimidation in a transaction; using an unconscionable practice in a transaction; and making any other false representation in a transaction (NRS 598.0915(15), 598.0923(1)). No statute says whether renting a dwelling is a lease of goods or services, but the practices tied to a transaction are not limited to goods or services, so treat the Act as applying to your rental business. A victim may sue for damages, equitable relief, costs and attorney's fees (NRS 41.600). Public enforcers may seek civil penalties of up to $15,000 for each willful violation, and more for conduct aimed at an elderly person or a person with a disability; a knowing and willful violation can be a crime (NRS 598.0973, 598.0999). The door-to-door sales cancellation rules do not apply to the rental of real property (NRS 598.180(6)). Describe the unit, rent and fees accurately, disclose known material facts in writing, and never pressure a tenant. Case law was not reviewed.

title: Converting Rentals to Condominiums
bodyText: If you convert a building that was occupied by tenants into a common-interest community (condominiums or other units for sale), Nevada gives the residential tenants these rights. The declarant, and any dealer who intends to offer the units, must give each residential tenant and subtenant in possession written notice of the conversion, setting out generally their rights, together with the public offering statement, at least 120 days before they must leave, hand-delivered to the unit or mailed to the unit or another address the tenant gave. No tenant may be required to leave on less than 120 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste or conduct that disturbs other tenants, and the terms of the tenancy can't be changed during that period. Failing to give the notice is a defense to an action for possession. For 60 days after the notice you must offer to sell each residential unit to the tenant who leases it; if the tenant doesn't buy, for the next 180 days you may not offer that unit to anyone else at a price or on terms more favorable than those offered to the tenant. If a majority of tenants were made to leave in the 6 months before the declaration was recorded, for reasons other than nonpayment, waste or disturbance, the law presumes you already intended to convert. A conversion notice that states a move-out date and meets the eviction statutes' notice and service rules also serves as the notice to surrender. The conversion does not let you end a lease early in violation of its terms (NRS 116.4112). Nevada does not require a conversion statement as a lease clause, and no Nevada statute bars converting rental housing to hotel or other transient use or addresses local conversion moratoria. Mobile home park conversions and closures have separate rules for park tenants. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Criminal Activity by Tenants
bodyText: Nevada's eviction statute treats the most serious tenant crimes as grounds with no right to cure. A tenant who violates the controlled-substances laws on the premises (other than simple possession), carries on an unlawful business there, or maintains a nuisance that unreasonably obstructs others' use of the property and injures other tenants or occupants can be served a 3-day notice to surrender, and you may use the summary eviction procedure; if you win a drug-based case the tenant contested, you are entitled to reasonable attorney's fees (NRS 40.2514, 40.254). Other criminal conduct is handled as a breach of the lease or of the tenant's basic duty not to disturb neighbors: a 5-day notice to perform or surrender, with no notice needed if the breach cannot be cured (NRS 40.2516, 118A.310(1)(g), 118A.430). No Nevada statute requires, authorizes or limits a crime-free lease addendum, and none implies a no-crime term into every lease beyond those basic duties; a crime-free covenant is a lease term you choose to include. Your own exposure: letting a building while knowing it is used for a public nuisance, which includes any place where controlled substances are unlawfully sold, kept, used or made, is a misdemeanor (NRS 202.450(2)(e), 202.470(3)), and maintaining a place for unlawful drug sale or use is a felony (NRS 453.316). When a tenant is arrested for or convicted of a drug offense (other than simple possession) in which the rental was used, the prosecutor must notify you by certified or registered mail. After a notice of conviction, unless you serve a summary-eviction notice to surrender within 90 days or show the court good cause not to, you are rebuttably presumed in a later forfeiture case to have known of and consented to a further such use (NRS 453.305, 179.1164(3)). Counties and cities may also adopt chronic-nuisance ordinances under which the district attorney or city attorney can sue an owner over repeated criminal activity, close the property and seek civil penalties of up to $500 a day for residential property, after written notice and at least 30 days to abate when someone else's crime caused the problem (NRS 244.3603, 268.4124); local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed). Limits: you may not evict, fine or otherwise penalize a tenant based solely on a call for police or other emergency help that the tenant or another person in the home reasonably believed was needed (NRS 118A.515), and you may not retaliate against a tenant because the tenant, a co-tenant or a household member is a victim of domestic violence, harassment, sexual assault or stalking (NRS 118A.510(1)(h)). In federally assisted housing, criminal activity directly relating to such violence against the tenant is not a ground to deny the victim tenancy (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(b)(3)(A)).

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a landlord to disclose defective or corrosive drywall to a tenant. A drywall defect that makes the unit violate housing or health codes, or damages the plumbing, wiring or other facilities you must maintain, falls under your general habitability duty (NRS 118A.290(1)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Preset Deposit Deduction Schedule
bodyText: Nevada's statutes set no schedule of preset deposit deductions, no rule on fixing carpet-cleaning or other cleaning charges in advance, and no special notice for such a schedule. Whatever the lease lists, at the end of the tenancy you may keep only the amounts reasonably necessary to cover unpaid rent, to repair damage the tenant caused beyond normal wear, and to pay the reasonable costs of cleaning, and you must give an itemized written accounting and return the rest within 30 days (NRS 118A.242(4)). So treat any list of typical charges as an estimate and deduct the actual, reasonable cost. The one charge the statute lets the lease fix in advance is a nonrefundable cleaning charge in a reasonable amount (NRS 118A.242(8)); it is part of the security deposit, so it counts toward the three-months'-rent limit on all security (NRS 118A.240, 118A.242(1)). Any lease provision calling another part of the deposit nonrefundable, or modifying the tenant's deposit rights, is void. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Deposit Installment Right
bodyText: Nevada's statutes give a tenant no right to pay a security deposit in installments, and do not forbid you from agreeing to it. If you agree, put the schedule in the lease, because the lease must state the deposits required and the conditions for their refund (NRS 118A.200(3)(f)). Every installment is part of the security deposit, so the total of all deposits, any surety bond and any prepaid last month's rent still may not exceed three months' periodic rent (NRS 118A.240, 118A.242(1)), and the tenant may ask for a signed receipt for each payment (NRS 118A.250). An unpaid deposit installment is not rent: once you have served a pay-or-quit notice, you may not refuse a rent payment because a security deposit is unpaid (NRS 40.253(11)). Offer any installment option on the same terms to every applicant. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: If you collect the last month's rent in advance, it counts toward the limit on total security: all security deposits and any surety bond, including the last month's rent, may not exceed three months' periodic rent (NRS 118A.242(1)). Label each upfront payment in the lease as either prepaid rent for a named rental period or a security deposit, because any payment to be used to cover unpaid rent, damage or cleaning is a security deposit whatever it is called, with the refund, accounting and nonrefundability rules that go with it (NRS 118A.240, 118A.242). Prepaid rent must be returned if the tenant lawfully ends the lease because of your breach, a habitability or essential-services failure, your failure to deliver possession, an unlawful lockout or a fire or casualty (NRS 118A.350(3), 118A.355(3), 118A.370(1), 118A.390(3), 118A.400(2)). If a tenant ends the lease under the domestic-violence, harassment, sexual-assault or stalking provision, you may keep prepaid rent for the rental period in which the lease ends, refunding any excess (NRS 118A.345(5)). No statute lets a tenant use the security deposit as the last month's rent, or bars a lease from saying the deposit isn't to be used that way; if the last month goes unpaid, you may claim the deposit for the unpaid rent after the tenancy ends, with the itemized accounting due within 30 days (NRS 118A.242(4)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Deposit Refund Not Tied to a Move-Out Notice
bodyText: Nevada ties the deposit to the end of the tenancy, not to any notice from the tenant. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, whoever ends it and for whatever reason, you must give the tenant an itemized written accounting and return the balance, by handing it to the tenant at the place rent is paid or by mailing it to the tenant's present address, or to the last known address if the present one is unknown (NRS 118A.242(4)). The tenant does not have to give a forwarding address, a written demand or advance move-out notice first, and a lease can't make the refund depend on one, because any provision waiving or modifying the tenant's deposit rights is void (NRS 118A.242(8)). Asking for a forwarding address in writing is still sensible. When the tenancy ends is set by other rules: the end of a fixed term, a termination notice for a periodic tenancy (the lease may not require the tenant to give a different termination notice than you must give, NRS 118A.220(1)(e)), or abandonment (a tenant absent for half the rental period, with rent not current and no written notice of an intended absence, is presumed to have abandoned the unit, NRS 118A.450). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: Nevada's fair housing law has its own disability duties. You may not refuse to make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices or services when they are necessary for a person with a disability to use and enjoy the dwelling. You may not refuse to let a person with a disability make reasonable modifications to the dwelling they occupy or will occupy, if that person pays for them and they are necessary for the person to use and enjoy the dwelling. You may, as a condition of approving a modification, reasonably require the tenant to restore the dwelling at the end of the occupancy to its condition before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted. You may not raise your usual security deposit because a modification was requested. You may take an additional deposit only if it is necessary to ensure the restoration, does not exceed the actual cost of the restoration, and is held in an interest-bearing account, with the interest paid to the tenant. Nevada does not require this restoration condition to be written into the lease; it is set when you approve a modification (the optional lease clause on disability modifications states it in advance). The statute does not say whether the additional deposit counts toward the three-month limit on all security; the cautious course is to keep all deposits, including this one, within that limit. Federal fair housing law sets parallel duties. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Guests Displaced by a Disaster
bodyText: Nevada has no rule that lets a tenant house people displaced by a disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none that changes how long such a person can stay before becoming a tenant; the lease's occupant and guest terms control (the library's guest-policy clauses). Hotel and motel stays of less than 30 consecutive days are outside the landlord-tenant law unless the guest clearly shows an intent to stay longer, and there is no special rule for disaster-displaced hotel guests. If you choose to let people shelter on your property during a declared emergency or disaster, voluntarily and without compensation, you are not civilly liable for negligently causing their death or injury or loss of their property. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed); case law was not reviewed.

title: Leases After a Declared Disaster
bodyText: Nevada has no statute that ends a residential lease, suspends rent or sets special landlord duties when a disaster or state of emergency is declared, and none that addresses rent while a unit cannot be reached but is not damaged. The general rule for damage applies: if fire or casualty damages the unit so that the tenant's enjoyment is substantially impaired, you may end the lease, and the tenant may move out and give notice within 7 days to end it as of the move-out date, or, if staying is lawful, give up the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion; if the lease ends you must return prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit. That rule does not apply if the tenant, a household member or someone there with the tenant's consent caused the damage deliberately or negligently. During a declared emergency the Governor may order evacuations and take property for emergency use with compensation. In the first 75 days of a declared emergency or disaster, renting consumer goods or services in the disaster area at a price grossly above the usual price is a deceptive trade practice, with safe harbors for small increases; whether that reaches a rent increase on a home is not settled by the statute, so the cautious course is not to raise rent for homes in a declared disaster area during that period. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: No Nevada statute specifically addresses double letting, that is, renting the same room or unit to two tenants for the same period, or sets a special remedy for it. The general rule on delivering possession covers the practical result. If you fail to deliver possession as the lease requires, rent abates until you do, and the tenant may end the lease on at least 5 days' written notice and get back all prepaid rent, the recoverable deposit and any payment made to secure the lease; or demand performance and sue for possession against you or anyone wrongfully in possession and recover actual damages; or pursue any other remedy, including actual damages. The no-damages defense for a landlord who used due diligence to evict a holdover tenant or fix the condition keeping the new tenant out (NRS 118A.370) does not fit a unit you knowingly promised to someone else. Beyond that, the tenant left without the unit has ordinary contract claims against you, which case law (not reviewed here) governs. Keep one signed lease per unit and period, and don't accept a second applicant's deposit or rent for a unit already committed. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Drug-Free Housing Addenda
bodyText: No Nevada statute requires, authorizes or limits a drug-free housing addendum in a private residential lease. A drug-free term is an ordinary lease covenant; the library's optional Criminal Activity clause, which carries Nevada, makes unlawful manufacture, sale, distribution or possession of controlled substances on the property a breach. Nevada law already gives you a strong remedy without an addendum: violating the controlled-substances laws on the premises, other than simple possession, is a ground for a 3-day notice to surrender with no right to cure and supports summary eviction and an attorney's-fee award (NRS 40.2514(5), 40.254). A breach that rests only on the lease covenant, such as simple possession, goes through the 5-day notice to perform or surrender instead (NRS 40.2516). Cannabis needs separate thought: an adult 21 or older who stays within Nevada's limits is exempt from state prosecution for possessing or growing cannabis, so a term banning "illegal drugs" may not reach it. Nevada's cannabis law does not stop the owner or controller of private property from prohibiting or restricting smoking, cultivation, processing, manufacture, sale, delivery or transfer of cannabis there (NRS 678D.200, 678D.510(1)(c)), and growing cannabis without the consent of the person in lawful physical possession of the property is a crime (NRS 678D.310(1)(c)). The cannabis statute's list for private property does not mention eating or other non-smoked use, so a lease that restricts those relies on contract alone. If you want to restrict cannabis, say so expressly (the library's smoking policy already bans smoking marijuana). Federally assisted housing has its own program rules (not reviewed here). Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Domestic Violence: Confidentiality
bodyText: Once a tenant or cotenant gives you a termination notice under the domestic-violence, harassment, sexual-assault or stalking statute, you may not give the adverse party any information about where the tenant, cotenant or household member is (NRS 118A.345(7)). You also may not disclose, describe or characterize the termination to a prospective landlord as an early termination, and the tenant need not disclose it as one (NRS 118A.345(11)). Nevada's landlord-tenant law has no broader rule on keeping a victim's status or documents confidential; cautious course: treat the notice and the protection order, police report or affidavit as confidential and share them only with staff who need them to process the termination. The state's confidential-address program binds government agencies and utility providers, not private landlords (NRS 217.464). If the unit is in a federally covered housing program (for example housing choice vouchers, public housing or low-income housing tax credit housing), federal law requires you to keep information a tenant submits about victim status in confidence, out of any shared database, and undisclosed except with the tenant's written consent, for an eviction proceeding, or as otherwise required by law (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(c)(4)).

title: Domestic Violence Termination: Deposit Timing
bodyText: Nevada sets no special deposit deadline for a domestic-violence termination. When a tenant or cotenant ends the lease under the domestic-violence, harassment, sexual-assault or stalking statute, you may not withhold the deposit because of the early termination, though the ordinary claims for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and cleaning remain (NRS 118A.345(5), 118A.242(4)). The usual deadline applies: an itemized written accounting and the balance no later than 30 days after the tenancy ends (NRS 118A.242(4)); late return exposes you to the whole deposit plus up to the same amount again (NRS 118A.242(6)). The terminating tenant owes rent only through the termination date and other outstanding obligations, and you may keep prepaid rent for the final rental period, refunding only any excess (NRS 118A.345(5)). The statute does not say whether one cotenant's termination ends the tenancy for the others, what happens to a shared deposit when others stay, or whether the clock waits for every occupant to leave (case law not reviewed). Cautious course: get a written agreement signed by all cotenants on how the deposit is held, and give the accounting within 30 days after the tenancy ends for anyone it ends for.

title: Domestic Violence Victims: Eviction Protection
bodyText: You may not, in retaliation, terminate or refuse to renew a tenancy, raise rent, cut essential services, or bring or threaten an eviction because the tenant, a cotenant or a household member is a victim of domestic violence, harassment, sexual assault or stalking, or because the tenant ended the lease under the domestic-violence termination statute (NRS 118A.510(1)(h)). The tenant then has the remedies for an unlawful lockout and a defense to a retaliatory eviction (NRS 118A.510(2)). It is not retaliation if the tenancy is terminated with cause, such as nonpayment of rent or a breach of valid lease terms or rules (NRS 118A.510(3)(b), 118A.060), and the termination statute does not limit your right to terminate for reasons unrelated to the abuse (NRS 118A.345(10)). You also may not evict, fine or punish a tenant based solely on the tenant or someone in the home calling for police, fire or medical help with a reasonable belief it was needed (NRS 118A.515). In federally covered housing (for example housing choice vouchers, public housing or low-income housing tax credit housing), a tenant may not be evicted on the basis of being a victim, the abuse is not a serious or repeated lease violation by the victim or good cause to end the victim's tenancy, and criminal activity directly relating to the abuse by a household member or guest is not by itself grounds against the victim (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(b)).

title: Domestic Violence: Changing the Locks
bodyText: After a tenant or cotenant gives a termination notice under the domestic-violence, harassment, sexual-assault or stalking statute, the tenant, cotenant or a household member may require you to install a new lock if they pay the cost. You comply by rekeying the lock if it is in good working condition, or by replacing the entire locking mechanism with one of equal or better quality, and you may keep a copy of the new key. Whatever the lease says, you must refuse to give the adverse party a key to the new lock, and refuse the adverse party access to the dwelling to reclaim property unless a law enforcement officer is present, even if the adverse party is a tenant, cotenant or household member (NRS 118A.345(8), (9)). The right is tied to the termination notice: Nevada gives no stand-alone lock-change right to a victim who is staying, and the statute sets no special damages for a violation (general remedies and case law not reviewed). A court's protection order may separately exclude the adverse party from the home (NRS 33.030(1)(b)); follow any order you are shown.

title: Protection-Order Statutes: Current Citations
bodyText: Nevada's protection-order statutes have not been moved or renumbered. Orders for protection against domestic violence are still issued under NRS 33.017 to 33.100, and temporary or extended orders against stalking, aggravated stalking or harassment, and against sexual assault, under NRS 200.591 and 200.378. Those are the orders the domestic-violence termination statute accepts (NRS 118A.345(2)(a), (3)(b)). The 2023 and 2025 sessions amended several chapter 33 sections in place without moving them. One change matters to landlords: since January 1, 2026, the acts that count as domestic violence include kidnapping and an attempt or solicitation to commit any listed act (NRS 33.018(1)(h), (i)), and the landlord-tenant statutes borrow that definition (NRS 118A.345(12)(c), 118A.510(4)(b)). Harassment, sexual assault and stalking still take their meaning from the criminal statutes NRS 200.571, 200.366 and 200.575 (NRS 118A.345(12)).

title: Domestic Violence Termination: Qualifying Documents
bodyText: For a domestic-violence termination, the tenant's written notice must describe the reason and include one of: a copy of an order for protection against domestic violence issued to the tenant, cotenant or household member; a copy of a written law-enforcement report showing that person notified the agency of the domestic violence; or a copy of an affidavit in the statutory form, signed by a qualified third party acting in an official capacity, stating that the person is a victim and identifying the adverse party (NRS 118A.345(2), 118A.347). Qualified third parties are: a Nevada-licensed physician, psychologist or social worker; a Nevada-licensed psychiatrist certified by the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology or the American Osteopathic Board of Neurology and Psychiatry; a Nevada-licensed registered nurse with a master's degree in psychiatric nursing; a marriage and family therapist or clinical professional counselor licensed under NRS chapter 641A; a Nevada resident trained in domestic violence who either works for a domestic-violence advice or referral agency and is licensed to provide health care under NRS title 54, or is that agency's executive director or a board member; or a Nevada-resident member of the clergy of a 501(c)(3) church or religious organization (NRS 118A.345(12)(f)). For harassment, sexual assault or stalking, only a written law-enforcement report or a copy of a temporary or extended order under NRS 200.378 or 200.591 qualifies (NRS 118A.345(3)). The events must have happened within the 90 days before the notice (NRS 118A.345(4)). Don't demand more than the statute lists. Federally covered housing has its own documentation rules (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(c)).

title: Reselling Electricity to Tenants
bodyText: For Nevada's electric and natural gas provider statutes, a landlord who pays for electricity or gas delivered through a master meter and distributes or resells it to tenants is a retail customer, not a provider of electric service (NRS 702.090(2)(c), 704.7808(3)(b), 704.7818(2)(d)). The public-utility definitions do not expressly address landlord resale (Public Utilities Commission decisions and case law not reviewed). In the lease, an electric charge outside the single rent figure is allowed only as a monthly fee equal to the cost of the electricity provided in the tenant's own unit, when the utility cannot contract with the tenant directly, flagged by an asterisk or other symbol at least half the rent figure's font size that points to a same-page statement naming the utility and its phone number (NRS 118A.200(8)(a)). If a master-metered bill goes unpaid, regulations under NRS 704.1835(2) require the utility to use its best efforts to post a notice of the planned shutoff where tenants can see it.

title: Emergency Contacts
bodyText: Nevada requires the landlord to give the tenant, in writing at or before the start of the tenancy, a telephone number at which a responsible person who lives in the county or within 60 miles of the property can be called in an emergency, and to keep it current; the library's manager, agent and owner disclosure clause includes it. Posting the information in the building is an allowed alternative (in every elevator and one other conspicuous place, or two conspicuous places in a building without an elevator). If you fail to make the disclosure after the tenant demands it, the tenant may recover actual damages or $25, whichever is greater. No Nevada statute requires a tenant to give you an emergency contact, or limits asking for one; it is a lease matter. In an emergency you may enter the unit without the tenant's consent. Manufactured home parks have their own emergency-repair contract rule.

title: When the Property Is Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText: Nevada has no statute that ends a residential lease or reduces the rent when the property is taken by eminent domain, so the lease decides (the library's optional condemnation clause does so). In the condemnation case, a tenant in occupation may appear to protect its own interest, the court values each separate estate or interest in the property, including a leasehold, and it divides the award among the owner and the other interest holders in a separate hearing. A lease term giving the leasehold's share to the landlord settles the point between you and the tenant but does not take away the court's role. A government body that displaces a tenant from a dwelling must provide relocation assistance and payments at least equal to the federal relocation law, and month-to-month renters may receive them; those payments belong to the tenant. Ending a tenancy because the dwelling unit is condemned counts as ending it with cause, which matters if a tenant claims retaliation. Your security deposit duties apply as in any other move-out. Case law was not reviewed.

title: Background Checks for Property Staff
bodyText: Nevada has two employee-screening rules for landlords, each for particular properties. First, a landlord of a covered complex (more than 50 dwelling units on a single parcel in a county of 100,000 or more people, or more than 30 units in a smaller county) must have a policy requiring a criminal background check, as a condition of employment, for any job applicant whose position gives access to any dwelling unit key, including electronic keys and access codes; the same law requires written key policies and an on-site key log. Financial institutions and licensed real estate brokers and salespeople are not landlords for this rule. Second, a landlord of housing intended and operated exclusively for people 55 and older may not employ anyone who will work 36 or more hours a week with access to all units unless the person holds a current sheriff-issued work card; licensed property managers, independent contractors and some program workers are exempt. Outside these two rules, no Nevada statute requires or limits background checks of apartment staff; Nevada's employment-law limit on considering criminal history applies only to certain public employers. If you use a consumer reporting agency for an employee check, federal law requires a separate written disclosure and the applicant's written authorization first, and a copy of the report and a summary of rights before any adverse action. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Energy Benchmarking or Usage-Data Rule
bodyText: Nevada's statutes and the commission's utility rules do not require energy benchmarking of residential buildings, and they do not govern a lease term letting a utility release a tenant's usage data to you. The gas and electric rules give the account holder access: a customer applying for service may have the utility give the customer, or anyone the customer names in writing, a range of historical energy use at the address, and on request the utility must send the customer a statement of actual consumption for each billing period of the prior year. A utility may not give its customer lists or related customer information to others for commercial purposes. So if the tenant holds the account, get usage data through the tenant: the library's optional "Energy Usage Data Authorization" clause has the tenant sign the utility's own release on request, and lets the tenant withdraw it without breaching the lease. If you hold the account, the bills and usage records are yours. Water and local-government utilities have their own policies (not reviewed).

title: Who Can Appear in Court for an LLC or Corporate Landlord
bodyText: In Nevada the answer depends on the kind of case and the court. Summary eviction: the statutes let the landlord or the landlord's agent have the notices served and file the affidavit of complaint (NRS 40.253(1), (5)(a), 40.254(2)), though the notices themselves must be served by a sheriff, constable, licensed process server or an attorney's agent, apart from the in-person attempt for a short-term weekly tenancy (NRS 40.280(1), 40.253(2)), and a landlord's agent includes a person hired to manage the property, such as a licensed property manager (NRS 40.215(2)). Several justice courts' local rules say corporations and LLCs must be represented by an attorney, but those rules do not govern summary evictions: Henderson's and North Las Vegas's local rules exclude summary eviction cases, Las Vegas routes summary evictions to its separate local rules of practice, and Reno's local rules exclude landlord-tenant matters altogether. Formal unlawful-detainer suits and other civil cases: in the Henderson, Las Vegas and North Las Vegas justice courts a corporation or LLC must appear through a licensed Nevada attorney. Small claims (money claims up to $10,000): a corporation, partnership, trust or other business entity may be represented by its director, officer or employee (NRS 73.012). Practicing law without a license is a crime (NRS 7.285), and no rule in the sources reviewed says whether a non-attorney manager may argue legal issues for an entity landlord at a contested summary-eviction hearing; the cautious course is to use an attorney once the tenant files a contest, or at least have a manager with first-hand knowledge appear as the landlord's agent and confine the appearance to facts. Supreme Court rules on the practice of law and case law were not reviewed, and local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Rule
bodyText: No Nevada statute gives a landlord or tenant a specific right to end a residential lease because of an environmental or public-health event, such as contamination, a chemical spill, sewage backup, wildfire smoke, flooding or an evacuation order, and none authorizes an opt-in lease clause for it. The rules that come closest are general ones. If fire or another casualty damages the unit so that enjoyment of it is substantially impaired, you may terminate the lease and the tenant may leave and give notice within 7 days, or stay and pay reduced rent for the usable part if continued occupancy is lawful (NRS 118A.400); whether an event that damages the unit without fire counts as a casualty is not settled by the text, so treat physical damage from a flood or similar event as casualty only cautiously. If the event makes the unit unfit, your habitability duty and the tenant's repair remedies apply, including termination after 14 days' written notice if you don't fix it (NRS 118A.290, 118A.355). A former drug-lab property is a public nuisance until remediated. A lease may add a mutual termination right for such events, but because a lease can't waive the tenant's rights under the landlord-tenant act or shorten statutory notice periods, any such clause must leave those rights intact; the library offers none for Nevada. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: EV Chargers at Move-Out
bodyText: Nevada has no statute on who owns, removes or pays for a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when a tenancy ends, and tenants have no statutory right to install one. So the written agreement allowing the charger decides: say whether the tenant must remove it and repair the installation points, may leave it in place, or must sell it to you, and who pays for damage from removal. Two general rules apply. You have no lien on a tenant's household goods for unpaid rent, so you may not keep a tenant's removable charger to cover arrears. Personal property a tenant leaves behind must be stored safely for 30 days and may be disposed of only after written notice and the statutory waiting period. Whether a hard-wired charger has become part of the building is a fixtures question not answered by statute; settle it in writing before installation. Repair costs for damage the tenant causes in removing it may come from the security deposit like any other tenant-caused damage.

title: EV Charger Conditions
bodyText: Nevada's statutes set no conditions a tenant must meet to install an electric vehicle charger (insurance, licensed electrician, registration, separate metering) and do not require rental buildings to be EV-ready; tenants have no statutory right to install one, so any charger is by your agreement. A few general rules apply. A person who supplies electricity only to charge electric vehicles is not a public utility, so offering charging does not by itself make you a regulated utility. Nevada's weights-and-measures chapter does not address electricity, and we found no registration, accuracy or price-posting rule for chargers. New electric vehicle supply equipment within the ENERGY STAR specification must meet the state's efficiency standards before it is sold, leased or rented in Nevada, and before it is installed for compensation. Billing is the trap: every mandatory periodic charge must be inside the single rent figure, and the only utility charge allowed outside it is a qualifying unit-cost electric, gas or water fee, so the library's optional charger clause, which has the tenant reimburse charger electricity on your bill, is not offered for Nevada. If you allow a charger, connect it to electric service in the tenant's own name or build any fixed charge into the rent figure, and put consent, contractor, permit and removal terms in writing. Building codes and local permits were not reviewed.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking
bodyText: Nevada has no statute on tenant electric vehicle chargers in shared parking: nothing lets a tenant install one in a common area, sets a fee for reserving the charging space, or assigns responsibility for damage, so these are matters for your written agreement. Any fee follows the general fee rules: a mandatory periodic charge (such as a monthly space-reservation fee) must be included in the single rent figure, and a one-time required fee must be listed in the lease with its purpose. One statute does apply on private property: if a space is designated for charging electric or hybrid vehicles by a compliant sign or markings stating a minimum $100 fine, no one may park there without being connected to the charger, with fines of $100, then $200, then $400 to $750. In a condominium or planned community, the association's rules for common elements also apply. Local building and parking codes were not reviewed.

title: Stays and Delays of an Eviction
bodyText: Nevada lets a justice court stay the execution of any judgment, including an eviction, for up to 10 days (NRS 70.010(2)). The statute does not list reasons, so a tenant may ask for hardship reasons, but no Nevada statute gives a longer postponement for illness, age, children, weather or inability to find housing. In a summary eviction for a lease breach or after a no-cause or holdover notice, your notice must tell the tenant of the right to ask for this stay (NRS 40.254(1)(c)(2)). Under the statewide court rule the tenant asks in the contest affidavit, and a request made after the court has issued, or the sheriff or constable has executed, the removal order is untimely and may be summarily denied (JCRCP 110). Local rules vary: Las Vegas lets a tenant move for a stay after the order but before it is executed; Henderson, North Las Vegas and Pahrump allow one motion to stay or vacate per case and hold a pending eviction order until the court rules. Las Vegas and North Las Vegas may refer an eligible nonpayment case (not a breach or nuisance case) to an eviction diversion program before the hearing, and the Reno Justice Court runs a Housing Court that refers nonpayment cases to rental-assistance agencies. Other delays come from specific statutes: on appeal from a summary eviction order a tenant can stay execution by posting a $250 bond, but must keep paying rent as it comes due (NRS 40.385); in a formal unlawful-detainer trial the court may adjourn up to 5 days for good cause, or up to 30 days for a missing witness if the tenant posts a bond for rent, costs and damages (NRS 40.340); and a tenant 60 or older or with a disability, or a qualifying government worker during a shutdown, can ask for more time under a no-cause notice. The Las Vegas rule still refers to a 2021 law that let a tenant with a pending rental-assistance application stop a nonpayment eviction, and the Reno court still posts a form for that defense, but that law expired on June 5, 2023 and was not renewed; a 2023 bill to bring back a similar stay was vetoed and is not law. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Eviction Fees in the Lease
bodyText: No Nevada statute expressly bans, authorizes or caps a lease clause charging the tenant a fixed fee because you start or win an eviction. The rules that limit one: attorney's fees may be shifted only through a prevailing-party clause (NRS 118A.220(1)(c)), so a clause making the tenant pay your legal costs whatever the outcome risks being void as a one-way fee term; court costs already go by statute to the prevailing party in an action to recover real property (NRS 18.020(1)); any required fee must be stated in the lease with its purpose (NRS 118A.200(3)(e)); after a pay-or-quit notice you may not refuse rent because collection fees, attorney's fees or other non-rent costs are unpaid (NRS 40.253(11)); and a fixed charge unrelated to actual cost risks being struck as a penalty or as unconscionable (NRS 118A.230; case law not reviewed). Separately, in a formal unlawful-detainer action the court itself enters judgment for the rent found due and three times the damages it assesses for the unlawful detainer (NRS 40.360(2)); that is a statutory remedy, not a lease fee. The library offers no eviction-fee clause for Nevada; the prevailing-party sentence in the Default by Tenant clause covers fees.

title: Who Can Accept Eviction Papers
bodyText: Nevada does not let a lease name someone other than the tenant to receive eviction notices. Notices to surrender must be served on the tenant (and on any subtenant in actual occupation) by a sheriff, constable, licensed process server or an attorney's agent: personally; or, if the tenant is away from home or work, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion there and mailing a copy; or, failing that, by posting, delivering a copy to a resident if one can be found, and mailing (NRS 40.280(1), (3)). Short-term weekly tenancies have their own delivery rule. A lease clause pointing notices to a third party does not replace these methods, and a notice of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of a primary residence can't be given electronically (NRS 719.250(4)(b)). For the summons and complaint in a formal unlawful-detainer case, the court rules allow service on an agent "authorized by appointment or by law to receive service of process" (JCRCP 4.2(a)(3)), but whether a designation in a lease counts as such an appointment is not settled in the sources reviewed, so serve the tenant directly. A minor must be served personally if 14 or older and through a parent or guardian (JCRCP 4.2(b)(1)). The rule runs the other way for you: the lease or another writing must name a person in Nevada authorized to accept service of process, notices and demands for you, and service on your manager or that person counts as service on you (NRS 118A.260(1), (4)). Nevada's confidential-address program for victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking or human trafficking gives a participant a substitute address for government agencies and utilities; it does not reroute eviction service, which goes to the rental. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Exculpation or Indemnity for Your Own Fault
bodyText: A lease may not make the tenant agree to excuse or limit any liability you have under law, or to indemnify you for that liability or its costs, where the liability is based on an act or omission of you or your agent or employee. Such a term is void, and the tenant may recover any actual damages its inclusion caused (NRS 118A.220(1)(d), (2)). The ban is keyed to your own conduct and that of your agents and employees. Making the tenant answer for harm the tenant, a household member or a guest causes is not an exculpation of your liability, and the law lets you charge for repairs needed because of the tenant's own deliberate or negligent conduct (NRS 118A.290(5)). Even so, keep any liability, indemnity or insurance clause from reaching your own negligence, for example by saying the tenant's indemnity does not cover claims caused by you, your agents or your employees. A court may also refuse to enforce an unconscionable term (NRS 118A.230). Case law was not reviewed.

title: Fast-Track Eviction for Drug Activity and Nuisance
bodyText: Nevada has no separate criminal-eviction statute, but its general eviction law gives a fast, no-cure route for the usual criminal grounds. If a tenant violates the controlled-substances laws on the premises (other than simple possession), carries on an unlawful business there, commits or permits waste, or maintains a nuisance that unreasonably obstructs others' use of the property and injures other tenants or occupants, you may serve a 3-day notice to surrender, and the tenant has no right to cure (NRS 40.2514). You may then use the summary eviction procedure: the written notice to surrender must also name the court and tell the tenant that he or she may contest it by filing an affidavit before the court closes on the fifth judicial day after service, or ask the court to stay removal for up to 10 days (NRS 40.254(1)). If the tenant does not contest, no hearing is required; if the tenant does, the court holds an informal hearing, and if it finds a legal defense the case must go forward as a formal unlawful-detainer action instead (NRS 40.253(6); JCRCP 103, 105). A removal order directs the sheriff or constable to post it within 24 hours and remove the tenant between 24 and 36 hours after posting (NRS 40.253(5)(a)). If you win a drug-based case the tenant contested, you are entitled to reasonable attorney's fees for the hearing (NRS 40.254(3)), and if the court refuses summary relief on a drug ground, you may still end the tenancy with a periodic no-cause notice (NRS 40.253(6)). Notices must state the ground specifically and be served by a sheriff, constable, licensed process server or an attorney's agent (JCRCP 101; NRS 40.280(1)). Only the landlord or its agent brings the case: no Nevada statute lets a tenant organization, neighbor, district attorney or the Attorney General evict a tenant for drug or other criminal activity. Public involvement is indirect: prosecutors must notify owners of tenants' drug arrests and convictions, and local chronic-nuisance ordinances let public attorneys sue owners. In the Las Vegas and North Las Vegas justice courts, cases under these breach statutes are not eligible for the eviction diversion program. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Nevada's statutes set no fast-track procedure for security-deposit disputes and no special early-return rule. The only deadline is the general one: within 30 days after the tenancy ends, give the itemized written accounting and return the balance (NRS 118A.242(4)). You may return the deposit sooner, but you may not deduct a processing fee for doing so: you may keep only amounts reasonably necessary for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and reasonable cleaning (NRS 118A.242(4)). The same 30-day rule governs the deposit when a tenant lawfully ends the lease early because of your breach, a habitability or essential-services failure, your failure to deliver possession, an unlawful lockout or a fire or casualty; in those cases you must also return all prepaid rent (NRS 118A.350(3), 118A.355(3), 118A.370(1), 118A.390(3), 118A.400(2)). The statute's expedited court procedure is for unlawful lockouts and interruption of essential services, not deposits (NRS 118A.390(4)-(7)). A deposit dispute is an ordinary money claim; the justice court's small-claims procedure covers claims of up to $10,000 (NRS 73.010(1)), and a landlord who keeps the balance past 30 days risks the whole deposit plus up to the same amount again (NRS 118A.242(6)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Tenant Absences and the Abandonment Presumption
bodyText: No Nevada statute requires a tenant to tell you before an extended absence, so any such duty comes from the lease; the library's optional Notice of Extended Absence clause, which carries Nevada, supplies it. A tenant's written notice matters under Nevada law in one way: if you have no notice that the tenant has abandoned the unit, the tenant is presumed to have abandoned it after being absent for half a rental period (for example, about 15 days under monthly rent), unless the rent is current or the tenant has notified you in writing of an intended absence (NRS 118A.450). So a written absence notice keeps that presumption from arising, and you should not treat a tenant who gave one, or whose rent is current, as having abandoned the unit on absence alone. A separate abandonment-notice procedure applies when rent is unpaid and you reasonably believe the tenant has left. Nevada gives a landlord no extra right to enter during a tenant's absence: outside an emergency you need the tenant's consent on at least 24 hours' notice for an inspection, repairs or services, or a court order, the tenant's abandonment or surrender, or the remedial-work procedure (NRS 118A.330). Damages for a tenant's failure to give a notice the lease requires are ordinary lease damages (NRS 118A.420). Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Child Care Businesses in a Rental Home
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a landlord to allow a tenant to run a child care business in a rented home, and set no conditions (insurance, liability waivers, notice) on doing so, so the lease controls; the library's residential-use clause applies. A 2025 bill (AB 185) that would have limited association and lease restrictions on licensed child care in homes was vetoed and is not law; vetoed bills can be reconsidered in the 2027 session. The state child care rules regulate the provider, not the landlord: caring for five or more children for pay is a child care facility that the state licenses, and caring for up to four unrelated children for pay outside their parents' presence for at least 6 hours a day, 4 days a week and more than 3 weeks in a row is a small child care establishment that may register with the state. If you allow it, consider requiring proof of any license or registration and of liability insurance. A lease term may not release you from, or make the tenant indemnify you for, your own legal liability. Local zoning and business-license ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText: Nevada has no statute saying whether a tenant of rural land gets the hunting, fishing or trapping rights, so the lease decides (the library's optional clause reserves them to the landlord). Without a reservation, the tenant in possession matters: it is unlawful to hunt, fish in nonnavigable waters or trap on private land after a warning from the owner or occupant, or where signs forbid it without permission of the owner or occupant, so a tenant can both warn people off and give permission. A warning can be given by fencing, by orange paint or no-trespassing signs at the statutory intervals and corners, by cultivating the land, or by a direct demand. An owner, lessee or occupant who lets others hunt or fish owes them no duty to keep the land safe and is not liable for injuries caused by those people, except for willful or malicious failures, permission given for pay, or harm to people to whom a duty was otherwise owed. A lessee of private land, not only the owner, may apply for deer or antelope tags as compensation for wildlife damage. A lease of land used mainly for farming is outside the residential landlord-tenant law. Case law was not reviewed.

title: Surety Bonds and Other Deposit Alternatives
bodyText: Nevada regulates one alternative to a cash deposit: a surety bond. If you consent, a tenant may buy a surety bond instead of paying all or part of the security deposit, to secure unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear and cleaning; you don't have to accept one, and you may not require one (NRS 118A.242(2), (3)). The premium the tenant pays a qualified surety for the bond, or for a similar bond, guarantee or insurance coverage securing the tenant's obligations, is not a security deposit (NRS 118A.240(2)(b)), but the bond's value counts with any deposit and prepaid last month's rent toward the three-month limit (NRS 118A.242(1)). At the end of the tenancy you may claim against the bond only what is reasonably necessary for unpaid rent, tenant damage and cleaning, with the same itemized accounting within 30 days; if the tenant sends the surety a written dispute within 30 days after receiving the accounting, the surety may not report your claim to a credit reporting agency unless it gets a judgment (NRS 118A.242(4), (5)). No statute authorizes any other fee in lieu of a deposit. A fee you keep to cover unpaid rent, damage or cleaning is itself a security deposit, so it is capped and refundable except a reasonable cleaning charge (NRS 118A.240(1), 118A.242(8)). Because you may not require a bond, treat any bond or deposit-insurance product as the tenant's option, and keep an ordinary deposit available to every tenant. The library's Limit on Total Security clause already states the bond option.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: No Nevada statute expressly bars a fee for a service you don't provide, but several rules come close. Every mandatory periodic fee must be inside the single monthly rent figure the lease states, and you may not charge more periodic rent than that figure; the only add-on is a monthly utility fee equal to the cost of electric, natural gas or water service provided in the unit, where the utility can't contract with the tenant directly or the unit is on a master-metered water system, disclosed in the lease as the statute requires (NRS 118A.200(6)-(8)). A tenant harmed by a violation may sue for damages, equitable relief, costs and attorney's fees, plus $250 for each violation that involved deception (NRS 118A.405). The lease must list the services included and each required fee with its purpose (NRS 118A.200(3)(d), (e)). A fee for paying online may not exceed what the website or portal operator charges (NRS 118A.303(2)). You may not charge for repairs that are your habitability duty (NRS 118A.290(4)). If the lease or the law requires you to supply heat, air-conditioning, water, hot water, electricity, gas, a working door lock or another essential service and you willfully or negligently fail to, making the unit unfit, the tenant may after written notice buy the service and deduct the cost, recover damages, withhold rent without late fees or other charges, or move to comparable housing with the rent abated (NRS 118A.380). Cautious course: charge a service or amenity fee only for a service the tenant actually receives, describe it in the lease, and stop or credit it while the service is unavailable.

title: Which Fire and Building Codes Apply
bodyText: The State Fire Marshal enforces Nevada's fire-prevention laws and adopts regulations on fire safety and exits for, among others, all buildings occupied for sleeping purposes other than private residences, which includes apartment buildings (NRS 477.030(1)). By regulation the Fire Marshal has adopted the 2018 editions of the International Fire Code, International Building Code, International Existing Building Code, International Wildland-Urban Interface Code, Uniform Mechanical Code and Uniform Plumbing Code, with Nevada changes, plus listed NFPA standards (NAC 477.281, 477.283). These codes are privately published; you buy them from the International Code Council and IAPMO, though the NFPA standards are free to view online. Where these rules and a local code conflict, the more stringent applies, and local governments may adopt stricter codes (NAC 477.280). Who enforces depends on the county: in counties under 100,000 people it is the State Fire Marshal unless a local government has taken over by agreement; in counties of 100,000 or more (Clark and Washoe) and in a consolidated municipality it is the local government (NRS 477.030(1), NAC 477.052). In a county of 700,000 or more (Clark) the Fire Marshal's building-code rules do not apply at all while the county keeps its own fire, building and wildland codes at least as stringent as the latest International editions, updated within 2 years of each new edition (NRS 477.030(11)). Cities and counties also adopt their own building codes (NRS 278.580). A local ordinance requiring changes to existing structures for fire safety may not be less stringent than chapter 477, or more stringent without State Board of Examiners approval (NRS 477.110). Fire and building codes feed your habitability duty: a unit that violates a code concerning health, safety or fitness for habitation is not habitable (NRS 118A.050, 118A.290(1)), and knowingly violating chapter 477 or the Fire Marshal's regulations is a misdemeanor, each day a separate offense (NRS 477.250). Local codes and their editions were not reviewed.

title: When Sprinklers Are Required, and Keeping Them Working
bodyText: Nevada has no general sprinkler retrofit mandate for rental housing, but three rules can reach a rental. High-rise: the owner or operator of every apartment building or condominium with occupied floors more than 55 feet above the lowest ground a fire truck can reach must sprinkler each exit corridor as the State Fire Marshal's regulations require and, except in a condominium, put at least one sprinkler above each door opening into an exit corridor; the same statute requires elevator recall, floor numbers in stairwells and by elevators, an automatic HVAC shutoff and, except in condominiums, a posted evacuation route and a paging alarm in each sleeping room (NRS 477.150). Buildings over two stories: the Fire Marshal's Nevada amendments to the 2018 International Fire and Building Codes require an automatic sprinkler system throughout any building more than two stories high, in all occupancies except groups R-3 and U as those codes classify them (NAC 477.283); whether a given existing building must meet that depends on the codes' own applicability rules and the local code (not reviewed). Local governments may require sprinklers in new houses of 5,000 square feet or more, but in smaller new houses only after an independent cost-benefit finding or a finding that location would unreasonably delay firefighters; apartments, condominiums and townhouses sharing a wall with more than one other unit are outside that limit (NRS 278.586). Existing systems must be kept up: every automatic sprinkler system must be inspected quarterly, with an annual inspection by a licensed firm and records kept on site, and when a licensed firm reports a deficiency in writing the owner must correct it within 30 calendar days (NAC 477.335, 477.460). In a sprinklered one- or two-family dwelling the owner must test the system annually (NAC 477.540(2)). Local codes may require more (not reviewed).

title: Firearms: No State Limit on Lease Rules
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not limit a private landlord's lease terms or house rules about firearms. No statute protects a tenant's right to keep a firearm in a rental, and none protects a firearm locked in a vehicle in the parking area. The state firearm preemption statutes bar counties and cities from regulating the possession, carrying or storage of firearms; they are written to bind local governments, not private landlords (NRS 244.364, 268.418). A firearm term is therefore a matter for the lease, and a rule adopted after signing must meet the conditions for enforceable house rules (NRS 118A.320). Maliciously or wantonly discharging a firearm within a house or apartment is a crime (NRS 202.287), and in a manufactured-home park discharge of a weapon is a listed ground for terminating a tenancy (NRS 118B.200(1)(f)). Federal law and case law were not reviewed.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a landlord to tell a tenant that a rental is in a flood zone or has flooded, and they set no flood rider or flood-based termination right. The seller disclosure law covers sales of residential property, not leases (NRS 113.100(5), 113.130(1)). A licensed real estate agent acting for you in the lease must still disclose material and relevant facts it knows or should have known about the property (NRS 645.252(1)(a)). Flood damage that leaves the unit failing habitability standards is covered by your repair duty (NRS 118A.290(1)). Telling tenants about known flood risk in writing helps them decide on renter's insurance. Federal flood-insurance rules and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Foreign-Ownership Limit on Leasing
bodyText: Nevada has no foreign-adversary or alien land law. On the contrary, a statute provides that any nonresident alien, person or corporation may take, hold and enjoy real property or any interest in land in Nevada as fully and on the same terms as a resident citizen or domestic corporation. Whether or not a lease counts as an interest in land under that statute, no state statute bars or conditions a lease to a foreign national or a foreign-owned company, requires a lease to a nonresident alien to state that status, or puts any duty on you to find out whether a tenant is a foreign person. Nevada's fair housing law separately bars discrimination based on national origin or ancestry. Federal law was not reviewed for this row; case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Saving the Lease from Forfeiture
bodyText: Nevada gives a tenant several statutory chances to keep a lease after a default. Rent: a notice to pay or surrender must give at least seven judicial days to pay (in a short-term weekly tenancy, until noon of the fourth full day if you choose that notice), so full payment within the notice period ends that default (NRS 40.2512, 40.253(1)). Other breaches: within 5 days after service of a notice to perform or surrender, the tenant, a subtenant in actual occupation, a mortgagee of the lease or another person interested in its continuance may perform the broken covenant and so save the lease; no notice is needed if the breach cannot be performed afterwards (NRS 40.2516(1)). A tenant who cannot reasonably fix a breach can avoid termination by authorizing you to enter and fix it and paying the reasonable expenses or damages (NRS 118A.430(2)). After judgment: a judgment for an unlawful detainer after default in rent or breach of a covenant declares the lease forfeited (NRS 40.360(1)); but when the case is for unpaid rent and the lease has not expired by its terms, execution must wait 5 days after the judgment, and if the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the lease or another interested party pays the judgment and costs into court within that time, the judgment is satisfied and the tenant is restored to the lease (NRS 40.360(3)). The statute frames this 5-day right as following a trial and judgment; how it applies to a summary-eviction order has not been checked against case law, so the cautious course is to allow 5 days after any order for unpaid rent on an unexpired lease before seeking removal, or ask the court. No Nevada statute lets a tenant reinstate the lease later, for example by paying everything owed just before the sheriff or constable carries out the removal. No-cure grounds (drug violations, waste, an unlawful business, a qualifying nuisance or an unauthorized assignment or sublease) have no cure period (NRS 40.2514).
