A lease term that shortens the pay-or-quit or cure notice periods is void (NRS 40.252(1)), and a term waiving the landlord-tenant act's right to avoid termination by authorizing repairs is void as well (NRS 118A.220).

title: Which Edition of a Code Binds You
bodyText: Nevada borrows outside codes in three different ways, so the newest edition is not always the one that counts. Frozen in statute: in an apartment building or condominium of three or more stories with 15 or more units, fire alarms must comply with paragraph 2 of section 1202B of the 1979 Uniform Building Code (NRS 477.130); in an apartment building or condominium with occupied floors more than 55 feet up, elevator recall must meet the 1978 ANSI A17.1 standard with its 1981 amendments, and the HVAC system needs an automatic shutoff under the 1979 Uniform Mechanical Code and a smoke detector under the 1978 NFPA 90A (NRS 477.150). Frozen in regulation: the State Fire Marshal's rules adopt the 2018 International Fire, Building, Existing Building and Wildland-Urban Interface Codes, the 2018 Uniform Mechanical and Plumbing Codes and listed NFPA standards at named editions (NAC 477.281); sprinkler systems must meet the 2016 editions of NFPA 13, 13D and 13R (NAC 477.455(2)), though a sprinkler system in a one- or two-family dwelling is installed to the NFPA 13D and 13R edition in effect at the time of installation (NAC 477.483(4)). Moving with the latest edition: construction, alteration or change of use must comply with the Uniform Plumbing Code in the form most recently adopted by its publisher, subject to the State Public Works Board's review of amendments (NRS 444.350(1)); fire and smoke dampers and smoke control systems are inspected under the version of the International Fire Code most recently adopted by the local governing body (NRS 477.093, 477.097); and Clark County keeps its exemption from the Fire Marshal's building rules only by matching each new International code edition within 2 years (NRS 477.030(11)). Your habitability duty uses a fourth test: plumbing, heating and electrical systems must have conformed to applicable law when installed and be kept in good working order, so a later code edition does not by itself make an older system uninhabitable (NRS 118A.290(1)(b), (d), (e)). The model codes are privately published; local codes and their editions were not reviewed.

title: No Good-Cause Notice Requirement
bodyText: Nevada has no good-cause eviction law for houses and apartments, so there is no good-cause notice to give and no statement a lease must make about whether it is covered by one. A fixed-term lease ends at its expiration without notice, and a periodic tenancy can be ended without a stated reason on written notice of at least 7 days (week to week) or 30 days (other periodic tenancies), which must tell the tenant about the age-or-disability and shutdown-worker extension rights (NRS 40.250, 40.251). When you do rely on a breach, the notice must say what it is: a breach notice under the landlord-tenant act must specify the acts and omissions that make up the breach (NRS 118A.430(1)), and a summary-eviction notice must be specific about the ground it alleges (JCRCP 101). One federal exception: in a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, during the lease term you may end the tenancy only for a serious or repeated lease violation, a violation of law tied to the tenant's occupancy, or other good cause, and you must give the tenant a written notice specifying the grounds, at or before the start of the eviction case, and give the housing authority a copy of any eviction notice (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.310(a), (e)). During the initial term, "other good cause" can't be a business reason, owner use or the tenant's refusal of a new lease (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.310(d)(2)). Federally backed properties also face a separate 30-day notice to vacate. Retaliation, fair housing and domestic-violence protections still limit why you may end a tenancy. Mobile home parks have their own termination grounds. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: No Nevada statute authorizes or bars passing a local rental registration, licensing or inspection fee through to a residential tenant, and the statutes set up no statewide rental registration (local ordinances may impose such fees; not reviewed). The rent rules make a pass-through clause risky. The lease must list every required fee and its purpose (NRS 118A.200(3)(e)); every mandatory fee charged with the periodic rent must be inside the single all-in rent figure, and you may not charge more than that figure (NRS 118A.200(6)-(7)); a tenant can sue for damages, costs and attorney's fees plus $250 per deceptive violation (NRS 118A.405). A recurring government fee billed to the tenant on top of rent is the kind of charge those rules forbid. The safer course is to build expected government fees into the rent; if a new fee arises mid-term, a rent increase needs 60 days' written notice and, in a fixed-term lease, a lease provision that allows it (NRS 118A.300). Fines and abatement costs that the tenant, a household member or a guest caused are a different matter and may be reimbursed under a lease clause that excludes conditions you are responsible for. In a manufactured-home park, no fee, surcharge or rent increase may recover more than the cost of a governmentally mandated service or tax you actually paid (NRS 118B.140(1)(b)(9)).

title: Guarantors and Lease Renewals
bodyText: Nevada has no statute on whether a guarantor stays liable when a lease is renewed, extended or continues month to month, and none that requires a guaranty to state a maximum or an end date. A guaranty is a promise to answer for another person's debt, so it must be in writing and signed by the guarantor (NRS 111.220(2)). Whether a renewal, an extension or a rent increase releases a guarantor who did not agree to it is a question for case law, which was not reviewed, so the guaranty should say expressly whether it covers renewals, extensions, a month-to-month holdover (which continues on the same lease terms unless otherwise agreed, NRS 118A.470) and rent changes made under the lease. The deposit cap counts payments and surety bonds (NRS 118A.240, 118A.242(1)): a guarantor's promise is neither, but money a guarantor pays you to secure rent, damage or cleaning is a security deposit within the 3-month cap. Local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Guests Have No Separate Statutory Rights
bodyText: Nevada's landlord-tenant act gives a tenant's guests no rights of their own and does not limit how a lease regulates guests, so the lease and your house rules decide. The tenant answers for guests: the tenant must require persons on the premises with the tenant's consent not to disturb neighbors (NRS 118A.310(1)(g)), and you may charge the tenant for repairs of a condition a guest caused deliberately or negligently (NRS 118A.290(5)). A guest rule adopted as a house rule must meet the conditions for enforceable rules, including applying to all tenants fairly (NRS 118A.320). Two settings have special rules. In a homeowners' or condominium association, the association may not charge a fee for a tenant's visitor or invitee, or for a service provider, to enter the community (NRS 116.2111(2)(b)). In a manufactured-home park, the landlord may not prohibit guests, though it may require registration within 48 hours, and may not charge a fee for a guest who stays no more than 60 days in a calendar year (NRS 118B.150(1)(h)-(i)). Local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: How Serious a Defect Must Be for Each Tenant Remedy
bodyText: Nevada sets a different threshold for each tenant remedy, and none of them defines the word it uses. A unit is not habitable if it violates housing or health codes concerning health, safety, sanitation or fitness for habitation, or if it substantially lacks one of the listed features, such as weatherproofing, working plumbing, heat or electrical service, or floors, stairways and railings in good repair (NRS 118A.290(1)). Termination, damages, court relief and rent withholding under the habitability remedy require a material failure that you do not fix, or make a reasonable effort to fix, within 14 days after the tenant's written notice (NRS 118A.355(1)). The essential-services remedies (buying the service and deducting it, damages, withholding, or substitute housing) require a willful or negligent failure to supply heat, air-conditioning, water, hot water, electricity, gas, a working door lock or another essential item or service that makes the premises unfit for habitation (NRS 118A.380(1)). Two remedies carry no seriousness test in their text: the tenant may act on any failure to comply with the rental agreement that you leave unremedied for 14 days after written notice (NRS 118A.350(1)), and may repair and deduct for a lease or habitability failure costing less than $100 or one month's rent, whichever is greater (NRS 118A.360(1)). Fire or casualty damage gives the tenant (and you) a way out only if it substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit (NRS 118A.400(1)). Because no statute defines "material" or "substantially", treat any code violation affecting health or safety, and any loss of a listed feature or essential service, as one that counts. Case law was not reviewed.

title: What a Lease Can Change About Habitability
bodyText: Only two parts of Nevada's habitability law can be changed by agreement, and neither lowers the standard. Garbage and rubbish: you must arrange for removal from the premises unless the parties provide otherwise by written agreement, but you must still supply an adequate number of appropriate receptacles in clean condition and good repair at the start of the tenancy (NRS 118A.290(1)(f)). Tenant work: you and the tenant may agree that the tenant does specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling, but only in good faith and without reducing your duties to other tenants; it is not in good faith if you owed the work and the tenant agreed because you refused to do it (NRS 118A.290(2), (3)). Some duties depend on what you supply: ventilation, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, must be kept in good repair if you supply them or are required to (NRS 118A.290(1)(i)), and the hot-and-cold water supply may be under the control of either the tenant or you (NRS 118A.290(1)(c)). Nothing else in the habitability list can be waived or modified (NRS 118A.220(1)(a)), and you may not charge the tenant for your habitability work (NRS 118A.290(4)). The library offers an optional Garbage and Rubbish Removal clause and the Tenant-Performed Repairs clause for these two openings.

title: No Presumption of a Habitability Breach
bodyText: Nevada's statutes create no presumption that you breached the habitability duty, in an eviction or anywhere else, and none that you complied with it; the tenant who claims a failure must prove it, usually after giving you written notice (NRS 118A.355). Two related rules work in a similar way. First, if there is no written lease, the law presumes (rebuttably) that maintenance and waste removal services are provided without charge to the tenant and that, other than normal wear, the premises will be returned in the same condition as when the tenancy began (NRS 118A.200(5)). Second, written notice from a government agency authorized to inspect for building, housing or health code violations stands in for the tenant's notice: if you received one, the tenant may recover damages without giving you notice, and may withhold rent if you also fail to fix the condition, or try in good faith to, within the time the agency's notice allows; the same damages rule applies if you admit to the court that you knew of the condition (NRS 118A.355(4)). Under the act you have notice of a fact you actually know, were notified of, or reasonably should know from all the circumstances (NRS 118A.190(1)). A tenant who withholds rent for a habitability failure has a defense to eviction only after depositing the withheld rent in the court's escrow account (NRS 118A.355(5)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Required Habitability Statement in the Lease
bodyText: Nevada does not require your lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation. The duty applies whatever the lease says: at the start of the term you must deliver possession in compliance with the rental agreement and in a habitable condition, and you must keep the unit habitable at all times during the tenancy (NRS 118A.280, 118A.290(1)). The subjects every written lease must cover (NRS 118A.200(3)) do not include a fitness statement, but the lease must tell the tenant how to report a violation of a building, safety or health code or regulation to the appropriate authorities (NRS 118A.200(3)(m)). A lease sentence saying the tenant takes the unit as is, or that you make no promise about its condition, cannot remove these duties: a term by which the tenant waives rights or remedies under Nevada's landlord-tenant act is void, and the tenant may recover actual damages caused by including it (NRS 118A.220). A promise in the lease that goes beyond the statute becomes part of the rental agreement, which the tenant can enforce with the remedies for breach of the rental agreement (NRS 118A.350). A 2025 bill revising the habitability rules (AB 223) was vetoed and is not law. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Habitability Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A lease cannot waive the habitability requirements. You must keep the unit habitable at all times during the tenancy (NRS 118A.290(1)), and a term that makes the tenant give up that right, or the repair, rent-withholding and essential-service remedies that enforce it (NRS 118A.350 to 118A.380), is void; the tenant may recover any actual damages the term caused (NRS 118A.220). The law lets the parties move only who does some of the work, never the standard itself: a written agreement may make the tenant responsible for removing garbage and rubbish, though you must still supply clean receptacles in good repair at move-in; and the tenant may agree to do specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling only if the agreement is made in good faith and does not reduce your duties to other tenants. It is not in good faith if you owed the work and the tenant agreed because you refused to do it (NRS 118A.290(1)(f), (2), (3)). You may not charge the tenant for repairs that are your habitability duty, including a home-warranty deductible or copay, unless the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the condition deliberately or negligently (NRS 118A.290(4), (5)). Nevada has no statute letting a tenant accept listed defects in exchange for lower rent, and no separate-document rule for heat. A 2025 habitability bill (AB 223) was vetoed and is not law. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Contamination and Environmental Covenants
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a landlord to disclose environmental contamination to a tenant or to write recorded cleanup restrictions into a lease. Under the Uniform Environmental Covenants Act, a recorded environmental covenant runs with the land (NRS 445D.140(1)). When one is created, a copy must go to each person then in possession of the property, among others (NRS 445D.160(1)(c)), and the covenant itself may set notice requirements that apply when a specified interest in the property is transferred (NRS 445D.130(2)(a)). If your property is subject to a covenant, read it before leasing: it may require notice to a new tenant, and its activity and use limitations bind the property's use. One contamination fact is treated differently: a former methamphetamine lab is left out of the rule that makes certain facts immaterial to a lease or rental unless it has been remediated by a certified or licensed entity or deemed safe for habitation by the board of health (NRS 40.770(1)(b), (6)), and letting it be used for any purpose before then makes it a public nuisance (NRS 202.450(4)). Do not rent such a property until it has been remediated and deemed safe. Federal law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Heat: Working Facilities, No Temperature Number
bodyText: Heat is part of your habitability duty: the unit is not habitable if it substantially lacks adequate heating facilities that met the law when installed and are kept in good working order (NRS 118A.290(1)(d)). Nevada's statutes set no minimum indoor temperature and no heating season for rentals. If the lease or the law requires you to supply heat and you willfully or negligently fail to, making the unit unfit for habitation, the tenant's written notice gives you 48 hours (not counting weekends and legal holidays) to fix it or use best efforts; after that the tenant may buy reasonable amounts of heat and deduct the cost, recover damages, withhold rent if current when the notice was given, or move to comparable housing with rent abated; none of these remedies applies if the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the failure deliberately or negligently (NRS 118A.380). Willfully interrupting heat, or letting it be interrupted, exposes you to the lockout remedies, including up to $2,500 set by the court (NRS 118A.390). There is no special rule for shifting heat to the tenant: the lease may make the tenant responsible for paying the gas or electric bill (NRS 118A.200(3)(j)), but keeping the heating equipment working stays your duty, and you may not charge the tenant for that work unless the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the problem deliberately or negligently (NRS 118A.290(4), (5)). The tenant must use the heating system in a reasonable manner (NRS 118A.310(1)(e)). The only numeric room-temperature rule found (68 to 80 degrees) is a health regulation for hotels and motels serving the transient public (NAC 447.150), not a residential lease. Local codes may set temperatures (not reviewed).

title: Renting in a Homeowners' or Condominium Association
bodyText: If the rental is in a Nevada common-interest community (a homeowners' or condominium association), the association's rules reach your tenant directly. Fines: if the governing documents allow, the executive board may fine a tenant, or a tenant's guest, for violating the governing documents, but only after written notice of the rule at least 30 days before the violation, written notice of the violation and a hearing; a fine for a violation that does not threaten health, safety or welfare is capped at $100 per violation and $1,000 per hearing, a tenant is fined for a guest's violation only if the tenant took part, had prior notice or failed to stop it, and an uncured violation can draw continuing fines. The association may also assess against your unit the cost of damage caused by a tenant's willful misconduct or gross negligence. Limits that protect your tenant: the association may not charge a fee for a tenant's visitors or service providers to enter, and a planned-community association may interrupt a tenant's utility service only for nonpayment of utility charges, after at least 10 days' written notice. Rental restrictions: since July 1, 2026, if the declaration authorizes it, an association may adopt rules restricting or prohibiting rentals to the extent reasonably related to lender or insurer underwriting requirements, and a declaration amendment restricting leasing for those reasons is not limited to later buyers, although other use restrictions added by amendment still do not bind existing owners; an owner barred by a rental cap may seek a hardship waiver. The 2025 changes removed the former statutory limits on association lease approval, tenant registration information and registration fees. We found no Nevada statute capping a lease-approval fee, regulating an association-held tenant deposit, letting an association collect rent from your tenant when you are behind, or requiring you to give the tenant the governing documents (the library's association clause makes the tenant follow them, so give a copy). A 2025 bill on child care in homes (AB 185) was vetoed and is not law.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not regulate a holding deposit taken before the lease is signed: there is no cap, no deadline for refunding it if no lease results, and no rule on whether you may keep it if the applicant backs out. Put the terms in writing, signed by both of you, before you take the money: the amount, what it is for, how long you will hold the unit, whether it is applied to the first month's rent or the security deposit if a lease is signed, and when it is refunded. Three statutory rules still reach it. If the money is to be used to cover unpaid rent, damage or cleaning (for example, it becomes part of the deposit once the lease is signed), it is a security deposit, counts toward the three-months'-rent limit on all security and can't be made nonrefundable (NRS 118A.240, 118A.242(1), (8)). If you sign the lease but then fail to deliver possession, a tenant who ends the agreement on 5 days' written notice gets back all prepaid rent, any recoverable deposit and any payment, deposit, fee or charge paid to secure the signing of the rental agreement (NRS 118A.370(1)). An application, credit-report or background-check fee is separate: refund it if you rent to someone else without doing the work it paid for, and charge none for a minor in the applicant's household (NRS 118A.306). On request, give a prospective tenant a copy of the lease they would sign (NRS 118A.235). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Holdover Rent and Damages
bodyText: No Nevada statute sets or caps a holdover rate that a lease may charge. If a tenant stays after the lease ends without your consent, you may sue for possession and rent and recover your actual damages (NRS 118A.470); in an unlawful-detainer judgment the court must award the rent found due plus three times the damages it assesses for the unlawful detainer (NRS 40.250, 40.360(2)). That multiplier is a court award, not a daily figure the lease can fix, and no statute authorizes a lease-set per-day holdover charge, so rely on actual damages, including the fair rental value of the time the tenant stays, rather than a stipulated rate. If you consent to the tenant staying, the tenancy becomes week to week (weekly rent) or month to month on the same terms as the lease unless you have specifically agreed otherwise (NRS 118A.470). A different rent for a consented holdover must be specifically agreed and stated as a single all-in figure (NRS 118A.200(6)); whether a holdover rent fixed in the original lease is a rent increase needing 60 days' written notice (NRS 118A.300) is not settled, so give that notice. Manufactured-home parks have their own holding-over rules (NRS 118B.190). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Home Businesses: No State Rule
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not give a tenant a right to run a business from a rented home, and they do not limit a lease term that restricts one, so the lease decides. A residential-use clause can bar commercial use or allow it on stated conditions. If you adopt a home-business rule after the lease is signed, it must meet the conditions for enforceable house rules, and a rule that materially changes the bargain needs the tenant's written consent or 30 days' notice (NRS 118A.320). A tenant who carries on an unlawful business on the premises can be removed after a 3-day notice to surrender, with no chance to cure (NRS 40.2514(3)). Zoning, business-license and home-occupation rules are local and were not reviewed. A 2025 bill on child care in homes (AB 185) was vetoed; it is not law, though the Legislature could take it up again in 2027.

title: No Lease Waiver of Homestead or Exemptions
bodyText: Nevada's statutes give a landlord no way to have a tenant waive the homestead exemption or the exemptions from execution in the lease, and the library offers no such clause. The homestead exemption protects an owner's equity, up to $605,000, in land with a dwelling, in a mobile home (even on rented land) or in a condominium or other common-interest unit; an ordinary rented house or apartment is not a homestead, so a tenant has nothing to waive, and the only waiver the chapter describes is one signed by all holders of allodial title for a specific obligation. The personal-property exemptions (for example household goods up to $12,000 and up to $10,000 of other property) protect a tenant against collection of a judgment, and a judgment creditor may not require a judgment debtor to waive any exemption the debtor is entitled to claim. A security deposit is exempt from other creditors but not from the landlord enforcing the lease. A lien on a tenant's household goods for rent is also unenforceable unless created by attachment or garnishment. To collect unpaid rent, use the deposit as the law allows and then a court judgment. Case law was not reviewed.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code Orders
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a landlord to disclose open code-violation, inspection or condemnation orders to a prospective tenant. For a multifamily rental property (two or more rental units on a parcel), a county or city order to repair or abate a condition that substantially endangers health and safety must be posted on the property and mailed to each affected resident (NRS 244.36904(2)(b), 268.4283(2)(b)). Condemnation of the dwelling unit is cause for ending the tenancy (NRS 118A.060(4)). A unit that violates housing or health codes on health, safety, sanitation or fitness for habitation is not habitable (NRS 118A.290(1)), so tell a prospective tenant about an open order before signing. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: What Happens If You Inspect Without Notice
bodyText: Nevada sets no fixed penalty for entering or inspecting without the required notice; the tenant's remedies are actual. Outside an emergency you must give at least 24 hours' notice of intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times during normal business hours, unless the tenant expressly agrees to shorter notice or other hours for that particular entry (NRS 118A.330(3)). If you enter unlawfully, enter lawfully but in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated demands for entry that harass the tenant, the tenant may get an injunction against it happening again or terminate the lease, and in either case recover actual damages (NRS 118A.500(2)). An entry that turns into excluding the tenant or interrupting an essential service carries the separate lockout remedies, including up to $2,500 set by the court (NRS 118A.390). Nevada has no required notice of a move-out inspection; what matters for the deposit is the itemized accounting and refund within 30 days after the tenancy ends, and missing it makes you liable for the whole deposit plus up to the same amount again (NRS 118A.242(4), (6)).

title: Jury Waivers in a Nevada Lease
bodyText: No Nevada statute bans or authorizes a jury-trial waiver in a residential lease. The Nevada Constitution keeps the right to a jury and lets the parties waive it in civil cases in the manner prescribed by law (Nev. Const. art. 1, § 3). In an eviction case, a fact issue goes to a jury only if a party properly demands one under the court rules (NRS 40.310). In justice court, a party who does not file and serve a timely demand waives a jury, and a demanded jury can be dropped by stipulation (JCRCP 38(d), 39(a)). So a jury is not the default, and a lease waiver would mainly stop the tenant from demanding one. The landlord-tenant act's ban on waivers covers rights under that act (NRS 118A.220(1)(a)); the jury right comes from the Constitution and NRS 40.310 instead, so the act does not clearly reach it. A separate law voids jury waivers in standard-form consumer contracts unless the consumer agrees to arbitration or similar dispute resolution (NRS 97B.120(3)), but its definition covers leases of goods or services, which does not clearly include a lease of a home. Whether a court would enforce a jury waiver signed before any dispute is a case-law question not reviewed here. The library offers no jury-waiver clause for Nevada.

title: Using a Lease with an Unlawful Term
bodyText: Nevada sets no extra penalty for knowingly using a lease that contains a prohibited term. A prohibited term is void, and the tenant may recover any actual damages caused by including it, whether or not you knew it was unlawful (NRS 118A.220(2)). It is unlawful to use a written lease that does not meet the required-contents and single-rent-figure rules, and a contravening term is void (NRS 118A.200(9)). For a violation of the single-rent-figure rules the tenant may sue for damages, equitable relief, costs and attorney's fees, and the court must add $250 for each violation that involved deception (NRS 118A.405). A term calling a deposit nonrefundable, other than a reasonable cleaning charge, is void (NRS 118A.242(8)), and keeping a deposit balance past 30 days exposes you to the whole deposit plus up to the same amount again, with the court weighing your good faith (NRS 118A.242(6), (7)). Use the library's Nevada clauses as written and avoid adding your own one-sided terms.

title: What a Tenant Can Do When You Breach
bodyText: Nevada gives the tenant a separate remedy for each kind of landlord breach. Breach of the lease: the tenant gives written notice describing the breach and stating that the lease will end; if you do not fix a remediable breach, or make a reasonable effort to, within 14 days, the tenant may end the lease immediately, recover actual damages or ask the court for other relief, and you must return prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit if it ends (NRS 118A.350). Habitability failures, small repairs and essential services (heat, water, power, a working lock) have their own notice periods and remedies, including rent withholding, repair and deduct, and buying the service or substitute housing (NRS 118A.355, 118A.360, 118A.380). Failing to deliver possession abates rent and lets the tenant end the lease on 5 days' written notice or sue for possession (NRS 118A.370). A lockout or willful interruption of an essential service allows expedited court relief, damages and up to $2,500 (NRS 118A.390). Unlawful or harassing entry allows an injunction or termination plus damages (NRS 118A.500). Failing to disclose the manager and owner after the tenant asks costs actual damages or $25, whichever is greater (NRS 118A.410). A rent figure that leaves out mandatory fees can bring damages, equitable relief, the tenant's costs and attorney's fees, and $250 for each violation involving deception (NRS 118A.405). A void lease term lets the tenant recover the actual damages it caused (NRS 118A.220(2)). For a condition the tenant, a household member or a guest caused deliberately or negligently, the tenant may not end the lease for breach (NRS 118A.350(2)) and has none of the habitability, repair-and-deduct or essential-service remedies (NRS 118A.355(2)(a), 118A.360(3), 118A.380(5)); the habitability remedies are also barred if the tenant's refusal of lawful access kept you from fixing the problem within 14 days (NRS 118A.355(2)(b)). These remedies cannot be waived in the lease (NRS 118A.220(1)(a)).

title: No State Liability-Insurance Mandate for Landlords
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, and there is no statewide landlord registration that asks for proof of insurance. Insurance is a business choice, and a lender, an association or a property management agreement may require it. Two related rules: the lease may not shift your own legal liability to the tenant (no release, limit or indemnity for liability based on your or your agents' acts or omissions), so insurance, not the lease, is the way to cover that risk; and you may not charge the tenant the deductible or copayment under a home-warranty policy or service contract for a repair that is your duty, unless the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a household member or a person on the premises with the tenant’s consent. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed); case law was not reviewed.

title: Landlord Registration and Business Licenses
bodyText: Nevada has no statewide registry of residential landlords or rental units, and no state statute makes registration a condition of renting or of getting an eviction order. What the state does require is a state business license from the Secretary of State before conducting a business in Nevada. A natural person whose only business is renting four or fewer dwelling units to others is not a business for this purpose and needs no state business license; an LLC, corporation or other entity that owns rentals, or an individual with five or more units who reports the income on a federal Schedule E or C, generally does. Failing to get the license before doing business brings a $100 penalty plus the fee for each year, and a willful failure can bring a fine of $1,000 to $10,000. The state license is in addition to any local business license. Two other state filings can apply. Anyone doing business under an assumed or fictitious name different from each owner's legal name must file a certificate with the county clerk of each county where the business is conducted, and cannot bring an eviction on that business unless it was filed first; doing business without it is a misdemeanor (NRS 602.010(1), 602.070, 602.090). And an out-of-state LLC or corporation must register with the Secretary of State before doing business here, and cannot commence or maintain a suit until it does (NRS 86.544(1), 86.548(2); NRS 80.010(1), 80.055(2)). Short-term rentals are different: in a county of 700,000 or more people, and in its cities of 25,000 or more, anyone renting a residential unit or room for transient lodging must hold a county or city authorization and a state business license, display both in the unit and put both numbers in every listing. Counties and cities may also license businesses and may run their own rental programs; local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed). Separately, you must disclose in writing the names and addresses of the owner and of anyone authorized to manage the premises.

title: Landlord Remedies When a Tenant Defaults
bodyText: When a tenant breaks the lease or the landlord-tenant act, Nevada gives you money remedies and possession remedies, and you can pursue them together. Without ending the tenancy you may sue for damages and ask for an injunction (NRS 118A.420); for a fixable failure to keep the unit clean or undamaged you may give 14 days' written notice, then have the work done and bill it as rent (NRS 118A.440). To end the tenancy for a breach, give written notice specifying the breach; if the tenant does not adequately fix a fixable breach, or use best efforts to, within 5 days after receiving the notice, or it can't be fixed, you may terminate (NRS 118A.430). Possession comes only through the courts. Summary eviction is the fast route, but it decides possession: the court issues a removal or nonadmittance order (NRS 40.253(6), 40.254). A formal unlawful-detainer action lets the complaint claim damages and the rent due as well; the judgment restores the premises, declares the lease forfeited for a rent or covenant default, and awards the rent plus three times the damages assessed (NRS 40.300(1), 40.360(1)-(2)). A tenant who holds over without consent owes rent and your actual damages (NRS 118A.470). If the tenant abandons, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rent; the former tenant owes your actual damages, but only up to when you had reason to believe the unit was abandoned if you make no effort (NRS 118.175). No Nevada statute addresses rent acceleration clauses, so whether a lease can make all future rent due at once is a case-law question not reviewed here; the re-renting duty limits what you can recover after abandonment in any event. Attorney's fees are recoverable only under a prevailing-party lease term, never a one-way term (NRS 118A.220(1)(c)), or by statute in a contested drug eviction (NRS 40.254(3)). Money-only claims up to $10,000 can go to small claims, and justice court hears possession cases with damages up to $15,000 (NRS 73.010, 4.370(1)(g)).

title: Late Fee Caps by Type of Tenancy
bodyText: Nevada caps late fees by statute, with a different cap for each kind of tenancy. Dwelling leases under chapter 118A: the late fee must be reasonable and set forth in the lease, may not exceed 5% of the periodic rent, may not be charged until at least 3 calendar days after rent is due in a tenancy longer than week to week, and its maximum may not be increased because of an earlier late fee (NRS 118A.210(4)). No late fee may be charged on rent a tenant lawfully withholds for a habitability or essential-services failure (NRS 118A.355(1)(d), 118A.380(1)(c)). Manufactured-home-park lot rentals under chapter 118B: no late fee within 4 days after the rent is due, and no more than $5 for each day, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, that the payment is overdue, starting the day after it was due; no late fee at all on rent from a federal, tribal or state worker or household member during a shutdown; and a late charge on park utility bills may not exceed what the utility would charge for the same delinquency (NRS 118B.140(1)(b)(6)-(7); NAC 704.988). Commercial premises (chapter 118C) have no comparable cap. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Police, Crime and Your Lease
bodyText: Nevada has no crime-free lease statute and no general duty for landlords to cooperate with police investigations. Several rules do bear on it. You may not evict, fine or otherwise punish a tenant based solely on the tenant or someone in the unit calling police, fire or medical help with a reasonable belief that it was needed or that a crime may have occurred, however many earlier calls there were, but you may act on a nuisance or lease breach an officer discovers or reports. You may not retaliate against a tenant who complained in good faith to a law enforcement agency about a violation of the landlord-tenant law or of a criminal statute. A place where controlled substances are unlawfully sold, kept, made or used is a public nuisance, and anyone who lets or permits a building to be used knowing it is being used to maintain a nuisance commits a misdemeanor; unlawful drug activity on the premises (other than simple possession) is also a no-cure eviction ground. One reporting duty binds you as any person: if you know or have reasonable cause to believe that someone has committed a violent or sexual offense against a child 12 or younger, you must report it to a law enforcement agency as soon as reasonably practicable and within 24 hours, and a knowing and willful failure is a misdemeanor; close relatives of the child or offender, and anyone whom reporting would put in imminent danger, are exempt (NRS 202.876, 202.882, 202.888). Nevada's child-abuse and elder-abuse reporting duties otherwise bind listed professions only; anyone else may report (NRS 432B.220(4), (5); NRS 200.5093(4), (5)). Your right to enter is limited to the purposes, notice and exceptions in the access statute, which do not include letting police in; police entry otherwise depends on the tenant's consent or other lawful authority. In a federal voucher tenancy, the lease must make drug-related and certain other criminal activity grounds for termination. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No State Lead-Safe Certificate
bodyText: Nevada has no state lead-safe certificate, inspection certificate or registration that must be obtained for a rental or attached to a lease. For housing built before 1978, follow the federal disclosure: before the tenant is obligated under the lease, give the EPA lead hazard pamphlet and disclose any known lead-based paint or hazards and any available reports (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 4852d(a)(1)), and include in the lease or an attachment the Lead Warning Statement, your disclosure, a list of records, the tenant's acknowledgment, an agent's statement if an agent acts for you, and dated signatures (FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. § 745.113(b)). The federal rule covers target housing: housing built before 1978, except housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities and 0-bedroom units such as studios and single-room rentals; the EPA and HUD definitions place their exception for a child under 6 differently, so disclose for any such unit where a child under 6 lives or is expected to (FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. § 745.103; 24 C.F.R. § 35.86). Exempt leases are those of housing a certified inspector has found lead-based paint free, short-term leases of 100 days or less with no possible renewal or extension, and renewals where everything was disclosed before and you have no new information (FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. § 745.101(b)-(d); 24 C.F.R. § 35.82). A certificate is never required, but a certified inspector's finding that the housing is lead-based paint free removes the lease from the disclosure rule. You need not test or reduce hazards to comply (FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. § 745.107(a)). Keep the signed disclosure for at least 3 years from the start of the lease (FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. § 745.113(c)(1)).

title: No State Lead Notices
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead-based paint rules, Nevada law requires no state lead notice, certificate, pamphlet or packet with a lease, and sets no state lead-hazard rule for rentals. For housing built before 1978, use the federal disclosure in the lease: the Lead Warning Statement, your disclosure of known lead-based paint and hazards, the list of available records, the tenant's acknowledgment of the EPA pamphlet, any agent's statement and dated signatures (FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. § 745.113(b)). The federal rule covers target housing: housing built before 1978, except housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities and 0-bedroom units such as studios and single-room rentals; the EPA and HUD definitions place their exception for a child under 6 differently, so disclose for any such unit where a child under 6 lives or is expected to (FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. § 745.103; 24 C.F.R. § 35.86). Exempt leases are those of housing a certified inspector has found lead-based paint free, short-term leases of 100 days or less with no possible renewal or extension, and renewals where everything was disclosed before and you have no new information (FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. § 745.101(b)-(d); 24 C.F.R. § 35.82). A separate federal notice applies to renovation: within 60 days before a renovation firm works in a pre-1978 rental unit, it must give the pamphlet to you and to an adult occupant of the unit (FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. § 745.84(a)), and for common-area work in multi-unit housing it must notify each affected unit in writing or post signs (FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. § 745.84(b)). Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: You must give the tenant one copy of any written lease, free of cost, at the time it is signed, and give additional copies within a reasonable time when the tenant asks; you may charge a reasonable fee for the additional copies (NRS 118A.200(2)). On request, you or your agent must also give a prospective tenant a copy of the written lease they would be subject to (NRS 118A.235, in force since October 1, 2025). Nevada's statutes do not say that failing to deliver a copy makes the lease unenforceable or gives the tenant a defense, but using a lease that does not conform to the lease statute is unlawful (NRS 118A.200(9)), so deliver the copy and keep proof. A real estate licensee who handles the lease should make sure each party and the broker have a copy of the signed agreement; the Real Estate Commission weighs that in licensee discipline (NAC 645.605(7)).

title: No Initials Requirement for Lease Clauses
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a tenant to initial any clause of a residential lease. A few placement and type-size rules do apply. A single-family lease (up to four units) not signed by a licensed property manager must carry the occupancy-presumption disclosure at the top of the first page in type at least twice the size of any other type in the lease (NRS 118A.200(4)). A utility charge kept outside the single rent figure needs an asterisk or other symbol at least half the size of the rent figure, tied to a statement on the same page (NRS 118A.200(8)). An online-portal payment fee must be separately identified in the lease (NRS 118A.303(2)(b)). An arbitration clause is void unless the lease includes a specific authorization showing the tenant affirmatively agreed to it (NRS 597.995). Initials beside an important clause are still useful evidence that the tenant saw it, but they are optional and cannot save a term the law forbids. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: Nevada does not require a residential lease to be recorded or registered, and an unrecorded lease is fully binding between you and the tenant (NRS 111.315). A written lease creates an interest in land, so it can be recorded with the county recorder if it is acknowledged as the recording statutes require; once recorded, it gives everyone, including later buyers and lenders, notice of its contents (NRS 111.010(1), 111.315, 111.320). An unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good-faith buyer for value who records first (NRS 111.325); whether a tenant's possession alone gives such a buyer notice of the lease is a question for case law, which was not reviewed. Recording is unusual for an ordinary residential lease and does not change any right or duty under the landlord-tenant act.

title: Long Leases: Signatures and Approvals
bodyText: Nevada sets no maximum term for a private residential lease. A lease for more than one year must be in a writing signed by you or your authorized agent (NRS 111.210). Some owners need more. If the property is community property of a married owner, neither spouse may sell, convey or encumber community real property unless both sign and acknowledge the instrument (NRS 123.230(3)); no statute says whether a lease counts, so for a long lease of community real property the cautious course is to have both spouses sign and acknowledge it. A personal representative may lease estate property but must give notice of the proposed action before signing a lease of real property for more than one year, counting any extension option as if it were exercised (NRS 143.530(3)). A guardian must get a court order before leasing a protected person's property (NRS 159.113(1)(f), 159.161). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Leases: No Parity Rule
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require the same terms or rent for month-to-month and fixed-term tenants, and they do not cap a month-to-month premium. You may price and draft the two kinds of tenancy differently, within the general rules: a house rule binds a tenant only if, among other things, it applies to all tenants in the premises fairly (NRS 118A.320(1)(c)); a rent increase needs written notice at least 60 days ahead, or 30 days for a periodic tenancy of less than a month (NRS 118A.300); and fees must be built into the single rent figure (NRS 118A.200(6)). Raising rent for tenants who complained or organized is retaliation unless the increase applies uniformly to all tenants or another statutory exception applies (NRS 118A.510). Manufactured-home-park lots have their own same-rent rule (NRS 118B.150(1)(a)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Type Size and Placement Rules
bodyText: Nevada sets no minimum type size for a residential lease as a whole, and no rule that small print is unenforceable. Two layout rules apply to particular text: where required, the single-family occupancy disclosure goes at the top of the first page in a font at least twice as large as any other font in the lease (NRS 118A.200(4)); and if a utility is billed outside the single rent figure, the asterisk or other symbol on that figure must be at least half its font size and must point to a statement on the same page (NRS 118A.200(8)). Using a lease that does not meet these rules is unlawful (NRS 118A.200(9)). Other contracts, such as consumer vehicle leases and storage-unit rental agreements, have their own type-size rules.

title: Deadlines for Suing a Tenant
bodyText: Nevada's general statute of limitations sets how long you have to sue a tenant or former tenant for money. A claim on a written lease, such as unpaid rent or damage the lease makes the tenant pay for, must be brought within 6 years; a claim under an oral rental agreement within 4 years (NRS 11.190(1)(b), (2)(c)). A claim based on a liability created by statute, other than a penalty, has 3 years, as does a claim for waste or trespass to the property, for injuring or detaining personal property, or for fraud (counted from discovery of the fraud) (NRS 11.190(3)). A claim for a statutory penalty has 2 years unless the statute sets another period, and personal-injury claims have 2 years (NRS 11.190(4)). The time runs from the last transaction, item charged or credit given, and if the tenant makes a payment on an existing debt after it falls due, the period restarts from that payment; but a payment or acknowledgment after the period has expired does not revive the claim (NRS 11.200). Other promises or acknowledgments extend the time only if in a writing signed by the tenant (NRS 11.390). Time the tenant spends outside Nevada after the claim arises does not count (NRS 11.300). Once you have a justice-court judgment, execution may issue for 6 years after it is entered (NRS 70.010(1)). The same periods generally limit a tenant's claims against you. No Nevada statute addresses whether a lease may shorten these periods; that is a case-law question not reviewed here, and the library offers no clause doing so.

title: Pre-Set Damages in a Lease
bodyText: Nevada has no statute on liquidated (pre-set) damages in a residential lease; the statutes that use the term deal with sales of goods, leases of goods, public contracts and other subjects, not dwellings. Two lease amounts are governed by statute instead: a late fee must be reasonable, stated in the lease and no more than 5 percent of the periodic rent, and in a tenancy longer than week to week it can't be charged until rent is at least 3 calendar days late (NRS 118A.210(4)); and anything kept for unpaid rent, damage or cleaning is a refundable security deposit, except a reasonable cleaning charge (NRS 118A.240, 118A.242(8)). A tenant who ends the lease because of domestic violence, harassment, sexual assault or stalking owes only rent through the termination date and other outstanding obligations, and the named adverse party may be liable for your losses, including fees relating to early termination (NRS 118A.345(5), (6)). Any other pre-set damages clause, such as an early-termination fee, is judged under general contract law (case law not reviewed) and the court's power to refuse to enforce an unconscionable term (NRS 118A.230), and cannot take away the tenant's statutory rights, including your duty to make reasonable efforts to re-rent after abandonment, which limits the former tenant to your actual damages (NRS 118.175). If you use the library's optional Early Termination clause, never pair it with a waiver of the re-rent duty.

title: No Lockout for Late Rent
bodyText: Nevada does not let a residential landlord lock out a tenant who is behind on rent, and a lease can't create that right. You may recover possession of a dwelling only through a court action or summary proceeding in which the right to possession is decided, or after the tenant surrenders or abandons the unit; cutting or diminishing essential services to force a tenant out counts as taking possession too (NRS 118A.480). The summary-eviction statute mentions providing for a tenant's nonadmittance "by locking or otherwise" after an uncontested pay-or-quit notice, but only where NRS 118A.480 does not prohibit it, so treat any lockout without a court order, carried out by the sheriff or constable, as prohibited. A tenant who is unlawfully locked out or excluded may recover possession on an expedited complaint, terminate the lease, and recover actual damages and up to $2,500 (NRS 118A.390). A lease term giving you a lockout right would waive the tenant's rights under the landlord-tenant act and is void (NRS 118A.220). The opt-in lockout with advance notice and key access that some states allow exists in Nevada only for commercial premises (NRS 118C.200(3)(c)), not homes. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Shifting Repair and Maintenance Work to the Tenant
bodyText: Nevada lets you and the tenant agree that the tenant will perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling, but only if the agreement is made in good faith and does not reduce your obligations to other tenants. It is not in good faith if the work is part of your habitability duty and the tenant agreed because you or your agent refused to do it (NRS 118A.290(2), (3)). The statute does not require a separate document, a particular type size or a rent reduction; it does require the tasks to be specified, so list them. Separately, garbage and rubbish removal from the premises is yours unless the parties provide otherwise by written agreement, though you must still supply clean receptacles in good repair at move-in (NRS 118A.290(1)(f)). No agreement can make the tenant pay a fee or charge for work that is your habitability duty, including a home-warranty deductible or copay, unless the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the condition deliberately or negligently (NRS 118A.290(4), (5)). Whether the tenant may take over a habitability duty itself, rather than ordinary chores, is not settled by the text; the cautious course is to shift only defined tasks such as filter changes, yard care or pool upkeep and keep habitability with you. Without a written lease, maintenance and waste removal are presumed to be provided without charge to the tenant (NRS 118A.200(5)(b)). The library's optional Tenant-Performed Repairs and Maintenance clause recites these limits; its landscaping and snow-removal clauses rely on the same rule without restating it, so the good-faith conditions still apply when you use them.

title: No Meter or Conservation Surcharge
bodyText: Nevada has no energy-efficiency meter or conservation-charge program for rentals, and no statute that lets you add a meter, conservation or administrative surcharge to a tenant's utility bill. For a dwelling lease, a utility charge may be billed outside the single all-in rent figure only in two cases, each as a monthly fee equal to the cost of the electric, gas or water service in the tenant's own unit: where the utility can't contract directly with the tenant, or, for water, where the unit is on a master-metered water system; and the lease must mark the rent figure with an asterisk or symbol at least half its font size, tied to a statement on the same page explaining the charge (NRS 118A.200(8)). Any other mandatory utility-related fee, including a meter-reading, billing or conservation fee, must be inside the rent figure, and you may not charge more than that figure (NRS 118A.200(6)-(7)). The lease must also state who pays which utilities (NRS 118A.200(3)(j)). Manufactured-home parks follow separate rules: no markup over the landlord's rate, equal proration where lots aren't metered, itemized bills, and no charge to recover the cost of converting from a master water meter (NRS 704.940; NRS 118B.140(1)(b)(8)). Local utility rules and ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Military or Airport Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a landlord to disclose that a rental is near a military installation or in an aircraft noise or accident-potential zone, and give the tenant no termination right on that ground. Planning statutes require local governments to mail notice of a zoning hearing to the commander of a military installation within 3,000 feet of the property (for example, NRS 278.260(2)(c)); that is a government notice, not a landlord disclosure. A licensed real estate agent acting for you in the lease must still disclose material and relevant facts it knows or should have known (NRS 645.252(1)(a)). Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Minors as Tenants and Eviction Defendants
bodyText: In Nevada a person becomes an adult at 18: everyone 18 or older who is under no legal disability, and every minor declared emancipated by a court, can enter into any contract, including a lease (NRS 129.010). An emancipated minor's contracts and litigation are treated as an adult's, and obligations the minor incurs are enforceable by and against the minor (NRS 129.130(3)). There is no higher age of majority and no special rule for 18- to 20-year-olds. Because an unemancipated minor generally can't be bound by contract, have an adult sign as tenant or guarantor and list the minor as an occupant. You may not charge an application or screening fee for a prospective tenant's household member under 18 (NRS 118A.306). No Nevada statute or court rule bars naming a minor in an eviction case; only the tenant and any subtenant in actual occupation when the case is filed need be named, and people who enter under the tenant afterwards are bound by the judgment (NRS 40.290). If a minor is a party, the court rules require serving the summons on the minor personally if 14 or older and on a guardian, a parent or another responsible adult (JCRCP 4.2(b)(1)), and a minor without an appointed representative defends through a next friend or guardian ad litem (JCRCP 17(c)). Summary-eviction notices go to the tenant, so naming only the adult tenants is the cleaner course. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Local Utility Charges Can Become a Lien on Your Property
bodyText: Several Nevada statutes make unpaid local-government utility charges a lien on the property served, and none exempts an owner because a tenant used the service or held the account. Charges of a city-owned utility in a city organized under the general law become a lien once the city clerk records a statement of the amount. General improvement district rates and charges for services such as water, sewer, garbage and electricity become a perpetual lien once a notice is mailed to the owner and recorded, and the district may also sue the person who occupied the property when the service was rendered; a district may require deposits and the owner's guaranty of bills for service to the occupants. County service charges billed to anyone owning or occupying the property are a perpetual lien, as are municipal solid-waste fees once notice is mailed to the owner and recorded. Counties under 700,000 people and cities may also collect delinquent sewer, storm-drainage or water charges on the property tax roll, where they become a lien. We found no lease clause, affidavit or notice that keeps a tenant's unpaid bill off the property. Water districts and other providers created by special act, and local ordinances, were not reviewed. What to do: require proof that tenant-paid utilities are paid (the library's "Evidence of Utility Payment" clause), watch for lien notices mailed to you as owner, and treat an unpaid tenant utility bill as a lease breach.

title: Nonrefundable Fees and the Deposit
bodyText: Nevada decides what is a security deposit by what the money is for, not by its label. Any payment, deposit, fee or charge that is to be used to cover unpaid rent, repair damage beyond normal wear or clean the unit is a security deposit (NRS 118A.240(1)). So a "pet fee", "cleaning fee", "move-in fee" or prepaid amount that serves one of those purposes is part of the deposit: it counts toward the three-months'-rent limit on all security (NRS 118A.242(1)) and must be accounted for and refunded within 30 days after the tenancy ends (NRS 118A.242(4)). The only part a lease may make nonrefundable is a cleaning charge in a reasonable amount; any other provision calling a security deposit nonrefundable, or waiving or modifying the tenant's deposit rights, is void (NRS 118A.242(8)). State every required fee and its purpose, and every deposit and the conditions for its refund, in the lease (NRS 118A.200(3)(e)-(f)), and include any recurring mandatory fee, such as monthly pet rent, in the single total rent figure (NRS 118A.200(6)). Payments to secure an option to purchase and surety-bond premiums are not security deposits (NRS 118A.240(2)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Separate Notice for a Nonrefundable Charge
bodyText: Nevada's statutes require no separate notice, form or signature for a nonrefundable charge. The rule is in the deposit statute itself: the only nonrefundable amount allowed is a cleaning charge in a reasonable amount, and it must be provided for in the agreement (NRS 118A.242(8)). Put it in the lease with the other required fees and their purposes (NRS 118A.200(3)(e)); a nonrefundable label on any other deposit, or a waiver of the tenant's deposit rights, is void however conspicuously it is disclosed (NRS 118A.242(8)). The one statutory 'separately identified' rule nearby is for online payment-portal fees, which must be separately identified in any written rental agreement (NRS 118A.303(2)(b)). Manufactured-home-park lot rentals are governed by chapter 118B, not by these rules (NRS 118A.180(2)(a)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Out-of-State Owners: In-State Agent and Local Manager
bodyText: Nevada does not single out nonresident landlords, but three rules matter most to an owner who lives elsewhere. First, every landlord must tell the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of a person within Nevada authorized to accept service of process and receive notices and demands for the landlord, along with the names and addresses of the managers and the owner, and an emergency telephone number of a responsible person who lives in the county or within 60 miles of the property; the library's disclosure clause does this. If someone signs a lease for you without making these disclosures, that person becomes your agent for service of process and for performing your duties, and you remain liable. Second, anyone who manages your property for a fee under a property management agreement must hold a Nevada real estate license and a permit to engage in property management; you, your regular employees, and an on-site manager who manages no other property do not need one. Third, if you own through an out-of-state LLC or corporation, it must register with the Secretary of State before doing business here and keep a registered agent in Nevada, and until it registers it may not commence or maintain any action, an eviction included; an unregistered LLC doing business here is also deemed to have appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process for claims arising from that business (NRS 14.020(1); NRS 86.544(1), 86.548(2), (6); NRS 80.010(1), 80.055(2)). Owning property without more is not doing business (NRS 86.5483(1)(i); NRS 80.015(1)(i)); whether renting it out is, is a case-law question, so register before you file. Nevada's constitution bars an income tax on the personal income of natural persons, and no statute requires a tenant to withhold tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Charges for Serving Notices
bodyText: No Nevada statute authorizes or caps a lease charge for preparing or serving a notice, but the landlord-tenant act assumes a lease may authorize charges for notice: it bars them, together with late fees and other lease charges, on rent a tenant lawfully withholds because of a material habitability failure or a willful or negligent failure to supply an essential service (NRS 118A.355(1)(d), 118A.380(1)(c)). If your lease charges for a notice: state the charge and its purpose in the lease, using the Required Fees clause (NRS 118A.200(3)(e)); keep it reasonable and tied to actual cost, such as the fee of the sheriff, constable, licensed process server or attorney's agent who must serve most eviction notices (NRS 40.280(1)); do not fold attorney's fees into it (NRS 118A.220(1)(c)); and after serving a pay-or-quit notice do not refuse rent because the notice charge or other non-rent costs are unpaid (NRS 40.253(11)). Base a nonpayment notice on unpaid rent, not on an unpaid notice charge. A charge out of line with actual cost risks being struck as a penalty or as unconscionable (NRS 118A.230; case law not reviewed).

title: Notices to Quit Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A lease cannot waive or shorten Nevada's notices to quit. It is unlawful for a landlord to try, by contract or other agreement, to shorten the specified notice periods, and any such agreement is void (NRS 40.252(1)). That covers the notice to end a periodic tenancy (at least 7 days week to week, 30 days for other periodic tenancies), the 5-day notice where the tenant has failed to perform basic or lease obligations, the 7-judicial-day notice to pay rent or surrender, the 3-day notice to surrender for unlawful assignment or subletting, waste, an unlawful business, nuisance or drug-law violations, and the 5-day notice to perform or surrender (NRS 40.251, 40.2512, 40.2514, 40.2516). The summary-eviction notice for unpaid rent (NRS 40.253) sits just outside the range NRS 40.252 names, but a shortened notice would not support a summary eviction, so treat it the same way. Inside the landlord-tenant act, a lease may not make the tenant waive the 5-day written notice to remedy a breach (NRS 118A.430) or give you a different termination notice than you must give the tenant; such a term is void and carries actual damages (NRS 118A.220). The library offers no notice-waiver clause for Nevada. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Extra Terms and Work During a Notice to Vacate
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not regulate extra terms placed in a move-out form or notice to vacate, and they have no rule barring work on the unit while a notice to vacate runs. Each statutory notice must contain what its own section requires; for example, a notice ending a periodic tenancy must tell the tenant about the extension rights for tenants 60 or older or with a disability and for government workers during a shutdown (NRS 40.251(5)). A notice cannot change the lease. A new term binds the tenant only if the tenant agrees to it, and a term that waives the tenant's rights under the landlord-tenant act, or requires the tenant to give a different termination notice than you must give, is void however it is signed (NRS 118A.220). While the notice runs, the tenancy continues: you must keep the unit habitable (NRS 118A.290(1)), you may recover possession only through the court or after the tenant surrenders or abandons the unit (NRS 118A.480), and interrupting an essential service exposes you to the tenant's expedited court remedy, actual damages and up to $2,500 (NRS 118A.390). Keep notices to what the statute asks for, put anything you want agreed in a separate document the tenant signs, and schedule renovation for after the tenant leaves. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Where Nevada Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Nevada's landlord-tenant act lists subjects every written lease must cover but lets the lease contain more (NRS 118A.200(3)), so long as no term is prohibited (NRS 118A.220, 118A.242(8)) or unconscionable (NRS 118A.230). These choices exist only if the lease makes them: (1) when and where rent is paid (NRS 118A.210(1)); (2) a definite term, without which the tenancy is week to week or month to month (NRS 118A.210(2)); (3) a late fee, which may be charged only as set out in the lease and within the statutory limits (NRS 118A.210(4)); (4) attorney's fees to the prevailing party in a court action, the only fee clause allowed (NRS 118A.220(1)(c)); (5) a reasonable nonrefundable cleaning charge, the only nonrefundable deposit item allowed (NRS 118A.242(8)); (6) tenant garbage removal, which must be agreed in writing (NRS 118A.290(1)(f)); (7) specified tenant repairs or maintenance, agreed in good faith (NRS 118A.290(2)-(3)); (8) restrictions on children or pets, without which none are presumed (NRS 118A.200(3)(c), (5)(a)); (9) the place for the tenant's notices to you (NRS 118A.190(3)); (10) terms for a holdover other than the same lease terms (NRS 118A.470); and (11) an online-portal fee, separately identified (NRS 118A.303(2)). House rules can be adopted later, but a rule that materially changes the bargain needs the tenant's written consent or 30 days' notice (NRS 118A.320). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Nevada's statutes set none of these three disclosures: no duty to tell a prospective tenant that the property is near a former military ordnance site, no duty to disclose a planned demolition or demolition permit before signing, and no rule on a tenant's meter that also serves areas outside the unit. Related rules: a monthly utility fee outside the single rent figure may cover only the electric, natural gas or water service provided in the tenant's own dwelling unit, with the same-page statement the lease law requires (NRS 118A.200(8)); ending a tenancy because a code citation requires alteration, remodeling or demolition that cannot be done while the unit is occupied is not retaliation (NRS 118A.510(3)(c)); and tenants in a building being converted to a condominium or other common-interest community get at least 120 days' notice (NRS 116.4112(1)). Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Pools, Laundries and Other Shared Facilities
bodyText: Facilities you hold out for tenants' use, such as a pool, laundry room, gym, elevator, parking area or other common area, are part of the premises (NRS 118A.140). You must have the buildings, grounds and other areas under your control clean, sanitary and reasonably free of debris and vermin when the tenancy begins, keep floors, walls, stairways and railings in good repair, and keep ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, in good repair if you supply them (NRS 118A.290(1)(g)-(i)). Tenants must use these facilities in a reasonable manner (NRS 118A.310(1)(e)). You may adopt rules to fairly share facilities held out for tenants generally, if the rules meet the statutory conditions (NRS 118A.320). A pool used by the residents of an apartment complex is a public swimming pool supervised by the health authority (NRS 444.065, 444.070), and the state rules require, for example, a barrier at least 5 feet high with self-closing, self-latching gates around a pool serving multiple dwellings (NAC 444.136). Nevada has no statute on garage-door openers or similar building equipment. State any amenity fee and its purpose in the lease, and include any mandatory periodic fee in the single rent figure (NRS 118A.200(3)(e), (6)). Local codes may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Ending a Lease So the Owner Can Move In
bodyText: Nevada has no owner move-in statute. A periodic tenancy (month to month or week to week) can be ended without a reason on written notice of at least 30 days (7 for week to week), so owner occupancy needs no lease term there, though a tenant 60 or older or with a disability may ask for 30 more days and a qualifying government worker may stay until 30 days after a shutdown ends (NRS 40.251). A fixed-term lease, by contrast, ends at its expiration (NRS 40.250), and nothing in Nevada law lets you end it early for owner or family occupancy unless the lease reserves that right; a silent lease leaves you waiting for the term to end. The library's optional Owner Occupancy clause, which carries Nevada, reserves the right on at least 30 days' written notice ending on the last day of a monthly rental period, with possession recovered only through the courts. Cautions: a lease may not require the tenant to give you a different notice of termination than you must give the tenant (NRS 118A.220(1)(e)), so if the lease also lets the tenant end it early, set the owner-occupancy notice period equal to the tenant's notice period; serve the notice the way eviction notices must be served (NRS 40.280), with the extension statement the no-cause notice statute requires, so it can also support an eviction; and in a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy you may not end the tenancy during the initial lease term for personal or family use of the unit (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.310(d)(2)). Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Giving Tenants Your Parking Rules
bodyText: Nevada has no statute requiring you to deliver parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, to use a prescribed heading, to limit the vehicle information you ask for, or to make a parking permit last as long as the lease. Parking rules are landlord rules, so the general test applies: a rule binds the tenant only if it serves a legitimate purpose, is reasonably related to it, applies fairly to all tenants, is explicit, is in good faith, does not affect rent or other charges, and the tenant had notice of it when signing or after you adopted it; a rule adopted mid-lease that materially changes the bargain binds the tenant only with written consent or 30 days' advance written notice. Towing has its own preconditions: except at a single-family home, a sign in plain view must declare parking prohibited or restricted and show the police or sheriff's number, and you must give oral notice to law enforcement after the tow. A space designated for charging electric vehicles may be enforced only with compliant signs or markings. In an association, the association's parking rules also bind your tenant. What to do: attach your parking rules to the lease or give them at signing, and give 30 days' written notice before any material change. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Nevada's main landlord-tenant law is the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, NRS chapter 118A. A lease may not provide that the tenant: (1) waives or gives up any right or remedy the Act gives; (2) authorizes anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the lease; (3) agrees to pay your attorney's fees, except that the lease may say a court may award reasonable attorney's fees to whichever party prevails; (4) agrees to excuse or limit your legal liability, or to indemnify you for it or its costs, where the liability is based on an act or omission of you, your agent or your employee; or (5) agrees to give you a different termination notice than the one you must give the tenant. Any such term is void, and the tenant may recover any actual damages its inclusion caused; the statute does not require that you knew the term was unlawful (NRS 118A.220). Three more rules work the same way: no term may call a security deposit nonrefundable, except a reasonable nonrefundable cleaning charge, or waive or change the deposit rules (NRS 118A.242(8)); a lease that does not meet the required-contents and single-rent-figure rules is unlawful to use, and a term that contravenes them is void (NRS 118A.200(9)); and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease, strike an unconscionable term or limit it (NRS 118A.230). Some rights also apply whatever the lease says, such as early termination for domestic violence and for relocation or death of an older or disabled tenant's spouse or cotenant (NRS 118A.340, 118A.345). Where the Act leaves a point to the parties, the lease controls: for example, the time and place for paying rent, a late fee within the statutory limits, who removes garbage and rubbish, and specified repairs or maintenance tasks the tenant agrees in good faith to do (NRS 118A.210, 118A.290(1)(f), (2)). The waiver ban reaches rights under chapter 118A. Rights in other chapters carry their own rules: a contract may not shorten the eviction notice periods in NRS chapter 40 (NRS 40.252), and the duty to try to re-rent after a tenant abandons is in NRS 118.175, outside chapter 118A. Chapter 118A does not govern manufactured-home-park tenancies (chapter 118B) or the other occupancies NRS 118A.180 excludes. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText: Nevada has no rule allowing entry without notice for regularly scheduled services. Supplying necessary or agreed services is a lawful reason to enter, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent (NRS 118A.330(1)). But outside an emergency each entry needs at least 24 hours' notice and must be at a reasonable time during normal business hours, unless the tenant expressly agrees to shorter notice or other hours for that particular entry (NRS 118A.330(3)). Listing the services and their schedule in the lease helps show they are agreed services, but it cannot give blanket advance consent to shorter notice; a lease term waiving the 24-hour right is void (NRS 118A.220(1)(a)). You may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant, and repeated demands that harass the tenant let the tenant get an injunction or end the lease and recover damages (NRS 118A.330(3), 118A.500(2)). The statute does not say the entry notice must be written, but keep a written record of each notice.

title: No Pest Control Notice Rule
bodyText: Nevada law does not require a landlord to give tenants advance notice of pesticide application or pest control service, and sets no pest-control disclosure for rentals; advance notice before pesticide use is required only for schools. The pesticide regulations put a few duties on the licensed applicator, not on you: before applying a pesticide known to be harmful to animals, give the owner of any animals known to be on the property (for example, a tenant with pets) notice within a reasonable time so the owner can protect them (NAC 555.460(1)(a)); place rodenticides and insecticide baits where children and pets cannot reach them or in tamper-resistant stations (NAC 555.460(1)(d), (f)); follow the product label (NAC 555.440(4)); and, for a fumigation, keep a certified applicator on site until aeration is complete and the warning signs are removed (NAC 555.510(3)). Anyone you hire to apply pesticides for pay must be licensed (NRS 555.280). You must deliver the building, grounds and other areas under your control reasonably free of rodents, insects and vermin at the start of the tenancy (NRS 118A.290(1)(g)), and the tenant must keep its part of the premises as clean and safe as the condition of the premises permits (NRS 118A.310(1)(b)). Give at least 24 hours' notice before entering to treat a unit, except in an emergency (NRS 118A.330(3)). Local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Pet Fact Sheet Requirement
bodyText: Nevada's statutes require no state fact sheet or notice about pets, at lease signing or in an eviction. The written lease must address occupancy by pets (NRS 118A.200(3)(c)), and with no written lease the law presumes there are no restrictions on pets (NRS 118A.200(5)(a)).
