A rule adopted during the tenancy cannot affect, before the lease ends, a right the lease gives the tenant to keep a pet (NRS 118A.320(1)(g)). Local animal-control ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Pet Deposits and Pet Fees
bodyText: Nevada has no pet-fee statute; its general fee rules decide how a pet charge works. A pet deposit, or any pet charge that is to be used to cover unpaid rent, pet damage beyond normal wear, or cleaning, is a security deposit whatever you call it: it counts with all other deposits toward the three-month limit and must be refundable, except a reasonable nonrefundable cleaning charge (NRS 118A.240, 118A.242(1), (8)). So a nonrefundable pet fee is lawful only as a reasonable cleaning charge. A monthly pet fee the tenant must pay is a mandatory fee and must be included in the single monthly rent figure the lease states, not added on top (NRS 118A.200(6), (7)). The lease must address occupancy by pets and list each required fee with its purpose (NRS 118A.200(3)(c), (e)). At move-out you may claim against the deposit for pet damage beyond normal wear and for reasonable cleaning (NRS 118A.242(4)). A rule adopted later may not take away a pet right the lease gives before the lease ends (NRS 118A.320(1)(g)). Assistance animals are not pets; see the assistance-animal rows.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Rule
bodyText: Nevada has no plain-language or readability statute for residential leases, and no rule that a lease be divided into captioned sections. What the law does require: the written lease must be signed by both sides and must address the subjects NRS 118A.200(3) lists; a landlord who advertises and negotiates in a language other than English must give a full translation before signing (NRS 598.9733); and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term (NRS 118A.230). Plain-English rules in other statutes cover other documents, such as association bylaws and consumer vehicle leases. Writing the lease in clear, everyday language still helps it hold up.

title: No Consumer Restrictions Statement
bodyText: Nevada has no statute requiring a residential lease to open with a statement listing the landlord-protective terms or every waiver, no readability test and no Attorney General preapproval of lease forms. Instead, a lease term in which the tenant waives rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act is void, and the tenant may recover actual damages caused by including it (NRS 118A.220). One term needs its own sign-off: an agreement that requires a person to arbitrate disputes must include specific authorization showing the person affirmatively agreed to that provision, or the provision is void and unenforceable (NRS 597.995).

title: Candidates and Canvassers at Rental Properties
bodyText: For ordinary rentals, Nevada's statutes do not require you to let candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration workers into an apartment building or other multiunit property to reach tenants' doors, and they set no rule on campaign literature in common areas. The one access right is for manufactured-home parks: a park landlord may not stop a public officer, a candidate for public office or their representative from walking through the park to talk with tenants or distribute political material, and may not bar or charge for tenants' meetings, including political meetings, held in the park's community facility at reasonable hours when it is not otherwise in use. Related rights that do reach ordinary rentals: a tenant may display the U.S. flag in the tenant's exclusive area, subject to your reasonable placement rules; in a homeowners' or condominium association the association may not ban an occupant's political signs; and you may not retaliate against a tenant for organizing or joining a tenants' union. What to do: set your common-area access and literature rules in writing, apply them evenly to every campaign and cause, and don't interfere with tenants who invite a candidate in. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Pools and Spas at Rentals
bodyText: Nevada has no pool-safety notice to give a tenant and no pool rule in the landlord-tenant act, but its health laws reach shared pools. A public swimming pool is any structure holding an artificial body of water intended to be used collectively for swimming or bathing, whether or not a fee is charged; a pool at a private residence is excluded only if it is controlled by the owner or other authorized occupant and used only by that household's family and invited guests (NRS 444.065). So a pool or spa at an apartment complex, condominium or other multiple-dwelling property is regulated, while the private pool of a rented house used only by the tenant's household normally is not. Building or operating a public swimming pool without a permit from the health authority is unlawful (NRS 444.080), a noncompliant pool is a public nuisance (NRS 444.110), and violations are misdemeanors, each day a separate offense (NRS 444.120). The State Board of Health's rules require a barrier that completely encloses the pool area, is impenetrable for small children and, at an apartment, condominium or other multiple-dwelling facility, is at least 5 feet high, with no gates or doors opening from a dwelling unit directly into the pool enclosure and with self-closing, self-latching, lockable gates that the operator periodically inspects (NAC 444.136). Such a pool under 2,000 square feet needs no lifeguard if no fee is charged and use is limited to tenants or residents and their guests (NAC 444.270(1)). Local boards of health may adopt their own rules (NRS 444.070). The spa regulation excludes spas at single-family residences controlled by the homeowner (NAC 444.385(2)); if you rent out a house with a spa, confirm its status with the local health authority. If a lease makes the tenant clean or maintain a private pool, the library's Tenant-Performed Repairs clause lists the task. Local building codes may add barrier rules for private pools (not reviewed).

title: No Tenant Right to Install a Cooling Device, and No Cooling Standard
bodyText: Nevada's statutes give tenants no right to install a window or portable air conditioner or evaporative cooler, and set no rule on when a lease may restrict one; the lease and your rules on alterations govern. Nor do they require you to provide air-conditioning or set a maximum indoor temperature. But once you supply air-conditioning, or are required to, you must keep it in good repair as part of habitability (NRS 118A.290(1)(i)), and if the lease or the law requires you to supply it, a willful or negligent failure that makes the unit unfit lets the tenant use the 48-hour essential-services remedies: buying reasonable amounts of cooling and deducting the cost, damages, withholding rent, or comparable substitute housing with rent abated (NRS 118A.380(1)). Describe in the lease what cooling equipment comes with the unit, and if you allow tenant-supplied units, say where and how they may be installed. The tenant must use any air-conditioning in a reasonable manner (NRS 118A.310(1)(e)). Local ordinances and building codes may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Tenant Right to Plug-In Solar
bodyText: Nevada's statutes give a tenant no right to install a plug-in, balcony or other portable solar device, and they set no notice-and-response procedure for one. Nevada's solar-access laws protect property owners: a covenant, restriction or condition in a deed, contract or other instrument affecting real property is void if it prohibits or unreasonably restricts 'the owner of the property' from using a solar energy system on the owner's property, and local governments may not do so either. They do not by their terms give a tenant a right against the landlord, and whether a lease clause limiting a tenant's own device is such a restriction is not settled. Since October 1, 2025, an association may adopt rules for an owner's rooftop distributed generation system within statutory limits; those rules speak to unit owners. So a tenant's request is decided by your lease and your consent, subject to the lease's alterations clause and any association rules. One related duty: if you operate a solar-powered affordable housing system on a qualified multifamily affordable housing property, you must notify residents at least 30 days before installing it and tell each new tenant about it.

title: Nevada Rules That Depend on Property Size
bodyText: Nevada's landlord-tenant act applies the same way to every landlord, with no small-landlord exemption, but several rules turn on how many units you own or how big the building is. (1) Fair housing: Nevada's fair housing law does not reach a single-family house rented by an owner who owns no more than three single-family houses at a time AND rents without any licensed real estate broker or salesperson; both conditions must be met. It also does not reach rooms or units in an owner-occupied building of up to four families unless, in the last 12 months, the owner was the principal in three or more, or an agent in two or more, sale or rental transactions. The ban on discriminatory advertising still applies to both. (2) Lease form: a lease for a single-family residence (a structure of up to four units, not a manufactured home) that is not signed by a licensed property manager must carry the large-type occupancy disclosure at the top of page one. (3) Smoke detectors: an apartment building with three or more units must have a smoke detector in each unit. (4) Multifamily repair orders and receivership apply to two or more rental units on one parcel. (5) Key control and staff background checks apply to a complex of more than 50 units on one parcel in a county of 100,000 or more people, or more than 30 units in a smaller county. (6) A natural person whose only business is renting four or fewer dwelling units needs no state business license. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Possession Bond with a Confessed Judgment
bodyText: Nevada has no statutory end-of-term possession bond and no procedure for a tenant to sign a bond or warrant that confesses judgment for possession. A residential lease may not authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of it, and such a term is void, with the tenant able to recover any actual damages it causes (NRS 118A.220(1)(b), (2)). The bonds that do exist in Nevada possession cases are court-ordered. If you ask for a temporary writ of restitution in a formal unlawful-detainer action, the court must first hear the tenant and you must file a bond, in an amount the court fixes, to cover the tenant's probable loss (NRS 40.300(3)). A tenant who asks to adjourn a formal trial for a missing witness may get up to 30 days by giving a bond for the rent that accrues and your costs and damages (NRS 40.340). On appeal, a tenant can stay a formal judgment only by an undertaking of at least twice the judgment and costs (NRS 40.380), or stay a summary eviction order by a $250 cost bond while paying rent as it comes due (NRS 40.385). Separately, if you consent, a tenant may buy a surety bond instead of paying all or part of a security deposit, subject to the deposit cap; that secures the lease, not possession. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Tenant Property After an Eviction
bodyText: After an eviction, Nevada lets you deal with property left behind without civil or criminal liability only by following a set procedure. Store it safely for 30 days after the eviction; you may charge the reasonable and actual costs of inventory, moving and storage before releasing it to the tenant or the tenant's authorized representative, and you are liable only for your own negligent or wrongful acts in storing it. After 30 days you may dispose of it and recover your reasonable costs from it or its value, but only after reasonable efforts to locate the tenant, a written notice of your intent to dispose mailed to the tenant's present (or last known) address, and 14 more days. Vehicles go through the abandoned-vehicle law. For 5 days after the eviction or lockout you must give the former tenant a reasonable opportunity to retrieve essential personal effects, such as medication, baby formula, basic clothing and personal care items (NRS 118A.460). The tenant can challenge your charges by motion within 20 days after removal (or after asking for or receiving a copy of the charges, if later); the court hears it within 10 days and may set the costs and order the property released on payment. The tenant can also move within 5 days after removal about access to essential effects; the court hears that within 5 days and may order access and award up to $2,500 (NRS 40.253(7)-(10)). No Nevada statute sets special rules for pets left behind; they are not mentioned in the property-disposal procedure, and abandoning an animal is a crime, so contact the tenant and local animal control promptly rather than treating a pet as stored goods. When a formal writ of restitution is executed, the sheriff or constable carries it out like a writ of execution, after serving notice of the execution and the tenant's exemptions (NRS 40.420(2), 40.425). Nevada has no crime specific to returning after an eviction; a former tenant who re-enters may be removed through the forcible-entry route or reported for trespass after a warning. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Private Well Testing or Disclosure Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require you to test a private well that serves a rental, or to give tenants well test results. Your duty is the habitability one: the unit must have a water supply approved under applicable law, capable of producing hot and cold running water and furnished to the fixtures (NRS 118A.290(1)(c)), and running water is an essential service whose loss triggers the tenant's 48-hour remedies (NRS 118A.380(1)). A well that serves 15 or more service connections or regularly serves 25 or more people is a public water system regardless of who owns it (NRS 445A.235), and public water systems carry their own state monitoring and reporting duties set in regulations (NAC chapter 445A; its monitoring rules were not reviewed, and a search of the whole chapter found no rule addressed to landlords or tenants). If a well serves an accessory dwelling unit of a single-family home as a domestic use, the owner must get local approval, install a meter and keep withdrawals within 2 acre-feet a year (NRS 534.180(4)). Local health rules may add requirements (not reviewed).

title: Promises to Repair: No Writing or Date Rule, but They Bind You
bodyText: Nevada has no statute requiring your promises to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. But a promise you make becomes part of the rental agreement, and Nevada's act treats an oral agreement as a rental agreement too (NRS 118A.160). You must deliver possession at the start of the term in compliance with the rental agreement and in a habitable condition (NRS 118A.280). If you do not keep a promise, the tenant may give written notice of the breach; if you do not fix it, or make a reasonable effort to, within 14 days, the tenant may end the lease, recover actual damages or ask the court for relief (NRS 118A.350), and if the work would cost less than $100 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, the tenant may instead have it done and deduct the cost from rent (NRS 118A.360). A promise to supply heat, air-conditioning, water, power or another essential item or service also brings the 48-hour essential-services remedies (NRS 118A.380). Put any agreed pre-move-in work, and its target date, in the lease or the signed move-in inventory so both sides know what was promised. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: Nevada has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65: its statutes require no warning to tenants about exposure to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. Specific hazards have their own rules, such as the federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978 and the nuisance rule for former drug labs. Federal law beyond the lead rules and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Asking Applicants About Protected Characteristics
bodyText: Nevada's statutes have no separate rule that forbids asking an applicant or tenant about race, religion, national origin, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, ancestry, familial status or sex, or keeping a record of the answers. The fair housing law does bar any notice, statement or advertisement about renting a dwelling that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on those traits, and it bars refusing to rent or setting different terms because of them. A question on an application form is itself a written statement, so a question that signals a preference can break the advertising ban, and the answers can be evidence that a refusal was discriminatory. The cautious course: do not ask about these traits at all, except where the law lets you ask for proof, such as asking a person who requests an assistance animal for a health care provider's statement that the animal eases the effects of the disability. Federal fair housing law has the same statement ban. Federal rules also make it unlawful to ask whether an applicant, a future occupant or anyone associated with them has a disability, or about its nature or severity; questions asked of every applicant about meeting the requirements of the tenancy, eligibility for housing or a priority reserved for people with disabilities, current illegal drug use, or a conviction for making or distributing a controlled substance are allowed (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 100.202(c)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Unlawful Use of the Premises
bodyText: Nevada has no statute that makes a lease void or annulled when the premises are used for an unlawful purpose. Instead, a tenant who carries on an unlawful business on the premises, commits or permits waste, maintains a nuisance that unreasonably obstructs others' use and injures other tenants or neighbors, or violates the controlled-substances laws there (other than simple possession) can be removed after a 3-day notice to surrender, with no chance to cure (NRS 40.2514). A place used for unlawful drug activity, or regularly by a criminal gang, is a nuisance that can be enjoined or abated (NRS 40.140(1)). A person who lets a building, knowing it is being used to maintain a public nuisance, commits a misdemeanor (NRS 202.470), and renting a place within 400 yards of a school or church for use as a house of prostitution is separately punishable (NRS 201.380). A tenant's request for emergency help is not a nuisance (NRS 40.140(4)). State the permitted use in the lease, and act promptly when you learn of unlawful use. Local nuisance-abatement ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Landlord Recycling Notice
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a landlord to tell tenants where or how to recycle. Where a county or health district has adopted a recycling program, it must notify all occupants of residential premises in the program area of local recycling opportunities within 6 months and at least every 6 months after that (NRS 444A.050(1)(b)). Counties of 100,000 or more must offer a program that includes recycling containers at apartment complexes and condominiums where collection service is provided (NRS 444A.040(1)(a)), and plans for building or majorly renovating an apartment complex must provide for recycling containers (NRS 278.02315). Cities and counties enforce their programs by ordinance, which may place duties on owners of multifamily property (not reviewed).

title: Paying to Stop an Eviction
bodyText: Nevada's statutes give a tenant behind on rent two chances to pay and keep the home, and set one limit on what you may demand. First, the tenant may pay the rent within the pay-or-quit notice period (seven judicial days, or the shorter period for a new weekly tenancy). Once you have served that notice, you may not refuse rent the tenant submits because the tenant has not also paid collection fees, attorney's fees or other costs besides rent, a reasonable late or dishonored-check charge, or a security deposit (NRS 40.253(1), (11)). Second, after a judgment for an unlawful detainer for unpaid rent where the lease has not expired by its terms, the sheriff can't act for 5 days, and if the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the lease or another interested party pays the judgment and costs into court within that time, the judgment is satisfied and the tenant is restored to the lease (NRS 40.360(3)). Nothing else in Nevada's statutes lets a tenant redeem later, for example by paying everything owed up to a set time before removal. No statute requires you to accept a partial payment, prescribes wording for accepting one without waiving the default, or requires you to accept a charity's or government agency's payment for the tenant; whether accepting rent after a notice waives it is a case-law question not reviewed here (the Reno Justice Court's tenant affidavit form lists landlord acceptance of a partial payment as a defense a tenant may raise). Two special cases: in the Housing Choice Voucher program, the family is not responsible for the housing authority's share and its nonpayment is not grounds to end the tenancy (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.310(b)); and for a qualifying government worker during a shutdown, you must accept the shutdown-period rent for up to 30 days after it ends (NRS 118A.310(2)). Cautious course: if you take a partial payment after a notice, say in writing at the time whether you are reserving your right to proceed, and serve a fresh notice for any balance.

title: No Statewide Rent Control
bodyText: Nevada has no statewide rent control or rent-stabilization law for dwellings. Chapter 118A regulates how you raise rent, not how much: an increase needs written notice at least 60 days before the first increased payment (30 days for a periodic tenancy of less than a month) (NRS 118A.300), and may not be retaliatory, although an increase applied uniformly to all tenants is not retaliation (NRS 118A.510(1), (3)(d)). The statutes neither expressly preempt nor expressly authorize local rent control. Counties and cities may address matters of local concern, with doubts resolved in favor of local power unless the Legislature intended otherwise, but unless a statute authorizes it they may not prescribe the law governing civil actions between private persons (NRS 244.146, 268.0035); no statute settles whether that allows a local rent ordinance. Local ordinances were not reviewed. Rent can be limited in other ways: affordability restrictions on tax-credit and similar subsidized projects (NRS 319.410), federal program rules, and in manufactured-home parks, where an increase needs 90 days' written notice and the same rent as comparable lots, with listed discounts allowed (NRS 118B.150(1)(a)). During a declared state of emergency or disaster, renting consumer goods or services in the area at a price grossly in excess of the usual price is a deceptive trade practice for the first 75 days; whether dwelling rent is covered is not settled, and a contract price set before the proclamation is excluded (NRS 598.09235). Bills that would have temporarily capped rent increases for certain existing tenants (2025 AB 280) and set a maximum annual increase in manufactured-home parks (2023 SB 275) were vetoed and are not law.

title: When Rent Is Withheld, Abated or Deferred
bodyText: Nevada has no general rule that bars you from demanding rent for a unit with code violations. Instead the tenant's rent obligation is reduced, suspended or deferred in specific situations, and you may face a counterclaim if you sue for rent. (1) Habitability: after written notice and 14 days without a remedy or best efforts, a tenant may withhold rent without late fees or other charges until you remedy or try in good faith to remedy, but has no eviction defense on that ground unless the withheld rent is paid into the justice court's escrow (NRS 118A.355(1)(d), (5)). (2) Essential services you willfully or negligently fail to supply: after written notice and 48 hours (excluding weekends and holidays), a tenant may buy substitute services and deduct their cost, move to comparable housing while rent fully abates, or, if current on rent when giving notice, withhold rent without charges (NRS 118A.380). (3) Rent abates until you deliver possession (NRS 118A.370), and after a fire or casualty a tenant who vacates the unusable part owes rent reduced in proportion (NRS 118A.400(1)(b)). (4) During a government shutdown, a lease term requiring rent at a set time can't be enforced against a qualifying federal, tribal or state worker or household member, and you must accept that rent up to 30 days after the shutdown ends, unless a court grants relief (NRS 118A.310(2), 118A.315). (5) If a court appoints a receiver for a substandard multifamily property, you may not collect rent at all; the receiver does (NRS 244.36906(1), 268.4285(1)). The habitability, essential-services and casualty remedies are not available for a condition the tenant, a household member or a guest caused deliberately or negligently. In a suit for rent or possession the tenant may counterclaim for anything owed under the lease or the law (NRS 118A.490). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Raising Rent During the Term
bodyText: During a fixed term you may raise rent only if the lease provides for it; the notice rule limits increases but does not itself authorize one mid-term. If the lease sets a schedule, state each new rent as a single total figure that includes every mandatory fee (NRS 118A.200(6)), and still serve written notice at least 60 days before the first increased payment, or 30 days for a periodic tenancy of less than a month (NRS 118A.300), served as the eviction statutes provide (NRS 118A.190(2)). Avoid index (CPI) formulas and clauses that let you raise rent on short notice at your choice: the lease must state rent as the maximum total periodic rent and you may not charge more than that figure (NRS 118A.200(6)-(7)); a tenant can sue for damages, equitable relief, costs and attorney's fees, plus $250 for each violation involving deception (NRS 118A.405). A rent increase may not be retaliatory, but one applied uniformly to all tenants is not retaliation whether or not the lease mentions it (NRS 118A.510(1), (3)(d)). In a month-to-month tenancy, raise rent by the 60-day notice and use the new single figure from then on. No statute caps the amount or frequency of increases (local ordinances not reviewed).

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In an action for possession for nonpayment of rent, or an action for rent while the tenant is still in possession, the tenant may defend and counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease, the landlord-tenant act or other law, such as damages for an unrepaired habitability failure. Nevada does not make the tenant pay rent into court before raising a defense or counterclaim. But if money may come due to you after the hearing date, or the judgment is delayed for any reason, the court must require a tenant who stays in possession to deposit a just and reasonable amount with the court, no more than 1 day's rent for each day until the new hearing; it orders any undisputed rent paid to you and decides what each side owes. A tenant who fails to deposit the full amount within 24 hours after the original hearing loses the right to a hearing and the court grants judgment for eviction. Either side may ask the court to release deposited rent for good cause, and the court distributes it when it decides possession. A tenant no longer in possession may counterclaim without paying any rent into court (NRS 118A.490). Separately, a tenant who withheld rent for a habitability failure has that defense to eviction only after depositing the withheld rent in the justice court's escrow account (NRS 118A.355(5)). After an eviction judgment for unpaid rent on a lease that has not expired, the tenant has 5 days to pay the judgment and costs into court and be restored (NRS 40.360(3)). Justice-court local rules add procedure (not restated here).

title: Who Keeps the Repair Duty When Someone Else Collects Rent
bodyText: Nevada has no statute saying that whoever receives the rent keeps the landlord's habitability duties regardless of what a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage says. Related rules: the landlord is whoever provides the dwelling under a rental agreement, and the habitability duty and its remedies can't be waived by the lease (NRS 118A.100, 118A.220, 118A.290). A person who enters into a rental agreement for the landlord without giving the tenant the required written disclosure of the manager, the owner and an in-state agent for service becomes the landlord's agent for performing the landlord's obligations; the landlord's obligations devolve on the persons authorized to enter into rental agreements on the landlord's behalf; and an undisclosed landlord stays liable (NRS 118A.260(3)-(5)). After a voluntary sale or transfer, the new owner takes on the previous owner's obligations under the existing lease (NRS 118A.349(1)(a)). A lender collecting rents under an assignment of rents collects subject to the lease and to the tenant's claims and defenses arising from the landlord's nonperformance, and need not spend the rents on maintenance unless it agreed to, though the tenant may ask a court for a receiver (NRS 107A.320). Cautious course: if a manager or master tenant collects the rent, make the management agreement require it to handle repairs, and treat the duty as staying with whoever acts as landlord. Case law was not reviewed.

title: Rent Receipts on Request
bodyText: When the tenant asks, you must deliver a signed written receipt for the security deposit or surety bond and for any other payment, deposit or fee the tenant pays you, including rent; the tenant may refuse to pay rent until you tender the requested receipt (NRS 118A.250). The duty covers every payment method, not only cash, and arises on request. Nevada has no separate cash-receipt rule for dwelling tenancies and no presumption that a receipt for later rent shows earlier rent was paid (case law not reviewed). Because rent withheld until you tender a requested receipt is withheld lawfully, give receipts promptly and keep copies before serving any pay-or-quit notice. Manufactured-home-park tenancies have their own rule: a dated receipt for every rent payment within 5 days (NRS 118B.073).

title: Taxes on Rent
bodyText: Nevada's sales tax does not apply to residential rent: it is imposed on retail sales of tangible personal property, and a lease or rental counts as a sale only for tangible personal property (NRS 372.060(1), 372.105), not a dwelling. Do not add a sales-tax charge to rent. Short stays are different. Counties and cities tax the rental of transient lodging, and each defines by ordinance which lodging is taxed; in Clark County, and in its cities of 25,000 or more, the definition must include residential units and rooms in them (NRS 244.33565, 268.0195). If you rent a home or room for short stays, check the local room-tax ordinance and any short-term-rental permit rules (local ordinances not reviewed). Ordinary residential tenancies under chapter 118A exclude hotel and motel stays of under 30 consecutive days unless the occupant clearly intends to stay longer (NRS 118A.180(2)(f)). Separately, unless a written agreement makes the tenant pay the property tax or provides for calculating it and notifying the tenant of its amount, you must give tenants each July, and whenever rent changes, a statement of the part of each rent payment that represents property taxes (NRS 118.165).

title: Government Inspections of Rental Homes
bodyText: Nevada has no statewide program of routine inspections, certificates or permits for rental dwellings, and no statute that sets up or limits local rental-inspection programs (local ordinances may add rules, not reviewed). Inspections happen in narrower ways: a district board of health may inspect a unit after a tenant sends it a copy of an unanswered repair notice, a county or city may order repairs at a substandard multifamily property, housing authorities inspect units rented under the federal voucher program, and manufactured home parks need an annual health permit for their water and sewage systems. The lease cannot give a government inspector its own right to enter. Your right of entry is limited to the purposes the statute lists (inspecting, repairs, services and showing the unit), on at least 24 hours' notice at reasonable times, and outside an emergency, a court order, abandonment or surrender, you have no other right of access. The cautious course is to schedule any inspection as your own entry, with notice, and have the inspector come with you; the statute lets you show the unit to people with a bona fide interest in inspecting it. A tenant may also agree to a particular inspection directly. Case law was not reviewed.

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not regulate a landlord's requirement that a tenant carry renter's insurance: there is no rule on the tenant's choice of insurer, no force-placed coverage rule, no fee cap and no required notice that the landlord's insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings. A lease may require the tenant to carry renter's insurance (the library's renter's-insurance clause does so). The general lease rules still apply. The lease may not make the tenant release or limit your own liability for your acts or omissions or those of your agents or employees, or make the tenant indemnify you for it. Any required fee and its purpose must be stated in the lease. If you bill the tenant for insurance every rent period as a mandatory charge, it must be inside the single total rent figure, and you may not charge more than that figure. A charge meant to cover the tenant's damage to the unit is treated as a security deposit and counts toward the three-month limit. The cautious course is to require proof of the tenant's own policy rather than buying coverage and billing for it. Separately, an insurer may not refuse or raise the premium on a renter's policy because of a dog's breed alone. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Right to End a Lease Because a Repair Costs Too Much
bodyText: Nevada gives you no right to end a lease because a needed repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value, and cost is not an excuse from the habitability duty. Your statutory ways out are limited: you may end the lease if fire or casualty damage substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, unless the tenant, a household member or a guest caused it deliberately or negligently (NRS 118A.400(3)); you may end a periodic tenancy with at least 30 days' notice (7 days for week to week), or let a fixed term run out (NRS 40.251); and condemnation of the unit counts as cause for ending a tenancy (NRS 118A.060(4)). If a building, housing or health code citation requires alteration, remodeling or demolition that cannot be done unless the unit is vacant, ending the tenancy is not retaliation even if the tenant complained (NRS 118A.510(3)(c)). The cost limit in the repair statutes runs the other way: a tenant may repair and deduct only for work costing less than $100 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, and your liability for that remedy is capped at that amount in any 12 months (NRS 118A.360). A lease clause letting you end the tenancy early because of repair costs would have to work within these rules and could not waive the tenant's remedies (NRS 118A.220(1)(a)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Small-Landlord Exemption From Tenant Repair Remedies
bodyText: Nevada has no rule, and no notice you can give, that excuses a landlord with few units from the tenant's repair, rent-withholding or rent-escrow remedies. The landlord-tenant act applies to every rental agreement for a dwelling in the state except the listed situations, such as manufactured-home-park lots, public housing authority low-rent programs, hotel or motel stays under 30 days, employee housing conditional on employment and occupancy under a contract of sale; the number of units you own is not one of them (NRS 118A.180). So a tenant of a single house has the same remedies as a tenant in a large complex, and a lease term waiving them is void (NRS 118A.220). Rent withheld for a habitability failure goes through the justice courts' escrow mechanism: a tenant has that defense to eviction only after depositing the withheld rent into the court's escrow account (NRS 118A.355(5)). Unit counts matter only for other duties, such as smoke detectors in apartment buildings of three or more units, key-control policies for large complexes and receivership of multifamily properties. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Repair Notices: Written, With Two Exceptions
bodyText: Each of the tenant's repair remedies starts with written notice to you. For a lease breach or a habitability failure, the notice must specify the breach or each failure, and you then have 14 days to fix it or use best efforts (NRS 118A.350(1), 118A.355(1)); repair and deduct runs 14 days after the tenant notifies you in writing, or sooner in an emergency (NRS 118A.360(1)); and for heat, water, power, a working lock or another essential service, you have 48 hours, excluding weekends and legal holidays, after you receive the written notice (NRS 118A.380(1)). There are two exceptions: the tenant may recover damages without having given notice if you admit to the court that you knew of the condition, or if you received written notice of it from a government agency that inspects for building, housing or health code violations; and after such an agency notice the tenant may withhold rent if you do not fix the problem, or try in good faith to, within the time the agency's notice allows (NRS 118A.350(4), 118A.355(4), 118A.380(3)). A tenant's written notice may be delivered or mailed to the place of business the lease designates, or to any place you hold out for receiving rent, and is effective when delivered or mailed (NRS 118A.190(3)), so name that address in the lease. Nevada has no rule on oral repair requests: asking tenants to report problems in writing is consistent with the statutes, but it cannot take away the agency-notice and admitted-knowledge routes. Act on any report you receive, since under the act you have notice of what you actually know (NRS 118A.190(1)).

title: Required Lease Disclosures at a Glance
bodyText: Nevada's lease disclosure duties are: every written lease must address the subjects NRS 118A.200(3) lists, including a summary of the public-nuisance statute, how to report nuisances and code violations, and the tenant's flag and religious-display rights; rent must appear as one all-in figure, with a same-page asterisk statement for any separately billed utility (NRS 118A.200(6)-(8)); a single-family residence (up to four units, not a manufactured home) leased without a licensed property manager's signature needs the occupancy-presumption notice at the top of page one in type twice as large as any other (NRS 118A.200(4)); in writing at or before move-in, the names and addresses of the managers, an in-state agent for service and the owner, plus a local emergency phone number (NRS 118A.260), or posted notices instead (NRS 118A.270); in writing to a prospective tenant, any foreclosure proceedings (NRS 118A.275); on request, a copy of the lease to a prospective tenant (NRS 118A.235); a full translation before signing if you advertise and negotiate in another language (NRS 598.9733); each July and whenever rent changes, the property-tax share of each rent payment, unless a written agreement provides for the tax (NRS 118.165); on request, any district health board rental regulations (NRS 439.479(2)); and, for housing built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 4852d). Deaths, most crimes, non-transmissible illness and nearby sex offenders need not be disclosed (NRS 40.770). Nevada requires no notice of rent-regulation or just-cause coverage and no state form as the first page of the lease. If the lease gives the tenant an option to buy, the seller disclosure form is due at least 10 days before the property is conveyed, not at lease signing (NRS 113.130(1)(a)).

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: Nevada's statutes require no state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, before signing or at renewal, and no signed acknowledgment of one. The state's tenant handouts list help lines and legal aid; they are not required lease attachments. Two narrower duties exist: if your district board of health has adopted regulations on the condition of rental units, you must give a tenant a copy on request (NRS 439.479(2)); and a real estate licensee or property manager acting as an agent must give each party it acts for, and each unrepresented party, the Real Estate Division's form on the duties the licensee owes (NRS 645.252(3), 645.193).

title: No Duty to Give Tenants a Code Variance
bodyText: Nevada has no rule requiring you to give a tenant a copy of, or attach to the lease, a variance from a health, sanitation or fire code. Variances exist: the State Board of Health may grant one from its regulations if strict application would cause exceptional and undue hardship and the variance would not substantially harm the public welfare or the regulation's purpose (NRS 439.200(3)), and its regulations set the procedure, with applications going to the district board of health where that board enforces the regulation (NAC 439.200, 439.240); the State Fire Marshal may approve a variance from the adopted fire and building codes only for an alternate means and method at least equivalent in safety, requested by a licensed engineer or architect (NAC 477.287). A variance changes what the code demands of the property, but it does not change your habitability duty under the landlord-tenant act, which also covers the listed features (heat, plumbing, water, electrical, weatherproofing and the rest) whatever a code variance says (NRS 118A.290(1)). Follow any conditions the variance imposes. Local codes and their variance rules were not reviewed.

title: What the Landlord-Tenant Act Covers
bodyText: Nevada's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (NRS chapter 118A) governs every rental agreement, oral or written and wherever it is signed, for a dwelling in Nevada (NRS 118A.160, 118A.180(1)). It does not apply to: manufactured-home-park lot rentals under chapter 118B; low-rent programs run by public housing authorities under the federal Housing Act; residence in an institution for detention or for medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services; occupancy by a buyer under a contract of sale, or by a seller for up to 90 days under a purchase-and-sale agreement; occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in its building; a hotel or motel stay of less than 30 consecutive days unless the occupant clearly shows an intent to stay longer; employee housing that depends solely on employment in or about the premises; occupancy by a condominium owner or cooperative shareholder; premises used mainly for agriculture; and a person guilty of forcible entry or forcible detainer (NRS 118A.180(2)). Commercial premises, meaning any real property other than residential premises, are governed by chapter 118C (NRS 118C.040). Leases signed before July 1, 1977 and never renewed keep the earlier law, which no longer matters in practice because a month-to-month tenancy counts as renewed each month (NRS 118A.530). A lease cannot opt out of the act's protections (NRS 118A.220(1)(a)). Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Seasonal and Short-Term Rentals
bodyText: Nevada's statutes have no special rules for a seasonal or vacation lease of a dwelling. A rental for a fixed season is an ordinary fixed-term lease under the landlord-tenant act, with all of its rules, unless the occupancy falls outside the act, such as a stay in a hotel or motel of less than 30 consecutive days where the occupant has not clearly shown an intent to stay longer (NRS 118A.180(2)(f)). Renting a house or a room as short-term transient lodging is regulated mainly by local ordinance. In a county of 700,000 or more people, state law requires the county ordinance to require a permit, bar such rentals in apartment buildings, and set a minimum stay of 1 night for an owner-occupied unit and 2 nights otherwise, among other things (NRS 244.35351, 244.353545); the ordinances themselves, and city rules, were not reviewed. A manufactured-home-park lot rented for less than 3 months, or used only occasionally for recreation, is outside the park statute (NRS 118B.020). Case law was not reviewed.

title: Where the Deposit Is Held
bodyText: An owner who manages its own rentals has no statutory duty to hold an ordinary security deposit in a separate, trust or interest-bearing account, to name the bank, or to pay interest. The deposit is still the tenant's money in one respect: the tenant's claim to a deposit owed takes precedence over the claims of your creditors (NRS 118A.242(9)). Two rules do require a separate account. A real estate broker engaged in property management must keep client money in trust accounts in a Nevada bank or credit union, never commingled with the broker's own, and must keep two property-management trust accounts, one used solely for security deposits, with a ledger for each unit, reconciled monthly (NRS 645.310(3)-(5); NAC 645.655(8)-(9)). And if you require an additional deposit to secure restoration after a tenant with a disability makes a reasonable modification, it must be necessary for the restoration, may not exceed its actual cost, and must be held in an interest-bearing account with the interest paid to the tenant (NRS 118.101(4)). Keep records of every deposit you receive; a tenant may ask for a signed receipt (NRS 118A.250). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A lease cannot waive or change the tenant's security deposit rights. Except for a reasonable nonrefundable cleaning charge, no lease term may call any part of a security deposit nonrefundable, and any term waiving or modifying the deposit rules (the three-month cap, the 30-day itemized accounting and return, and the damages for late return) is void (NRS 118A.242(8)). Anything collected to cover unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear or cleaning is a security deposit whatever the lease calls it (NRS 118A.240), so a nonrefundable pet, damage or move-out fee is caught by the same rule. The general ban on waiving rights under the landlord-tenant act applies too, and the tenant may recover actual damages caused by a void term (NRS 118A.220).

title: The Deposit When the Property Changes Hands
bodyText: When your interest in a rental ends, by sale, assignment, death, appointment of a receiver or otherwise, you (or your agent) must within a reasonable time either (a) notify the tenant in writing of the successor's name, address and telephone number and that you have transferred the remaining deposit (after lawful deductions) to the successor, or (b) return the remaining deposit to the tenant. Doing one of these ends your liability for the deposit (NRS 118A.244(1)). Before you record a deed, you must also transfer the remaining deposits and other tenant money to the buyer in writing, or tell the buyer in writing that you have returned them (NRS 118A.244(2)). On a voluntary sale where the lease continues, the 2023 sale statute directs you to transfer the deposit with that written notice to the tenant, rather than refund it (NRS 118A.349(1)(c)). The successor takes on the deposit obligations owed at the time of transfer, must accept the tenant's existing deposit or surety bond, and may not require an additional deposit during the term of the rental agreement (NRS 118A.244(1), (3)); after a voluntary sale the new owner's 30-day notice to the tenant must state the amount of deposit it holds (NRS 118A.349(2)(b)). After a foreclosure sale of a building of up to four units, the new owner has the former landlord's chapter 118A obligations during the tenant's notice period (NRS 40.255(3)); how that applies to a deposit the buyer never received is not settled by statute, so a foreclosure buyer should get the deposit records and treat the deposit as owed. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Penalty for Keeping the Deposit
bodyText: If you fail or refuse to return the remainder of a security deposit within 30 days after the tenancy ends, you are liable to the tenant for an amount equal to the entire security deposit, plus a further sum the court may fix of up to the entire deposit again (NRS 118A.242(6)). In setting that further sum the court must consider whether you acted in good faith, the course of conduct between you and the tenant, and the degree of harm your conduct caused the tenant (NRS 118A.242(7)). The measure is the whole deposit, not just the part wrongly kept. Nevada's statutes do not add a separate forfeiture of your right to withhold or to sue for damage when the itemized accounting is late or missing, but the itemized accounting is a duty in its own right, due with the refund within the same 30 days (NRS 118A.242(4)). A lease term making the deposit nonrefundable (other than a reasonable cleaning charge) or waiving these rules is void (NRS 118A.242(8)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Rule on Posting Deposit Standards
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require any landlord, however many units it has, to post or hand out the standards it uses to set security deposits. You may set different deposits (for example by unit, credit result or pet) within the limits that do apply. The total of all deposits, any surety bond and any prepaid last month's rent may not exceed three months' periodic rent (NRS 118A.242(1)). You may not discriminate in the terms of a rental, expressly including the amount of deposits, because of race, religious creed, color, national origin, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, ancestry, familial status or sex (NRS 118.100(2)), and you may not raise your usual deposit because a tenant with a disability asks to make a reasonable modification, except for a separate restoration deposit held in an interest-bearing account (NRS 118.101(3)-(4)). Write your deposit standard down, apply it the same way to every applicant, and keep it on file. The lease must state each deposit required and the conditions for its refund (NRS 118A.200(3)(f)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Locks and Security Devices
bodyText: Nevada's statutes have no list of required security devices (deadbolts, door viewers, window latches) and no duty to rekey between tenants. Locks matter in three ways. First, a functioning door lock is an essential item: if the lease or the law requires you to supply one and you willfully or negligently fail to, making the unit unfit, the tenant's written notice gives you 48 hours (excluding weekends and legal holidays) before the essential-services remedies apply (NRS 118A.380(1)). Second, a tenant or cotenant who gives notice ending the lease because a tenant, cotenant or household member is a victim of domestic violence, harassment, sexual assault or stalking may require you to install a new lock at the tenant's cost; you comply by rekeying a lock in good working condition or replacing the whole mechanism with one of equal or better quality, you may keep a key, and you must refuse a key, and any access to reclaim property without a law enforcement officer present, to the adverse party (NRS 118A.345(8), (9)). Third, a complex of more than 50 units on one parcel in a county of 100,000 or more (more than 30 elsewhere) must have written key-control policies, a key log and background checks for staff with key access (NRS 118A.332). A 2025 bill that would have added locks on exterior doors and openable windows to the habitability list (AB 223) was vetoed and is not law. Locking a tenant out unlawfully is an exclusion that brings the lockout remedies (NRS 118A.090, 118A.390). Local building codes and ordinances may require specific hardware (not reviewed).

title: Refusing an Assistance Animal: Penalties
bodyText: Nevada's statutes set no criminal penalty aimed at a landlord who refuses to rent to a person with a disability because of an assistance, support or service animal. The consequences are civil: refusing to rent solely because such an animal will live with the person is barred by the fair housing law, and the person may file a complaint with the Nevada Equal Rights Commission or sue for actual damages, punitive damages, court costs and attorney's fees. A section in the crimes title also makes it unlawful to refuse to rent solely because of disability, but it states no penalty of its own and is enforced through the same civil action. The misdemeanor for refusing admittance or service to a person with a service animal, and the damages owed for charging a fee or deposit for one, apply to places of public accommodation, which include hotels and motels that lodge transient guests but do not list residential rentals; whether a rental office open to the public counts is not settled by the statutes. Unlike a place of public accommodation, a landlord may ask for proof that the animal assists, supports or serves the person with a disability. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Sex Offenders Nearby: No Duty to Disclose
bodyText: In any sale, lease or rental of real property, the fact that a sex offender resides or is expected to reside in the community is not material to the transaction, and you and your agent have no duty to disclose it to a tenant (NRS 40.770(2)). You are not liable to a tenant for failing to disclose it (NRS 40.770(4)). Nevada's statutes do not require a lease to tell tenants about the sex offender registry or to include a registry notice; the registration chapter places no duty on landlords. The rule covers only silence, so do not give a false answer if a prospective tenant asks. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Registered Offenders as Tenants
bodyText: Nevada's statutes put no duty or restriction on a landlord about renting to a registered sex offender: there is no rule against leasing near schools or parks, no limit on offenders living together, and no landlord registration or notice duty. The residence limits Nevada does have bind the offender, not you. A court granting probation for a sexual offense, and the parole board for lifetime supervision, must require that the offender live only at a residence approved by the offender's parole and probation officer, and in some cases (a Tier III offender whose victim was under 14) not within 1,000 feet of a place designed primarily for children; it is the offender and the supervising officer who must comply. You also have no duty to tell a tenant that a sex offender lives or is expected to live in the community, and that fact is not material to a lease. The registration statutes are duties of the offender and law enforcement, and they create no landlord duty. A residence that provides housing and a living environment for people released from prison who need help reintegrating is a separately regulated facility (not reviewed here). Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed); case law was not reviewed.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require a landlord to disclose shoreline, beach or water-access rights or restrictions to a tenant. Limits on lakefront or riverfront property come from recorded documents, association rules and regional or local rules, none reviewed here. If the property is in a common-interest community, the association's rules bind the tenant. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Advance Waiver of Showing Notice
bodyText: Nevada sets a fixed entry notice: except in an emergency you must give the tenant at least 24 hours' notice of intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times during normal business hours, and that applies to showing the unit to prospective tenants, buyers, lenders, contractors or others with a genuine interest (NRS 118A.330(1)(d), (3)). The tenant may agree to shorter notice or to entry outside business hours only by expressly consenting for the particular entry. A lease clause giving blanket advance consent to short-notice showings does not meet that test and would waive a right under the landlord-tenant act, so it is void and carries actual damages (NRS 118A.220); a separate signed document does not change that. The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to a properly noticed showing. If the tenant refuses lawful access you may get a court order compelling access or terminate the lease, and recover actual damages; an unlawful or harassing entry, or repeated harassing demands for entry, gives the tenant the same remedies against you (NRS 118A.330(1), 118A.500). Ask for the tenant's consent to each shorter-notice showing and keep a written record of it.

title: Renting Homes in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not limit long-term renting of a home in a single-family zone, and do not require the owner to live on the lot. The one state zoning rule on the point favors renting: in a county of 100,000 or more people or a city of 60,000 or more, the required accessory dwelling unit ordinance may not prohibit the owner from renting an accessory unit as housing, though it may prohibit renting it as short-term (transient) lodging. Short-term rentals are regulated separately: in a county of 700,000 or more people, the county's short-term rental ordinance must set a minimum stay of 1 night for an owner-occupied unit and 2 nights for one that is not owner-occupied, and must bar short-term rental of units in apartment buildings (its larger cities have parallel rules). A homeowners' association may restrict or cap rentals only as its declaration and the common-interest community law allow. Local zoning ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Smart Locks and App-Based Entry
bodyText: Nevada has no statute written specifically for smart locks, keypads or app-based entry systems in rentals, but existing rules reach them. At a large complex (more than 50 units on one parcel in a county of 100,000 or more people, or more than 30 units in a smaller county), your written key-control policies must cover electronic keys, combinations and access codes, including their use and deactivation, and you must keep a key log and background-check staff with key access (NRS 118A.332). Entry by code or app is still entry: outside an emergency you need at least 24 hours' notice and must enter at reasonable times during normal business hours, unless the tenant expressly agrees otherwise for that particular entry (NRS 118A.330(3)). Disabling or changing a tenant's code or credential to keep the tenant out is an unlawful exclusion, which includes prohibiting entry by locking doors, and lets the tenant seek expedited court relief, actual damages and up to $2,500 (NRS 118A.090, 118A.390, 118A.480). A functioning door lock is an essential item when the lease or the law requires you to supply it (NRS 118A.380). Privacy and data-security laws on information an entry system collects, and local ordinances, were not reviewed.

title: Smoke Drift and Smoke-Free Common Areas
bodyText: Nevada has no statute on tobacco or other smoke drifting between rental units, and none that lets a lease make the tenant waive complaints about it. The Nevada Clean Indoor Air Act bans smoking in any form, including vaping, in indoor places of employment, which it defines as enclosed areas under an employer's control that employees frequent during work, expressly including hallways, lobbies and restrooms; private residences are exempt (NRS 202.2483(1), (3)(g), (13)(j)). The Act does not mention apartment buildings, so whether it reaches a building's common hallways is not settled. Cautious course: treat enclosed common hallways, lobbies and other enclosed common areas that your employees frequent as smoke-free, post No Smoking signs at their entrances and remove ashtrays (NRS 202.2483(10)); the units themselves are private residences. Counties, cities and towns may adopt stricter smoking rules (NRS 202.2483(9)); local ordinances were not reviewed. No smoke-drift waiver clause is offered for Nevada: no statute authorizes one, and a term making the tenant give up rights under the landlord-tenant act, or excusing your own liability, would be void (NRS 118A.220). The library's Smoking Policy clause bans smoking on the property instead.

title: No Defense for a Late Benefit Check
bodyText: No Nevada statute or court rule gives a tenant a defense, a continuance or reinstatement in an eviction because a Social Security check, other government benefit or a housing-voucher payment arrived late. The ordinary nonpayment rules apply: the tenant can pay within the pay-or-quit period, and the court may stay removal for up to 10 days. Two narrower protections exist. In the Housing Choice Voucher program, the family is not responsible for the housing authority's share of the rent, the authority's failure to pay is not a lease violation by the tenant, and during the lease term you may not end the tenancy for the authority's nonpayment (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.310(b)); pursue the authority under your payment contract instead. And during a federal, state or tribal government shutdown, a qualifying government worker or household member who gives you proof is outside the pay-or-quit summary-eviction process, a lease term requiring rent at a set time can't be enforced against that tenant, and you must accept the rent for the shutdown period for up to 30 days after it ends (NRS 40.2512(2), 40.253(12)(b), 118A.310(2)). That protection turns on the tenant's government job, not on receiving benefits. Bills in 2023 and 2025 that would have added protections for tenants who rely on Social Security were vetoed and are not law. Some justice courts refer nonpayment cases to rental-assistance or eviction diversion programs. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Special Districts: No Lease Statement Required
bodyText: No Nevada statute requires a lease to disclose that the property lies in a special district or improvement district, or to address the tenant's role in one. Tenants are not shut out, though. When a city or county forms a district for a neighborhood improvement project, it must mail notice of the hearing to each owner and to each tenant who lives or owns a business in the proposed district, and a tenant may object at the hearing. In a general improvement district, the trustees are elected by the district's qualified electors, meaning people registered to vote in district elections. Special assessments are levied on the owner's land; if you pass a share to the tenant as a mandatory periodic charge, it must be included in the single total rent figure. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure in the Lease
bodyText: Nevada's statutes and the state fire regulations do not require you to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, whether the building has a sprinkler system or when it was last inspected. The rules on sprinklers that do exist govern installation and upkeep, not disclosure: high-rise apartment buildings must have sprinklers in exit corridors (NRS 477.150), and every automatic sprinkler system must be inspected quarterly, with records kept on site and deficiencies corrected within 30 days of a licensed firm's written notice (NAC 477.460). Nevada also has no state grant or loan program for sprinkler retrofits in private rentals in the statutes searched. You may describe fire-safety equipment in the lease if you choose. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be in Writing
bodyText: A lease for more than one year is void unless the lease, or a note or memorandum of it stating the rent or other consideration, is in writing and signed by the party making the lease, which is you or your authorized agent (NRS 111.210). No interest in land other than a lease for a term of one year or less can be created except by operation of law or a signed writing, and an agent signing for you under that section must be authorized in writing (NRS 111.205(1)). An agreement that by its terms cannot be performed within one year, and a promise to pay another person's debt, such as a guaranty of the tenant's rent, must also be in writing and signed by the person bound (NRS 111.220(1)-(2)). A lease for one year or less may be oral, and an oral rental agreement is covered by the landlord-tenant act (NRS 118A.160). Any written lease must be signed by you or your agent and by the tenant or the tenant's agent, and the tenant gets a free copy (NRS 118A.200(1)-(2)). Whether part performance can save an unsigned long lease is a question for case law, which was not reviewed: put every lease in writing and have every party sign it.

title: Nevada's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Nevada's money limits for dwelling leases, at a glance. Rent: no cap on amount or frequency of increases, but the lease must state rent as one all-in figure including every mandatory fee, you may not charge more than that figure, and an increase needs 60 days' written notice (30 for a periodic tenancy under a month) (NRS 118A.200(6)-(7), 118A.300). Security: all deposits, any surety bond and prepaid last month's rent together may not exceed 3 months' periodic rent; only a reasonable cleaning charge may be nonrefundable; return the balance with an itemized accounting within 30 days, or owe the whole deposit plus up to the same again (NRS 118A.242(1), (4), (6), (8)). Late fee: reasonable, stated in the lease, no more than 5% of the periodic rent, and in a tenancy longer than week to week not until 3 calendar days after the due date (NRS 118A.210(4)). Returned check: the check amount plus damages of 3 times the check, at least $100 and at most $500, after a certified-mail demand unpaid for 30 days (NRS 41.620(1)); a $25 cap on a seller's dishonored-check fee whose reach to rent is unsettled (NRS 597.960). Payment portal fee: no more than the operator charges, with at least one fee-free method (NRS 118A.303). Application fees: no cap, but refund in the stated case and none for a minor in the household (NRS 118A.306). Interest on money owed: without a written rate, the prime rate at Nevada's largest bank plus 2% (NRS 99.040(1)); a written agreement may set another rate (NRS 99.050(1)). Remedies with fixed figures: tenant repair-and-deduct up to $100 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, in 12 months (NRS 118A.360); up to $2,500 for an unlawful lockout or utility shutoff (NRS 118A.390(1)); $250 per deceptive rent-figure violation (NRS 118A.405). Manufactured-home parks have their own limits (chapter 118B). Local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: When the Law Lets a Tenant End the Lease Early
bodyText: Whatever the lease says, Nevada law lets a tenant end a residential lease early in these situations. Health or age: a tenant 60 or older or with a physical or mental disability who must move for care or treatment, or who loses a spouse or co-tenant, may end it on written notice (NRS 118A.340). Violence: a tenant, co-tenant or household member who is a victim of domestic violence, harassment, sexual assault or stalking may end it on written notice with the required documentation (NRS 118A.345). Your breach: if you fail to comply with the lease, or to keep the unit habitable, and don't fix a remediable problem or make best efforts within 14 days after the tenant's written notice, the tenant may terminate immediately (NRS 118A.350, 118A.355). Possession and lockouts: if you fail to deliver possession, the tenant may end the lease on 5 days' written notice (NRS 118A.370); if you unlawfully lock out the tenant or willfully cut off essential services, the tenant may terminate (NRS 118A.390). Casualty: if fire or other casualty substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may leave and give notice (NRS 118A.400). Foreclosure: after a foreclosure sale of a building of up to four units, the tenant may leave at any time during the notice period without further obligation to the new owner (NRS 40.255(6)(a)). Military service: federal law lets a servicemember end a residential lease after entering service or receiving qualifying orders, and lets a spouse or dependent end it after the servicemember's death in service or a catastrophic service injury or illness (FEDERAL: 50 U.S.C. § 3955(a)). Nevada has no statute letting a tenant end a lease for the landlord's fraudulent misrepresentation (ordinary contract law and case law, not reviewed here, govern that), and none that makes a landlord forfeit accrued rent for leaving a required statement out of the lease; instead, a lease that omits required terms is unlawful to use and a nonconforming provision is void, and a tenant may sue over a rent figure that does not include all mandatory fees (NRS 118A.200(9), 118A.405).

title: No Radiator Cover Rule or Lease Rider
bodyText: Nevada's statutes and the state regulations reviewed have no requirement to cover steam radiators on request and no radiator-cover rider or notice for a lease. Heating equipment falls under the general habitability duty: the unit must not substantially lack adequate heating facilities that met the law when installed and are kept in good working order (NRS 118A.290(1)(d)), and a heating hazard that violates a housing or health code concerning health or safety also makes the unit not habitable (NRS 118A.290(1)). Local building and housing codes may address heating equipment safety (not reviewed).

title: Stigmatized Property: Deaths, Crimes and Illness
bodyText: In any sale, lease or rental of real property, three kinds of fact are not material to the transaction: that the property is or has been the site of a homicide, suicide or death from any other cause, except a death that results from a condition of the property; the site of a felony, other than methamphetamine manufacture; or occupied by a person exposed to or suffering from a disease that is not known to be transmitted through occupancy (NRS 40.770(1)). A licensed transitional-living facility for released offenders near the property is also not material (NRS 40.770(3)). You and your agent are not liable to a tenant for failing to disclose such a fact, or one you had no actual knowledge of (NRS 40.770(4)). The rule does not reach a death caused by a condition of the property, or a former methamphetamine lab that has not been remediated by a certified or licensed entity or deemed safe for habitation by the board of health (NRS 40.770(6)): disclose a death caused by a condition of the property, and do not rent a former methamphetamine lab at all until it has been remediated and deemed safe: while it has not been deemed safe, letting it be used for any purpose before a certified or licensed entity has remediated it makes it a public nuisance (NRS 202.450(4)). The statute protects only silence, so do not give a false answer if a prospective tenant asks. A real estate licensee acting as an agent in the lease must still disclose material and relevant facts it knows or should have known about the property (NRS 645.252(1)(a)). The seller disclosure form law applies to sales, not leases (NRS 113.100, 113.130). Case law was not reviewed.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator, but Supplied Appliances Must Work
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require you to supply a stove, oven or refrigerator in a rental, and the habitability list does not name them. What you do supply counts: ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, must be kept in good repair if you supply them or are required to (NRS 118A.290(1)(i)), and you may not charge the tenant a fee for that repair work, including a home-warranty deductible or copay, unless the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the problem deliberately or negligently (NRS 118A.290(4), (5)). If the lease says you will supply an appliance, failing to supply it is a breach of the rental agreement the tenant can act on after written notice (NRS 118A.350). The tenant must use appliances in a reasonable manner (NRS 118A.310(1)(e)). List the appliances that come with the unit in the lease so both sides know which ones you maintain. A 2025 state law on accessory dwelling units requires large counties and cities not to prohibit separate kitchen facilities (sink, refrigerator and a cooking appliance) in an accessory unit; it governs zoning approval, not what a landlord must supply (NRS 278.257). Local codes may require cooking facilities (not reviewed).

title: Renting to Students
bodyText: Nevada has no special rules for renting to students: no student-housing license or certification, no rule on parental guarantors or academic-year leases, and no special termination right for students. Renting to students is ordinary renting, and the landlord-tenant law applies in full. Two points to note. Residence in an institution incident to the provision of educational or similar services is outside the landlord-tenant law, so a college dormitory is governed by the institution's own terms, not by this lease. And student status is not a protected class under Nevada's fair housing law, but familial status, disability and the other listed classes still apply to student applicants. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed); case law was not reviewed.

title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText: Nevada has no statute about refusing a voucher tenancy because of the program's inspection, and no special remedy when a subsidized tenant refuses to let the inspector in. Source of income is not a protected class under Nevada's fair housing law, so declining to join a voucher program is not itself a state fair housing violation, as long as the real reason is not race, disability, familial status or another protected trait (local ordinances may add rules, not reviewed). Nevada does require each housing authority to inspect units leased under the federal voucher program on the schedule the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) requires, to have the tenant sign to confirm the inspection, and, if repairs are needed, to see that they are made as soon as practicable, in coordination with the private owner. If the tenant blocks entry, the state access rule is the ordinary one: a tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to the landlord's entry to inspect, on at least 24 hours' notice at reasonable times. That rule names the landlord, not a housing authority inspector, so attend or send your agent to the inspection. The voucher family also has its own federal program duty to allow the housing authority to inspect the unit at reasonable times after reasonable notice (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.551(d)). A refusal is handled through the ordinary access remedies (court order or termination). Under the federal program rules, the housing authority may withhold and then abate its payment if you do not fix deficiencies in time; you may not end the tenancy because the payment was withheld or abated, and the authority's failure to pay is not the tenant's lease violation.

title: No Rule for Splitting a Rent Reduction With a Subsidy
bodyText: Nevada's statutes have no special rule for reducing rent when part of a subsidized unit becomes uninhabitable, and do not say whether a reduction is measured on the tenant's share or on the full contract rent including the subsidy. The general rules apply to every tenant: after a fire or casualty, a tenant who vacates the unusable part owes rent reduced in proportion to the drop in fair rental value or lack of use (NRS 118A.400(1)(b)); rent abates fully while you fail to deliver possession (NRS 118A.370) or while the tenant uses substitute housing after an essential-service failure (NRS 118A.380(1)(d)). The act defines rent as all periodic payments to be made to you for occupancy (NRS 118A.150), which does not settle who bears the reduction when an agency pays part. For a housing choice voucher tenancy, federal rules govern the agency's share: if you do not correct a housing quality standards deficiency within 24 hours (life-threatening) or 30 days of the agency's notice, the agency must abate its assistance payment, does not repay it for the abated period if you later make the repairs, and you may not end the tenancy because the payment was withheld or abated (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(d)). Check your HAP contract and the agency's administrative plan. Public housing authority low-rent programs are outside Nevada's landlord-tenant act (NRS 118A.180(2)(b)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Late Fees for Subsidized Tenants
bodyText: Nevada's statutes set no special late-fee rule for tenants whose rent is partly paid by a housing subsidy; the general rule applies: a reasonable late fee stated in the lease, no more than 5% of the periodic rent, and in a tenancy longer than week to week not until at least 3 calendar days after rent is due (NRS 118A.210(4)). The statute doesn't say whether the 5% is measured on the full contract rent or on the tenant's share; measure it on the tenant's share. For a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) tenancy, federal rules also apply: the family is not responsible for the part of the rent covered by the housing assistance payment, the housing agency's failure to pay is not a lease violation and is not grounds to end the tenancy, and you may not demand or accept from the tenant more than the rent to owner minus the assistance payment (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. §§ 982.310(b), 982.451(b)(4)). So charge a late fee only when the tenant's own share is late, never because the agency paid late. The voucher contract must provide penalties against the agency for its late payments if they follow local practice, you charge them to assisted and unassisted tenants alike, and you also charge them to the tenant for late family rent, though the agency owes no penalty if HUD finds the late payment was due to factors beyond its control (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.451(b)(5)(ii)). Public-housing-authority low-rent programs are outside chapter 118A (NRS 118A.180(2)(b)); follow the program's rules and the lease addendum for any subsidized unit.

title: Passing Tax and Insurance Increases to Tenants
bodyText: No Nevada statute authorizes or regulates passing property-tax or insurance increases through to a residential tenant, but the rent rules make a pass-through clause risky.
