Every mandatory fee must be inside the single figure the lease states as the maximum total periodic rent, and you may not charge more than that figure (NRS 118A.200(6)-(7)); a share of a later tax or premium increase, billed on top of rent, is the kind of extra charge those rules forbid, and a tenant can sue for damages, costs and attorney's fees plus $250 for each violation involving deception (NRS 118A.405). Any rent increase also needs 60 days' written notice (NRS 118A.300). The safer course is to build expected tax and insurance costs into the rent, or schedule fixed increases in the lease with each amount stated as a single all-in figure. If a written agreement does make the tenant pay the property tax, or provides for calculating it and notifying the tenant of its amount, you are excused from the annual property-tax statement (NRS 118.165(3)(a)); otherwise give it each July and whenever rent changes (NRS 118.165(1)). In a manufactured-home park, no fee, surcharge or rent increase may recover more than the cost of a governmentally mandated service or tax you actually paid (NRS 118B.140(1)(b)(9)). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Cable, Satellite and Antenna Access
bodyText: Nevada law protects a tenant's choice of video service. You may not interfere with a tenant's receipt of service from a video service provider or discriminate against a tenant for getting it, and you may not demand or accept a fee or anything of value from the provider or the tenant for granting the provider access, except the reasonable compensation the statute allows for the direct economic effect of access (presumed to be the greater of $1,000 or $1 per dwelling unit, unless you notify the provider of a larger claim). The provider must give you 30 days' written notice before acting, and you may impose reasonable safety, function and appearance conditions, make the provider bear installation and removal costs and require indemnity for damage. Federal law adds the antenna rule: a lease provision, rule or similar restriction that impairs a tenant's installation, maintenance or use of a satellite dish or fixed-wireless antenna one meter or less across, or a TV broadcast antenna and its mast, on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control is prohibited, except restrictions needed for a clearly defined safety objective or historic preservation, and any fee must be reasonable. That rule does not give a tenant a right to install on common areas or the roof. If you develop a property and shut out the incumbent telephone carrier, commission rules may require written notice to tenants about possible construction charges for that carrier's service.

title: Tenancy at Will
bodyText: For a dwelling covered by the landlord-tenant act, a tenancy with no definite term is week to week if the tenant pays weekly rent and month to month in every other case (NRS 118A.210(2)), and a tenant who stays on with your consent after the lease ends becomes a periodic tenant the same way (NRS 118A.470). So an ordinary residential tenant who pays rent is not a tenant at will. To end such a tenancy without cause you serve the 7-day (week-to-week) or 30-day (other periodic) notice, with the required statement of the tenant's extension rights; a 5-day notice applies only where the tenant has failed to perform basic or lease obligations (NRS 40.251(1)(b), (2)-(5)). The eviction statute's 5-day notice for a tenancy at will sits in the separate paragraph for real property in general (NRS 40.251(1)(a)(3)); it can matter for an occupancy outside the landlord-tenant act, and whether a particular arrangement is a tenancy at will is a question for case law, which was not reviewed. When in doubt, treat the occupant as a periodic tenant and give the longer notice.

title: When a Tenant Files Bankruptcy
bodyText: Bankruptcy is federal law, and Nevada's statutes add nothing specific about a residential tenant's bankruptcy. Under the Bankruptcy Code, the tenant's filing automatically stays most actions against the tenant: starting or continuing a court case, including an eviction, on a claim that arose before the filing, enforcing a judgment obtained before the filing, any act to obtain possession of property of the bankruptcy estate, and any act to collect a pre-filing debt (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)). There are two residential exceptions. If you obtained a judgment for possession before the filing, you may continue the eviction, but if the tenant certifies with the petition that state law lets the tenant cure the entire money default after judgment and deposits the next 30 days' rent with the clerk, the stay continues for 30 days, and if the tenant certifies a full cure within those 30 days, the exception does not apply; you may object to either certification and get a hearing within 10 days (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(b)(22), (l)). Nevada's 5-day right to pay a rent judgment on an unexpired lease (NRS 40.360(3)) is the kind of state cure right the tenant may cite. And you may pursue an eviction based on endangerment of the property or illegal drug use there by filing and serving a sworn certification; it takes effect 15 days later unless the tenant objects (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(b)(23), (m)). Otherwise ask the bankruptcy court for relief from the stay (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(d)). A willful violation exposes you to actual damages, costs and attorney's fees, and sometimes punitive damages (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(k)(1)). A lease term that ends the lease because the tenant files bankruptcy or becomes insolvent can't be enforced after the case begins (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 365(e)(1)); in a chapter 7 case, a residential lease the trustee does not assume within 60 days is deemed rejected, and a trustee can assume a lease in default only by curing it and giving adequate assurance of future performance (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 365(b)(1), (d)(1)). Rent for the period after the filing is not a pre-filing claim, but whether and how you may collect it or evict for it is a bankruptcy-court question; get advice before acting.

title: Protecting Tenant and Applicant Information
bodyText: Nevada's landlord-tenant act has no general rule that bars you from sharing tenant information or sets a consent rule for disclosing it; its one disclosure ban is for domestic violence: once a tenant gives notice ending the lease under NRS 118A.345, you may not give the adverse party any information about where the tenant, cotenant or household member is (NRS 118A.345(7)). Nevada's general data-security law does reach the personal information you collect from applicants and tenants, meaning a name together with a Social Security number, driver's license or ID card number, a financial account or card number with its access code, a medical or health insurance ID number, or an online user name or e-mail address with its password or security question and answer. A business entity that handles that information must keep reasonable security measures to protect it, and any contract under which you disclose it (for example to a screening company or a property manager) must require the recipient to do the same. A business must take reasonable measures to destroy customer records containing personal information, such as shredding or erasing them, once it decides not to keep them. If unencrypted computerized personal information you own or license is, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person, you must notify each affected Nevada resident in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, and also notify the nationwide consumer reporting agencies if more than 1,000 people must be notified at one time. A lease term waiving these rules is void, and a violation is a deceptive trade practice. Whether an individual owner who is not a business entity is a data collector (security and breach-notice duties) is not settled by the statute; the destruction duty reaches any proprietorship doing business in Nevada (NRS 603A.200(2)(a)). The cautious course is to follow all these rules. Federal rules separately require anyone who holds information from consumer reports to dispose of it properly. If a tenant ends a lease because of domestic violence, harassment, sexual assault or stalking, you may not describe that termination to a prospective landlord as an early termination. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: Nevada has no statute that ends a residential lease when a tenant dies, and none that sets a special procedure for a sole tenant's death, a deceased tenant's belongings or the deposit. Two rules touch the subject. The death of one tenant does not by itself give you a right to end the lease. And a surviving tenant who is 60 or older or has a physical or mental disability may end the lease on 60 days' written notice given within 3 months after the death of a spouse or co-tenant (NRS 118A.340(2), (4)). Otherwise the lease's terms, contract law and estate law govern: the deceased tenant's obligations and rights pass to the estate, and you deal with the personal representative or, for a small estate with no Nevada real property, a successor who presents the statutory affidavit at least 40 days after the death (available when the estate's Nevada property is worth no more than $25,000, or $150,000 for a surviving spouse). If you rely in good faith on an affidavit containing the required information when you release money or property to the affiant, you are immune from civil liability for that reliance (NRS 146.080(1), (4)). The abandoned-property procedure covers property left after an eviction, abandonment or the end of the rental period, so once the tenancy has ended, use it for belongings no one claims. No statute lets the lease require a tenant to name someone with authority to remove property or receive the deposit on death; an emergency contact named in the lease is only a person to call. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Housing Provided to an Employee
bodyText: Nevada's landlord-tenant act does not apply to occupancy by your employee whose right to occupy is solely conditional on employment in or about the premises (an on-site manager or maintenance worker housed as part of the job). An employee who rents under an ordinary lease, not tied to the job, is a regular tenant. So decide which you intend and say so in writing. If the housing is part of the employment, the employment contract governs, with wage-law limits: lodging may count as part of wages only if you and the employee agree to it in the employment contract, and its value may not be computed at more than five times the state minimum hourly wage for each week (agricultural employees excepted). For a domestic worker who lives in your household, you may deduct for lodging only if the worker freely accepts it and consents in writing, never if living there is required; and if you end the employment without cause, you must give written notice and at least 30 days of lodging, on site or comparable. Even where the landlord-tenant act does not apply, entry onto property must be peaceable, so remove a former employee through the courts, not by force. In a company town, utility charges to occupants are limited to their share of your cost.

title: Renter's Insurance and Insurance Claims
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not require renter's insurance, bar a lease from requiring it, cap the coverage you may require, or govern how a tenant's or your insurance claim is handled between you, so the lease decides. The library's "Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" clause, which carries Nevada, requires coverage without a landlord disclaimer. Limits that apply: a lease may not make the tenant release you from, limit, or indemnify you for liability based on your own or your agents' acts or omissions, and such a term is void; you may not charge the tenant a home-warranty deductible or copayment for repairs that are your duty; a premium a tenant pays for a surety bond or similar insurance securing the tenant's obligations is not a security deposit. Insurers may not refuse, cancel, refuse to renew or raise the premium on a renter's or homeowner's policy because of a dog's breed (they may act on a dog known or declared to be dangerous or vicious). What to do: state any required coverage and minimum in the lease, ask for proof, and keep your own property and liability coverage.

title: Online Tenant Portals
bodyText: Nevada has no portal statute as such, but three rules shape one. Payment: you must always offer at least one way to pay rent and other charges that costs the tenant nothing to use and does not require bank-account information (a check is allowed), so a portal can't be the only way to pay if it charges a fee or needs bank details; any portal fee you pass on may not exceed what the portal operator charges and must be separately identified in the written lease. Electronic dealings: the Electronic Transactions Act applies only between parties who have agreed to deal electronically, and a tenant who agreed may refuse to conduct later transactions electronically, a right the lease cannot waive. Notices: written notices to a tenant under the landlord-tenant act must be served in the way the eviction statutes prescribe, and a notice of default, eviction or the right to cure for a tenant's primary residence never satisfies a writing requirement if given electronically. So use a portal as a convenience, keep a fee-free payment method and paper notices, and don't make portal use for notices or signatures mandatory. The library's optional portal clause is drafted that way.

title: Tenant Records, Receipts and Data Security
bodyText: Nevada does not require a landlord who manages its own rentals to keep a rent ledger, to give a tenant a ledger or payment history, or to attach one to a nonpayment notice; a real estate broker who manages the property must keep a ledger account for each unit and reconcile its trust accounts monthly (NAC 645.655(8)-(9)). It does require a signed written receipt, on the tenant's request, for any deposit, surety bond, fee or rent payment, and the tenant may withhold rent until you tender the requested receipt. Data security: Nevada's data-security law covers any business entity that handles nonpublic personal information, which includes a name combined with a Social Security, driver's license or ID number, a financial account or card number with its access code, a medical or health insurance identification number, or an online username or e-mail address with its password or security question and answer. Such a business must keep reasonable security measures for those records, must require anyone it discloses the information to by contract to do the same, must notify affected Nevada residents of a breach of computerized data in the most expedient time possible (and the nationwide credit bureaus if more than 1,000 people must be notified), and must take reasonable measures to destroy customer records it will no longer keep (shredding or erasing). These duties cannot be waived. Federal law adds a disposal rule for information derived from consumer reports, such as tenant-screening reports: dispose of it by reasonable measures, such as shredding paper or erasing electronic files. The destruction duty reaches a proprietorship doing business in Nevada (NRS 603A.200(2)(a)); whether an individual owner renting one home is a data collector for the security and breach-notice duties is not settled, so follow those rules anyway.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: Nevada protects tenant organizing through its retaliation law: you may not, in retaliation, end a tenancy, refuse to renew it, raise rent, cut essential services the lease or the landlord-tenant act requires, or bring or threaten an eviction because a tenant has organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization. A tenant who suffers retaliation gets the same remedies as for an unlawful lockout, including actual damages and up to $2,500, and has a defense to a retaliatory eviction. Acting with cause, or raising rent uniformly for all tenants, is not retaliation. For ordinary rentals, Nevada's statutes give no affirmative right to meet in common areas or to distribute organizing literature there; in manufactured-home parks, the landlord may not bar or charge for tenants' meetings in the park's community facility at reasonable hours, may not ban the distribution of meeting notices, and may not stop tenants from soliciting membership in a tenants' association. What to do: treat organizing as protected, apply common-area rules evenly, and document the real reason for any non-renewal or rent change.

title: No State Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Nevada's statutes require no state-agency statement of tenant rights attached to the lease or signed by the tenant, and providing one is not a condition of suing. The lease itself must carry certain tenant-facing information: a summary of the public-nuisance statute, how to report a nuisance or a building, safety or health code violation, and the tenant's rights to display the U.S. flag and religious or cultural items (NRS 118A.200(3)(l)-(o)). The only first-page notice is the single-family occupancy disclosure, where it applies (NRS 118A.200(4)). Eviction notices carry their own required statements.

title: Screening Applicants
bodyText: Nevada has no tenant-screening statute: nothing limits criminal-history checks to after a conditional offer, sets look-back periods, limits income tests, or shields you for renting to someone with a record. The rules that do apply: screening criteria may not treat applicants differently because of race, religious creed, color, national origin, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, ancestry, familial status or sex; you must refund an application, credit-report or background-check fee if you rent to someone else without doing what the fee paid for, and you may not charge those fees for a minor in the applicant's household. A person whose criminal record a court has sealed may properly answer an inquiry as if the proceedings never happened, so don't penalize an applicant for that answer; a sealed eviction file is treated as never having occurred. Federal law: you may obtain a consumer report for a business transaction the applicant initiates, and if you deny an application or take other adverse action based even partly on a consumer report, you must give the applicant notice of the adverse action, the reporting agency's contact details, a statement that the agency did not make the decision, and notice of the right to a free report and to dispute it, plus any credit score used. Keep and dispose of screening reports securely.

title: Tenant's Duties Under the Landlord-Tenant Act
bodyText: Nevada's landlord-tenant act gives every tenant basic obligations whatever the lease says: comply with the lease; keep the part of the premises the tenant occupies and uses as clean and safe as its condition permits; dispose of ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste cleanly and safely; keep plumbing fixtures as clean as their condition permits; use electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, reasonably; not deliberately or negligently make the premises uninhabitable or damage, deface or remove any part of them, or knowingly let anyone else do so; and behave, and require guests to behave, so as not to disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment. One exception: a lease term setting a rent due date is unenforceable against a federal, tribal or state worker or household member during a government shutdown, subject to the landlord's petition right. If a tenant breaches, you may recover damages and seek an injunction; give a written notice specifying the breach, and if a remediable breach is not remedied (or best efforts begun) within 5 days, you may terminate; for a failure you can fix by repair, replacement or cleaning, after 14 days' written notice you may do the work and bill the actual, reasonable cost, payable as rent on the next due date. The library's tenant-maintenance clause restates these duties in the lease.

title: Changing Lease Terms: Notice Rules
bodyText: Nevada sets notice rules for two kinds of change and none for the rest. Rent: you may not increase rent without written notice served at least 60 days before the first increased payment, or 30 days for a periodic tenancy of less than a month (NRS 118A.300). Because every mandatory periodic fee must be included in the single rent figure and you may not charge more than that figure (NRS 118A.200(6)-(7)), the cautious course is to treat raising a mandatory fee as a rent increase and give the same notice. House rules: a rule adopted after the tenant signs that materially changes the bargain binds the tenant only if the tenant agrees in writing or has 30 days' advance written notice, and no rule may change rent, utilities or other charges, or take away a pet the lease allows before the lease ends (NRS 118A.320). Anything else: no statute lets you change a lease term by notice. During a fixed term, a change needs the tenant's written agreement. In a periodic tenancy, the lawful routes are a signed amendment or ending the tenancy with the 7-day or 30-day notice and offering a new lease (NRS 40.251). Notices are served as the eviction statutes require (NRS 118A.190(2)), and no change may be made in retaliation for protected tenant activity (NRS 118A.510). Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Purchase-Right Exemption Notice
bodyText: Because Nevada has no general tenant opportunity-to-purchase law, and no rent-limit or just-cause law with an exemption scheme, there is no exemption notice, filing or statement of exempt status to give tenants or record. The only tenant purchase right, on a condominium or other common-interest conversion, has built-in limits: the offer to the tenant does not apply to a unit that will be restricted to nonresidential use or whose boundaries do not substantially match the residential unit before conversion. A good-faith buyer who pays value without knowing of a violation takes the unit free of the tenant's purchase right if the deed states that the seller complied with the offer requirement, though the tenant can still sue the seller for damages. What to do: on an ordinary sale there is nothing to file or send; on a conversion, document which units fall outside the tenant offer and why, and have the deed recite compliance.

title: Tenant Purchase Rights on Conversion
bodyText: Nevada gives residential tenants no general right to buy, and no right of first refusal, when an owner sells a rental building, and no notice of sale is owed to tenants of an ordinary rental (the lease continues; see the library's sale-of-property row). The exception is a condominium or other common-interest conversion: the declarant, and any dealer who intends to offer units, must give each residential tenant and subtenant in possession notice of the conversion and the public offering statement at least 120 days before requiring them to vacate, hand-delivered or mailed; no tenant may be required to vacate on less than 120 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste or conduct disturbing other tenants, and the tenancy's terms may not change during that period. For 60 days after the notice, the unit must be offered to the tenant who leases it, and if the tenant does not buy, it may not be offered to anyone else for the next 180 days at a better price or on better terms. Failing to give the notice is a defense to an action for possession. Manufactured-home parks (chapter 118B) have their own rules: a landlord converting a park into lots for sale must offer each tenant the lot at the public price for at least 90 days, and a landlord listing a park for sale must notify a tenants' association that has asked for notice.

title: No Sunset on Nevada Tenant Laws
bodyText: No section of Nevada's landlord-tenant act, its fair-housing chapter, its manufactured-home-park chapter or its eviction statutes carries a dated repeal or expiration clause, and none of the 2023 or 2025 acts in our corpus puts a tenant protection on a repeal clock. Treat these rules as permanent until the Legislature changes them. Two dated items to watch: three fair-housing complaint sections exist in two versions, and the second takes effect only when the Governor declares that the federal government has found Nevada's fair-housing law substantially equivalent; until then the current version applies. And thirteen 2025 vetoed bills, several on tenancy (including AB 283 on summary eviction), go to the 2027 session, where two-thirds of each house could override the vetoes; until then they are not law. Court-rule deadlines (for example, a summary-eviction order expiring if not executed within 30 days in some justice courts) are procedural, not sunsets.

title: Trespass Warnings on Rental Property
bodyText: Nevada's trespass statute makes it a misdemeanor to go onto land or into a building of another to vex or annoy the owner or occupant or to commit an unlawful act, or to willfully go onto or stay on land or in a building after the owner or occupant has warned the person not to trespass within the previous 36 months (NRS 207.200(1)). A sufficient warning can be given by posting "no trespassing" signs (at each corner and at intervals of no more than 500 feet), fencing, fluorescent orange paint marks, or, for a guest, by an oral or written demand to vacate; being found on posted or fenced property without lawful business with the owner or occupant is prima facie evidence of trespass (NRS 207.200(2)-(3)). So you or your manager may warn a non-tenant who has no business on the property to stay out of common areas you control, and a person who returns after the warning can be reported to police. Limits: the statute's "guest" demand method excludes a tenant, so trespass is not a way to remove a tenant, who must be evicted through the courts; and a tenant's dwelling is in the tenant's possession, so the tenant, as occupant, decides who may visit the unit, subject to the lease's guest terms. No Nevada statute says whether a landlord's trespass warning can bar a tenant's invited guest from common areas, or lists defenses for invitees; that is a case-law question not reviewed here, so warn only people who have no tenant's invitation or who have broken property rules, and document why. Squatters in a vacant unit are handled under the unlawful-occupancy and forcible-detainer laws. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: No Truth-in-Renting Statement
bodyText: Nevada has no truth-in-renting law requiring landlords to distribute a state statement of tenants' rights. It polices lease content directly: using a written lease that does not conform to the lease-content statute is unlawful, and a provision that contravenes it is void (NRS 118A.200(9)); prohibited terms, such as a tenant's waiver of rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act, are void, and the tenant may recover actual damages caused by their inclusion (NRS 118A.220); and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease or term (NRS 118A.230).

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Nevada's statutes don't require you to rent parking separately from the dwelling or to offer a rent reduction to tenants who don't need a space, and don't forbid charging separately for parking. What matters is whether the parking charge is mandatory. If every tenant must pay for parking, that fee is a mandatory fee and must be inside the single total rent figure the lease states; you may not charge periodic rent above that figure (NRS 118A.200(6)-(7)). If parking is optional, a tenant who chooses it can pay a separate parking fee, and the lease should state it with its purpose (NRS 118A.200(3)(e)). Local zoning and parking ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: If a court finds as a matter of law that a lease or any of its terms was unconscionable when made, it may refuse to enforce the lease, enforce the rest without the unconscionable term, or limit the term to avoid an unconscionable result. When unconscionability is raised by a party or by the court on its own, both sides get a reasonable chance to present evidence of the setting, purpose and effect of the lease or settlement (NRS 118A.230). The statute gives no list or test, and case law was not reviewed. Terms the library treats as exposed include large fixed charges unrelated to actual cost (such as a steep early-termination fee), terms keeping a tenant liable for rent on an unusable unit, and terms waiving the duty to re-rent after abandonment. Separately, some terms are void outright whatever their fairness (NRS 118A.220, 118A.242(8)).

title: Interest on Money a Tenant Owes
bodyText: Money a tenant owes you under the lease earns interest even if the lease says nothing: when there is no written agreement fixing a different rate, interest runs from the time the money becomes due at the prime rate of Nevada's largest bank plus 2%, using the rate on the January 1 or July 1 before the transaction and adjusted every January 1 and July 1 (NRS 99.040(1)). A written agreement may set any other rate, and must state the rate and whether interest compounds (NRS 99.050(1)); a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term (NRS 118A.230). A judgment draws interest at the contract rate or, if none, at prime plus 2% (NRS 17.130(2)). Don't add interest to late rent. A charge for late payment of rent is a late charge: it must be stated in the lease, is capped at 5% of the periodic rent, and can't be increased because of an earlier late fee (NRS 118A.200(3)(g), 118A.210(4)); and no late fee or other charge may be added to rent lawfully withheld for a habitability or essential-services failure (NRS 118A.355(1)(d), 118A.380(1)(c)). Use an interest clause, if at all, for amounts other than rent, such as damage costs beyond the deposit. Case law and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: Leases Granted by Life Tenants and Co-Owners
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest Nevada law does not use, so the rule about what happens to a lease granted by a usufructuary does not arise here. The closest Nevada situations are a lease granted by someone holding only a life estate, and a lease of community property. Nevada's statutes say nothing about whether a lease granted by a life tenant survives the life tenant's death; that is left to general property law, not reviewed here, so if you lease from a life tenant, get the remainder owners to join or consent in writing, or limit the term. For community real property, neither spouse may sell, convey or encumber it unless both join in the signed and acknowledged instrument; whether a lease counts as an encumbrance is not settled by statute, so the cautious course is to have both spouses sign a lease of community property, especially a long one. Case law was not reviewed.

title: Utility Allowances and Overage Charges
bodyText: Nevada has no statute on utility allowances in private leases, but the single-rent-figure rule decides how one can work. Every mandatory periodic fee must be inside the one rent figure the lease states, and you may not charge more periodic rent than that figure. The only exception is a monthly fee equal to the cost of the electric, natural gas or water service provided in the tenant's unit, where the public utility cannot contract directly with the tenant or the unit is on a master-metered water system, flagged by an asterisk with the required statement on the same page. A term under which you pay a utility up to a monthly allowance and the tenant reimburses any excess creates a variable periodic charge outside the rent figure. Unless the charge is that qualifying unit-cost fee, it conflicts with the rule, and a nonconforming lease term is void. So the library does not offer its allowance-with-overage clause for Nevada. Workable choices: include the utility in the rent figure with no overage charge, or, where the exception applies, pass the whole unit bill through at cost using the asterisk statement in the library's rent clause. Any utility fee you bill must equal the actual cost, with no markup. Utility allowances in the federal Housing Choice Voucher program are set by the public housing agency under federal rules not reviewed here.

title: Splitting Shared Utility Bills
bodyText: Nevada has no statute that sets a formula (floor area, number of occupants or any other ratio) for splitting a shared utility bill among units, but the single-rent-figure rule limits what you can bill. Every mandatory periodic fee must be included in the one rent figure the lease states, and you may not charge more periodic rent than that figure. The only utility charge you may bill outside it is a monthly fee equal to the cost of the electric, natural gas or water service provided in the tenant's own unit, and only (1) where the public utility is unable to contract directly with the tenant for that service, or (2) for water, where the unit is on a master-metered water system. Either way the rent figure must carry an asterisk or other symbol at least half its font size, tied to the required statement on the same page. Because the fee must equal the cost of the service in the tenant's unit, a ratio estimate of a shared bill may not meet that test; the cautious course is to bill outside the rent figure only from a unit meter or submeter reading at your actual cost, with no markup or administrative charge, or else to build the utility into the rent figure. Sewer, trash and other services are not in the exception, so a mandatory periodic charge for them belongs inside the rent figure. A lease that does not conform is unlawful to use and the nonconforming term is void. Separate rules apply in manufactured-home parks, where a landlord without lot meters must prorate the cost equally among the tenants who use the service, never collecting more than the landlord's own cost. Commission rules also generally bar master-metering electricity in a new multiunit building where occupants control their own use and separate meters are cost-justified.

title: Utility Deposits
bodyText: Utility deposits are between the utility and its customer, so if the account is in the tenant's name the utility refunds the tenant and you have no refund duty. The commission's gas and electric rules cap a deposit at 150% of the customer's estimated average monthly bill for each service (half that for an elderly customer), excuse it for customers with satisfactory credit, a qualifying guarantor or retirement or Social Security income (unless they have had a shutoff or repeated late payments), let the utility apply it to amounts owed when service ends, and require the utility to return it after 12 consecutive months of timely payments. Every regulated public utility must pay interest on customer deposits at the six-month Treasury bill rate. Local-government utilities set their own deposit rules; a general improvement district may require a deposit of up to one year's charges from the user or the property owner. If you collect money from a tenant to secure utility charges you bill, treat it as part of the security deposit: any payment to be used to remedy a default in rent, repair damage or clean is a security deposit, counted toward the three-month cap and refunded with an itemized accounting, and a deposit held against unpaid utility charges risks being treated the same way. In manufactured-home parks, a park landlord must refund a tenant's utility deposit with interest through the next utility bill or by mail.

title: Utility Terms Belong in the Lease
bodyText: Nevada requires no separate utility disclosure form or attachment for a residential lease. Utility terms go in the lease itself: who pays which utility charges (NRS 118A.200(3)(j)), the services included with the rental (NRS 118A.200(3)(d)), and, for a utility billed outside the single rent figure, a statement on the same page as that figure, not on an attachment (NRS 118A.200(8)). With no written lease, the law presumes maintenance and waste removal are provided at no charge (NRS 118A.200(5)(b)). If you customarily pay a utility and bill the tenant separately, nonpayment of that bill is cause for ending the tenancy (NRS 118A.060(2)).

title: Getting Copies of a Tenant's Utility Shutoff Notices
bodyText: Only the account holder can arrange for you to receive copies of a utility's shutoff notices. Under the commission's gas and electric rules, a utility must, on a customer's written request, send a duplicate of any notice of intended shutoff to a third person the customer names, who may be any person or agency; that person does not have to pay the bill, and the utility is not liable if it fails to notify them. Utilities must tell elderly and disabled customers about this option when they apply. The water rules have no such designation. So if the tenant holds the account, you learn of a pending shutoff only if the tenant names you (the library's optional clause invites this, without making it a lease condition) or tells you. If you hold the account yourself, the notices come to you, and for a multiunit complex the utility also posts notices on each unit's door. A tenant's nonpayment of a utility the lease makes the tenant's responsibility is a lease breach handled by the usual notice process; it never lets you shut off or restore service yourself. Municipal and district utilities may have their own forms (not reviewed).

title: No Shutoffs of Submetered or Landlord-Billed Utilities
bodyText: Nevada gives a landlord of an ordinary rental no procedure to shut off electricity, gas or water that the landlord submeters or bills to the tenant. If the lease or the landlord-tenant act requires you to supply the service, willfully interrupting it, or causing or permitting it to be interrupted, is treated like a lockout: the tenant may get an expedited court order restoring it, end the lease, or use the essential-services remedies, and may recover actual damages and up to $2,500 fixed by the court. You also may not cut essential services in retaliation. Unpaid utility charges that you customarily pay and bill separately to the tenant are "cause" for ending the tenancy (NRS 118A.060(2)), so the remedy is an eviction notice and the court process, never a shutoff. The utility commission's shutoff rules bind public utilities, not apartment landlords. Manufactured-home parks are different: a park landlord who charges tenants for utility service may interrupt it for nonpayment only in a manner consistent with the utility's tariffs and the law, and a park landlord who resells water must follow the commission's water-termination rules (notice, extreme-heat and health postponements). A utility fee may be billed outside the rent figure only where the public utility cannot contract directly with the tenant, or for water in a master-metered system, with the required same-page asterisk statement, and the fee must equal the cost of the service in the tenant's unit (NRS 118A.200(8)); otherwise the charge must be inside the single all-in rent figure (NRS 118A.200(6)). Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Utilities in the Landlord's Name
bodyText: When a utility account is in your name and you distribute or resell the gas, water or electricity to residential tenants, state law requires the Public Utilities Commission to make the utility use its best efforts to post, in a conspicuous place, notice of its intent to shut off service because you did not pay, with enough information for tenants to contact the utility if a shutoff would threaten an occupant's health. The commission's rules go further for a multiunit residential complex: when a utility plans to shut off the complex, it must use its best efforts to post a notice on each unit's door, at the same time it notifies you, giving the reason, the deadline to pay or cure and the shutoff date; it must postpone a nonpayment shutoff during a forecasted period of extreme temperature (for water, extreme heat); and once you pay, it must restore every unit on a priority basis. A utility may not cut a new occupant's own service for a previous occupant's unpaid bill. On your side: if the lease makes you responsible for a utility and you willfully or negligently fail to supply it so the unit becomes unfit, the tenant may, after written notice and 48 hours (not counting weekends and holidays), buy the service and deduct the cost from rent, recover damages, withhold rent or move to comparable housing; a willful interruption adds the lockout remedies, including up to $2,500. We found no separate Nevada procedure letting tenants petition for a receiver because a landlord did not pay a utility. What to do: pay landlord-held utilities on time, and if you fall behind, expect the utility to notify your tenants directly.

title: Utility Shutoff Protections for Residential Customers
bodyText: Nevada's shutoff protections are Public Utilities Commission rules that bind regulated public utilities, and a utility may not shut off gas, water or electricity without following them. For residential gas and electric customers: written notice at least 10 days before a nonpayment shutoff (48 hours after a missed deferred-payment installment), followed by a second notice if there is no response; no shutoff on a weekend, a holiday or the day before one; no nonpayment shutoff for $50 or less ($100 or less for an advanced-meter electric customer); postponement during a forecasted period of extreme temperature, with thresholds set by service territory; postponement for 30 days, renewable once, when a physician, public health official or advanced practice registered nurse certifies that a shutoff would be especially dangerous to a resident's health and the customer certifies inability to pay; no shutoff where the utility knows a confined household member on life support is likely to die without it; and in-person or telephone notice at least 48 hours ahead for an elderly or disabled customer. Residential water customers have parallel rules, including postponement when 105°F or more is forecast. We found no winter-only extension or emergency moratorium in the statutes or the commission's rules. These protections belong to the account holder: if the tenant holds the account they protect the tenant, and they never let you shut off service yourself. City-, county- or district-owned utilities may follow their own rules (not reviewed).

title: Billing Tenants for Utilities
bodyText: Every mandatory periodic fee must be inside the lease's single rent figure, with one exception for utilities. You may charge a separate monthly fee equal to the cost of the electric, natural gas or water service provided in the tenant's own unit only if the public utility cannot contract directly with the tenant for that service, or, for water, the unit is on a master-metered water system. In either case the rent figure must carry an asterisk or other symbol at least half its font size, pointing to a statement on the same page that explains the arrangement, names each utility and its phone number where the utility cannot contract with the tenant, and says the fee equals the cost of the service, separate from the rent (NRS 118A.200(8)). The fee may not exceed that cost. Billing a share of a building-wide bill by a formula is not clearly the cost of service in the unit, so use a meter for each unit or build the charge into rent. The lease must also say who pays which utility charges (NRS 118A.200(3)(j)). A tenant can sue over a violation of the single-figure rule for damages, equitable relief, costs and attorney's fees, plus $250 for each violation involving deception (NRS 118A.405). Manufactured-home parks have separate utility rules.

title: Moving Utilities into the Tenant's Name
bodyText: Nevada's statutes do not set a deadline for a tenant to put utilities in the tenant's own name, and they give you no right to shut off a utility still in your name because the tenant has not transferred it. The lease decides who holds each account; it must state who pays which utility charges, and the library's "Utilities Paid by Tenant" clause has the tenant arrange and pay tenant-paid services directly. Ending service yourself is risky: willfully interrupting, or causing or permitting the interruption of, an essential service the lease or the landlord-tenant act requires you to supply exposes you to the lockout remedies, including up to $2,500, and running hot and cold water, heat and working electrical service are part of habitability. If you keep an account in your name after move-in and bill the tenant, the charge must fit the single-rent-figure rule (only a monthly fee equal to the cost of electric, gas or water service in the unit, where the utility cannot contract directly with the tenant or the water system is master-metered, may be billed outside the rent figure). A utility may not refuse or cut the tenant's own new service because of a previous occupant's unpaid bill. What to do: give a move-in transfer deadline in the lease, close your account only after the tenant's account is open, and treat a failure to transfer as a lease breach handled by written notice. Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Renting to Veterans
bodyText: Nevada's statutes give landlords no tax credit, fee waiver or other incentive for renting to veterans, and they neither require nor regulate a veterans' rent discount or preference in private housing. Veteran or military status is not among the classes protected by Nevada's fair-housing statute. State veterans' programs run through the Department of Veterans Services and state housing plans, not through landlord incentives. Federal protections for servicemembers who are active-duty tenants are covered separately in the library. What to do: you may offer a voluntary discount to veterans if you wish, but apply it consistently and make sure it does not work as a preference based on a protected class such as familial status or disability.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice
bodyText: Nevada has no statute saying whether accepting rent after a breach or after a notice waives the breach or the notice; that is a case-law question not reviewed here. Two statutes shape the practice. After you serve a pay-or-quit notice under the summary-eviction statute, you may not refuse rent the tenant submits because the tenant hasn't paid collection fees, attorney's fees or other non-rent costs, a reasonable late or dishonored-check charge, or a deposit (NRS 40.253(11)). And for a qualifying government worker or household member during a shutdown, a term requiring rent at a set time can't be enforced, and you must accept the rent for the shutdown period for up to 30 days after it ends (NRS 118A.310(2)). Cautious course: if you accept full payment of the rent a pay-or-quit notice demanded, treat that notice as satisfied; if you accept a partial payment, tell the tenant in writing at the time whether you are reserving the right to go forward, and serve a fresh notice for any balance. The library offers no Nevada rent-acceptance non-waiver clause, because its effect would rest on case law that was not reviewed.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Nevada's statutes and the state regulations reviewed set no maximum or minimum temperature for a rental's water heater and no duty to reset it before a new tenant moves in. Your duty is the habitability one: an approved water supply capable of producing hot and cold running water, furnished to the fixtures (NRS 118A.290(1)(c)), and hot water is an essential service, so a willful or negligent failure to supply it that makes the unit unfit triggers the tenant's 48-hour remedies (NRS 118A.380(1)). The state boiler and pressure-vessel law does not reach an ordinary household water heater that stays within its limits of 199,999 BTU per hour of heat input, 210 degrees and 120 gallons (NRS 455C.090). The only 120-degree figure found is energy-saving advice that utilities must give eligible customers, not a landlord duty (NAC 704.808). The fixed 110-degree hot-water limits in the health regulations apply to schools, not homes. The plumbing code the State Fire Marshal adopts and local building codes may regulate water heater installation (not reviewed).

title: Waterbeds: No State Rule
bodyText: Nevada's statutes say nothing about waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in a rental: there is no tenant right to have one, no ban, and no insurance or installation rule. The lease may prohibit or condition them, and a rule adopted later must meet the conditions for enforceable house rules (NRS 118A.320). The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises (NRS 118A.310(1)(f)), and you may claim from the security deposit what is reasonably necessary to repair damage beyond normal wear (NRS 118A.242(4)). Any extra deposit you take because of a waterbed is a security deposit and counts toward the 3-month cap on all deposits (NRS 118A.240(1), 118A.242(1)). Local building codes were not reviewed.

title: No Window Guard Requirement
bodyText: Nevada's statutes and the state regulations reviewed have no window-guard or window-fall-prevention requirement for rentals, and no window-guard notice to put in a lease. The only state window rule for landlords is part of habitability: the unit must not substantially lack effective waterproofing and weather protection of the roof and exterior walls, including windows and doors (NRS 118A.290(1)(a)). A 2025 bill that would have added doors and windows in good repair, and locks on windows that open, to the habitability list (AB 223) was vetoed and is not law. Building codes adopted locally, and the building and fire codes the State Fire Marshal adopts, may set window and opening requirements for construction (not reviewed). Local ordinances may add rules (not reviewed).

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Nevada requires writing for most notices that change or end a tenancy. From you to the tenant: a pay-or-quit notice for unpaid rent (NRS 40.2512, 40.253(1)); a notice to perform a lease covenant or surrender (NRS 40.2516); a summary-eviction notice to surrender for a breach, no-cause or holdover case (NRS 40.254(1)); a notice specifying a breach under the landlord-tenant act (NRS 118A.430(1)); a 14-day notice before you do remedial work and bill it (NRS 118A.440); a rent increase, at least 60 days ahead (30 for a periodic tenancy shorter than a month) (NRS 118A.300); a new rule that materially changes the bargain, unless the tenant consents in writing, 30 days ahead (NRS 118A.320(2)); the managers, agent for service and owner disclosure (NRS 118A.260(1)); a foreclosure disclosure to a prospective tenant (NRS 118A.275); notice of a transferred deposit when your interest ends (NRS 118A.244(1)); and notice before disposing of property left behind (NRS 118A.460(1)(b)). The no-cause termination notice is a notice served by delivering or posting a copy (NRS 40.251, 40.280), so it too is in practice a written document. From the tenant to you: notice of your breach or a habitability failure (NRS 118A.350, 118A.355), notice of an essential-service failure (NRS 118A.380), termination for failure to deliver possession (NRS 118A.370), early termination for age, disability or a co-tenant's death (NRS 118A.340), termination for domestic violence or related crimes (NRS 118A.345), and a request for a 30-day extension under a no-cause notice (NRS 40.251(2)). A notice of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of a primary residence can't be given electronically, even if the tenant agreed to electronic notices (NRS 719.250(4)(b)). The statute sets no writing requirement for your 24-hour notice of entry (NRS 118A.330(3)) or for consenting to a holdover (NRS 118A.470), but written notice is the safer practice.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Nevada follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (NRS 104.3311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (NRS 104.1308(2)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Nevada's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (NRS ch. 118A searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Nevada's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
